quote: And Trypho said, "I believe, however, that many of those who say that they confess Jesus, and are called Christians, eat meats offered to idols, and declare that they are by no means injured in consequence." And I replied, "The fact that there are such men confessing themselves to be Christians, and admitting the crucified Jesus to be both Lord and Christ, yet not teaching His doctrines, but those of the spirits of error, causes us who are disciples of the true and pure doctrine of Jesus Christ, to be more faithful and stedfast in the hope announced by Him. For what things He predicted would take place in His name, these we do see being actually accomplished in our sight. For he said, 'Many shall come in My name, clothed outwardly in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.'" And, 'There shall be schisms and heresies.' And, 'Beware of false prophets, who shall come to you clothed outwardly in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.' And, 'Many false Christs and false apostles shall arise, and shall deceive many of the faithful.' There are, therefore, and there were many, my friends, who, coming forward in the name of Jesus, taught both to speak and act impious and blasphemous things; and these are called by us after the name of the men from whom each doctrine and opinion had its origin.

author: Justin Martyr
quote: And that God the Father of all would bring Christ to heaven after He had raised Him from the dead, and would keep Him there until He has subdued His enemies the devils, and until the number of those who are foreknown by Him as good and virtuous is complete, on whose account He has still delayed the consummation-hear what was said by the prophet David. These are his words: "The Lord said unto My Lord, Sit Thou at My right hand, until I make Thine enemies Thy footstool. The Lord shall send to Thee the rod of power out of Jerusalem; and rule Thou in the midst of Thine enemies. With Thee is the government in the day of Thy power, in the beauties of Thy saints: from the womb of morning have I begotten Thee." That which he says, "He shall send to Thee the rod of power out of Jerusalem," is predictive of the mighty word, which His apostles, going forth from Jerusalem, preached everywhere; and though death is decreed against those who teach or at all confess the name of Christ, we everywhere both embrace and teach it. And if you also read these words in a hostile spirit, ye can do no more, as I said before, than kill us; which indeed does no harm to us, but to you and all who unjustly hate us, and do not repent, brings eternal punishment by fire.

author: Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius
quote: Wherefore, if they were not wise who were so called, nor those of later times, who did not hesitate to confess their want of wisdom, what remains but that wisdom is to be sought elsewhere, since it has not been found where it was sought. But what can we suppose to have been the reason why it was not found, though sought with the greatest earnestness and labour by so many intellects, and during so many ages, unless it be that philosophers sought for it out of their own limits? And since they traversed and explored all parts, but nowhere found any wisdom, and it must of necessity be somewhere, it is evident that it ought especially to be sought there where the title of folly appears; under the covering of which God hides the treasury of wisdom and truth, lest the secret of His divine work should be exposed to view.

author: Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius
quote: Since, therefore, human wisdom has no existence (Socrates says in the writings of Plato), let us follow that which is divine, and let us give thanks to God, who has revealed and delivered it to us; and let us congratulate ourselves, that through the divine bounty we possess the truth and wisdom, which, though sought by so many intellects through so many ages, philosophy

author: Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius
quote: But this consideration may perhaps have influenced them, that if there were any true religion, it would exert itself and assert its authority, and not permit the existence of anything opposed to it. For they were unable to see at all, on what account, or by whom, and in what manner true religion was depressed, which partakes of a divine mystery and a heavenly secret. And no man can know this by any means, unless he is taught.

author: Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius
quote: For, having left God, the parent and founder of all things, men began to worship the senseless works of their own hands. And what were the effects of this corruption, or what evils it introduced, the subject itself sufficiently declares. For, turning away from the chief good, which is blessed and everlasting on this account, because it cannot be seen, or touched, or comprehended, and from the virtues which are in agreement with that good, and which are equally immortal, gliding down to these corrupt and frail gods, and devoting themselves to those things by which the body only is adorned, and nourished, and delighted, they sought eternal death for themselves, together with their gods and goods relating to the body, because all bodies are subject to death.

author: Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius
quote: But let us suppose it possible that any one, by natural and innate goodness, should gain true virtues, such a man as we have heard that Cimon was at Athens, who both gave alms to the needy, and entertained the poor, and clothed the naked; yet, when that one thing which is of the greatest importance is wanting-the acknowledgment of God-then all those good things are superfluous and empty, so that in pursuing them he has laboured in vain. For all his justice will resemble a human body which has no head, in which, although all the limbs are in their proper position, and figure, and proportion, yet, since that is wanting which is the chief thing of all, it is destitute both of life and of all sensation.

author: Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius
quote: These things are near to the truth. For the soul, when separated from the body, is, as the same poet says, "No vision of the drowsy night, No airy current half so light," because it is a spirit, and by its very slightness incapable of being perceived, but only by us who are corporeal but capable of being perceived by God, since it belongs to Him to be able to do all things.

author: Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius
quote: But that he may obtain the favour of God, and be free from every stain, let him always implore the mercy of God, and pray for nothing else but pardon for his sins, even though he has none.

author: Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius
quote: There would be no adulteries, and debaucheries, and prostitution of women, if it were known to all, that whatever is sought beyond the desire of procreation is condemned by God. Nor would necessity compel a woman to dishonour her modesty, to seek for herself a most disgraceful mode of sustenance; since the males also would restrain their lust, and the pious and religious contributions of the rich would succour the destitute.

author: Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius
quote: What, then, is it? Truly religion is the cultivation of the truth, but superstition of that which is false. And it makes the entire difference what you worship, not how you worship, or what prayer you offer. But because the worshippers of the gods imagine themselves to be religious, though they are superstitious, they are neither able to distinguish religion from superstition, nor to express the meaning of the names.

author: Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius
quote: Before all things, it is befitting that we should know both that He Himself and His ambassadors foretold that there must be numerous sects and heresies, which would break the unity of the sacred body; and that they admonished us to be on our guard with the greatest prudence, lest we should at any time fall into the snares and deceits of that adversary of ours, with whom God has willed that we should contend.

author: Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius
quote: For if our souls are mortal, if virtue is about to have no existence after the dissolution of the body, why do we avoid the goods assigned to us, as though we were ungrateful or unworthy of enjoying the divine gifts? For, that we may enjoy these blessings, we must live in wickedness and impiety, because virtue, that is, justice, is followed by poverty. Therefore he is not of sound mind, who, without having any greater hope set before him, prefers labours, and tortures, and miseries, to those goods which others enjoy in life. But if virtue is to be taken up, as is most rightly said by these, because it is evident that man is born to it, it ought to contain some greater hope, which may apply a great and illustrious solace for the ills and labours which it is the part of virtue to endure.

author: Macarius of Egypt
quote:
We Are Not Irremediably In Error 

"It is not true, as some maintain who are led astray by error, that the human being is irremediably dead and can no longer do anything good. A small child is incapable of anything; it cannot run to its mother on its own legs; it tumbles on the ground, cries out, sobs, calls out to her. And she is gentle with it, she is touched to see her baby seeking her so impatiently with so many sobs. It cannot reach her but cries out to her tirelessly, and she goes to it overcome with love, she kisses it, presses it to her heart and feeds it, with unspeakable tenderness. God loves us and he behaves like her towards the soul that seeks him and cries out to him. In the eagerness of that infinite love that is his… He takes hold of our spirit, unites Himself to it, and we become 'one spirit with Him', as the apostle says (I Corinthians 6.17). The soul is linked with the Lord, and the Lord, full of compassion and love, unites Himself to it and it dwells in his grace. Then the soul and the Lord are one spiritually, they form one life, one heart." - "Homily 46"

author: Macrina the Younger
quote: Love is first among all the activities connected with virtue and all the commandments of the law. If, therefore, the soul ever attains this love, it will need none of the others, having reached the fullness of its being. It seems that love alone preserves in itself the character of the divine blessedness. And knowledge becomes love because what is known is by nature beautiful.
source_title: [THE TEACHING OF MACRINA] ON THE SOUL AND THE RESURRECTION

author: Macrina the Younger
quote: The seed does not germinate unless it is dissolved in the earth, rarefied and made for us, so that it is mixed with the moisture nearby and dust changes into root and sprout, and it does not stop there but changes into a stalk with sections in between which are surrounded by chains, as it were, so as to be able to hold the grain in an upright position.… Thus the apostle says that the mystery of the resurrection is presignified before us in the miracles performed in the seeds. The divine power in its surpassing excellence not only gives back to see but adds many great and more wonderful features with which nature is magnificently adorned.
source_title: [THE TEACHING OF MACRINA] ON THE SOUL AND THE RESURRECTION

author: Macrina the Younger
quote: At her death Macrina prayed: "O Lord, you have freed us from the fear of death. You have made the end of life here the beginning of a true life for us. You give rest to our bodies in sleep, and you awaken us again with the last trumpet. The dust from which you fashioned us with your hands you give back to the dust of the earth for safe keeping, and you who have relinquished it will recall it after reshaping with incorruptibility and grace our mortal and graceless substance." … As she said this, she made the sign of the cross upon her eyes and mouth and heart, and little by little, as the fever dried up her tongue, she was no longer able to speak clearly. Her voice gave out and only from the trembling of her lips and motion of her hands did we know that she was continuing to pray. Then the evening came on and the lamp was brought in.… When she had completed the thanksgiving and indicated that the prayer was over by making the sign of the cross, she breathed a deep breath and with the prayer her life came to an end.

author: Marcus Minucius Felix
quote: See, therefore, how for our consolation all nature suggests a future resurrection. The sun sinks down and arises, the stars pass away and return, the flowers die and revive again, after their win-try decay the shrubs resume their leaves, seeds do not flourish again. unless they are rotted: thus the body in the sepulchre is like the trees which in winter hide their verdure with a deceptive dryness. Why are you in haste for it to revive and return, while the winter is still raw? We must wait also for the spring-time of the body.

author: Martyrdom Of Polycarp
quote: And, looking to the grace of Christ, they despised all the torments of this world, redeeming themselves from eternal punishment by [the suffering of] a single hour. For this reason the fire of their savage executioners appeared cool to them. For they kept before their view escape from that fire which is eternal and never shall be quenched, and looked forward with the eyes of their heart to those good things which are laid up for such as endure; things "which ear hath not heard, nor eye seen, neither have entered into the heart of man," but were revealed by the Lord to them, inasmuch as they were no longer men, but had already become angels.

author: Maximus of Turin
quote: What took place, as the apostle says, was the mystery of baptism. Clearly this was a kind of baptism, where the cloud covered the people and water carried them. But the same Christ the Lord who did all these things now goes through baptism before the Christian people in the pillar of his body—he who at that time went through the sea before the children of Israel in the pillar of fire.… Through this faith—as was the case with the children of Israel—the one who walks calmly will not fear Egypt in pursuit.

author: Maximus of Turin
quote: He wishes, then, for all our actions to be accomplished with Christ as companion and witness, that we may do good things for him as the author and avoid what is evil for the sake of his fellowship. One who knows that Christ is his companion is ashamed to do evil. In good things, however, Christ is our helper, and in the face of evil things he is our defender.

author: Maximus of Turin
quote: In Christ's resurrection, all his members have necessarily risen with him. For while he passes from the depths to the heights, he has made us pass from death to life.

author: Maximus of Turin
quote: Therefore Christ is not to be hoped in for this life only, in which the bad can do more than the good, in which those who are more evil are happier, and those who lead a more criminal life live more prosperously.

author: Maximus of Turin
quote: Adam is formed from mire by the hands of God. Christ is formed in the womb by the Spirit of God.

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: Blessed is He that cometh in the name of the Lord: the King against the tyrant; not with omnipotent power and wisdom, but with that which is accounted the foolishness

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: The apostle certainly, after assigning the planting and watering to art and earth and water, conceded the growth to God alone, where he says, "Neither is he that planteth anything, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase."
source_title: Methodius From the Discourse on the Resurrection

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: Now we should consider the case of the renowned Paul, that when he was not yet perfect in Christ, he was first born and suckled, Ananias preaching to him, and renewing him in baptism, as the history in the Acts relates. But when he was grown to a man, and was built up, then being moulded to spiritual perfection, he was made the help-meet and bride of the Word; and receiving and conceiving the seeds of life, he who was before a child, becomes a church and a mother, himself labouring in birth of those who, through him, believed in the Lord, until Christ was formed and born in them also. For he says, "My little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you;" and again, "In Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the Gospel."

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote:
Desiring with all his might that believers in Christ should be chaste, endeavours by many arguments to show them the dignity of chastity, as when he says.
Come, now, and let us examine more carefully the very words which are before us, and observe that the apostle did not grant these things unconditionally to all, but first laid down the reason on account of which he was led to this. For, having set forth that "it is good for a man not to touch a woman"

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote:
He added immediately, "Nevertheless, to avoid fornication, let every man have his own wife".
and come together again, that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency. But I speak this by permission, and not of commandment."

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: I have now brought to an end what I have to say respecting continence and marriage and chastity, and intercourse with men, and in which of these there is help towards progress in righteousness; but it still remains to speak concerning virginity-if, indeed, anything be prescribed on this subject. Let us then treat this subject also; for it stands thus:

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote:
For this is acceptable to God, he does not wish these things to be said as by authority, and as the mind of the Lord, with reference to the giving of a virgin in marriage; for after he had said.
So, immediately after he had said, "if a virgin marry, she hath not sinned "he added, "such shall have trouble in the flesh: but I spare you."

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote:
But yet if it shall please you who find chastity hard to bear, rather to turn to marriage; I consider it to be profitable for you to restrain yourselves in the gratification of the flesh, not making your marriage an occasion for abusing your own vessels to uncleanness. "Then he adds.
But those who are goaded on by their lusts, although they do not commit fornication, yet who, even in the things which are permitted with a lawful wife, through the heat of unsubdued concupiscence are excessive in embraces, how shall they celebrate the feast? how shall they rejoice, who have not adorned their tabernacle, that is their flesh, with the boughs of the Agnos, nor have listened to that which has been said; that "they that have wives be as though they had none? "

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: But if our opponents say, How then is it, if the universe be not destroyed, that the Lord says that "heaven and earth shall pass away;" and the prophet, that "the heaven shall perish as smoke, and the earth shall grow old as a garment;" we answer, because it is usual for the Scriptures to call the change of the world from its present condition to a better and more glorious one, destruction; as its earlier form is lost in the change of all things to a state of greater splendour; for there is no contradiction nor absurdity in the Holy Scriptures. For not "the world" but the "fashion of this world" passeth away, it is said; so it is usual for the Scriptures to call the change from an earlier form to a better and more comely state, destruction; just as when one calls by the name of destruction the change from a childish form into a perfect man, as the stature of the child is turned into manly size and beauty. We may expect that the creation will pass away, as if it were to perish in the burning, in order that it may be renewed, not however that it will be destroyed, that we who are renewed may dwell in a renewed world without taste of sorrow.
source_title: From the Discourse on the Resurrection

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: Then he adds, "But this I say, brethren, the time is short: it remaineth, that both they that have wives be as though they had none." And again, going on and challenging them to the same things, he confirmed his statement, powerfully supporting the state of virginity, and adding expressly the following words to those which he had spoken before, he exclaimed, "I would have you without carefulness. He that is unmarried careth for the things that belong to the Lord: but he that is married careth for the things that are of the world, how he may please his wife. There is a difference also between a wife and a virgin. The unmarried woman careth for the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and in spirit: but she that is married careth for the things of the world, how she may please her husband." Now it is clear to all, without any doubt, that to care for the things of the Lord and to please God, is much better than to care for the things of the world and to please one's wife.

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: For then am I plainly consecrated altogether to the Lord, when I not only strive to keep the flesh untouched by intercourse, but also unspotted by other kinds of unseemliness. For "the unmarried woman "it is said,

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: Now it is clear to all, without any doubt, that to care for the things of the Lord and to please God, is much better than to care for the things of the world and to please one's wife. For who is there so foolish and blind, as not to perceive in this statement the higher praise which Paul accords to chastity? "And this," he says, "I speak for your own profit, not that I may cast a snare upon you, but for that which is comely."

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: Wherefore he rejects those of the more incontinent, who, under the influence of vain-glory, would advance to this state, advising them to marry, lest in their time of manly strength, the flesh stirring up the desires and passions, they should be goaded on to defile the soul. For let us consider what he lays down:

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: But for him who of his own free will and purpose decides to preserve his flesh in virgin purity, "having no necessity"

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: For when one thoroughly examines and understands those things which happen to man according to his nature, he will know not to despise the procreation of children, although he applauds chastity, and prefers it in honour. For although honey be sweeter and more pleasant than other things, we are not for that reason to consider other things bitter which are mixed up in the natural sweetness of fruits. And, in support of these statements, I will bring forward a trustworthy witness, namely, Paul, who says, "So then he that giveth her in marriage doeth well; but he that giveth her not in marriage doeth better." Now the word, in setting forth that which is better and sweeter, did not intend to take away the inferior, but arranges so as to assign to each its own proper use and advantage. For there are some to whom it is not given to attain virginity; and there are others whom He no longer wills to be excited by procreations to lust, and to be defiled, but henceforth to meditate and to keep the mind upon the transformation of the body to the likeness of angels, when they "neither marry nor are given in marriage," according to the infallible words of the Lord; since it is not given to all to attain that undefiled state of being a eunuch for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, but manifestly to those only who are able to preserve the ever-blooming and unfading flower of virginity.

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: But if any one should venture to oppose this statement, and reply, that the apostle teaches that we hate not only the evil which is in thought, but that we do that which we will not, and we hate it even in the very act of doing it, for he says, "The good which I would, I do not; but the evil which I would not, that I do;" if he who says so speaks the truth, let us ask him to explain what was the evil which the apostle hated and willed not to do, but did; and the good which he willed to do, but did not; and conversely, whether as often as he willed to do good, so often he did not do the good which he willed, but did the evil which he willed not? And how he can say, when exhorting us to shake off all manner of sin, "Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ?" Thus he meant the things already mentioned which he willed not to do, not to be done, but only to be thought of. For how otherwise could he be an exact imitation of Christ?
source_title: Methodius From the Discourse on the Resurrection

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: And he asks what will be the appearance of the risen body, when this human form, as according to him useless, shall wholly disappear; since it is the most lovely of all things which are combined in living creatures, as being the form which the Deity Himself employs, as the most wise Paul explains: "For a man indeed ought not to cover his head, forasmuch as he is the image and glory of God; "
source_title: Methodius From the Discourse on the Resurrection

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: For "though I sell all my goods and give to the poor, and though I yield up my body to the fire, and though I have so great faith that I can remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing."

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: Whence we, having received Christ, saying, "I am the truth," know that shadows and figures have ceased; and we hasten on to the truth, proclaiming its glorious images. For now we know "in part," and as it were "through a glass," since that which is perfect has not yet come to us; namely, the kingdom of heaven and the resurrection, when "that which is in part shall be done away." For then will all our tabernacles be firmly set up, when again the body shall rise, with bones again joined and compacted with flesh. Then shall we celebrate truly to the Lord a glad festal-day, when we shall receive eternal tabernacles, no more to perish or be dissolved into the dust of the tomb.

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: For the law is indeed the figure and the shadow of an image, that is, of the Gospel; but the image, namely, the Gospel, is the representative of truth itself. For the men of olden time and the law foretold to us the characteristics of the Church, and the Church represents those of the new dispensation which is to come. Whence we, having received Christ, saying, "I am the truth," know that shadows and figures have ceased; and we hasten on to the truth, proclaiming its glorious images. For now we know "in part," and as it were "through a glass," since that which is perfect has not yet come to us; namely, the kingdom of heaven and the resurrection, when "that which is in part shall be done away."

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote:
Adam, should "all be made alive.".
he was changed into the nature of the latter, himself being neither the tree of life nor that of corruption; but having been shown forth as mortal, from his participation in and presence with corruption, and, again, as incorrupt and immortal by connection with and participation in life; as Paul also taught, saying, "Corruption shall not inherit in corruption, nor death life".
But if any one were to think that the earthy image is the flesh itself, but the heavenly image some other spiritual body besides the flesh; let him first consider that Christ, the heavenly man, when He appeared, bore the same form of limbs and the same image of flesh as ours, through which also He, who was not man, became man, that "as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive."

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: Let no one suppose that all the remaining company of those who have believed are condemned, thinking that we who are virgins alone shall be led on to attain the promises, not understanding that there shall be tribes and families and orders, according to the analogy of the faith of each. And this Paul, too, sets forth, saying,

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: Therefore, since the flesh is the boundary between corruption and incorruption, not being either corruption or incorruption, it was vanquished by corruption on account of pleasure, although it was the work and the possession of incorruption. Therefore it became subject to corruption. When, then, it had been overcome by corruption, and was given over to death for chastisement, He did not leave it to be vanquished and given over as an inheritance to corruption; but again conquering death by the resurrection, He restored it to incorruption, that corruption might not inherit incorruption, but incorruption that which is corruptible. And therefore the apostle answers, "This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal immortality." But the corruptible and mortal putting on incorruption and immortality, what else is this, but that which is sown in corruption rising in incorruption? For, "as we have borne the image of the earthly, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly."
source_title: Methodius From the Discourse on the Resurrection

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote:
-for the soul is not corruptible or mortal; but this which is mortal and corrupting is of flesh,-in order that, "as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly? ".
For, "as we have borne the image of the earthly, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly."
source_title: Methodius From the Discourse on the Resurrection

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote:
For He truly was made man, and died, and not in mere appearance, but that He might truly be shown to be the first begotten from the dead, changing the earthy into the heavenly, and the mortal into the immortal. When, then, Paul says that "flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God".
"Now this I say, brethren, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God; neither doth corruption inherit in corruption.".
a man not far removed either from the times or from the virtues of the apostles, says that that which is mortal is inherited, but that life inherits; and that flesh dies, but that the kingdom of heaven lives. When then, Paul says that "flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of heaven"
source_title: Methodius From the Discourse on the Resurrection

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote:
Therefore the apostle answers thus, "For this corruptible must put on in corruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.".
And therefore the apostle answers, "This corruptible must put on in corruption, and this mortal immortality."
source_title: Methodius From the Discourse on the Resurrection

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: For if the kingdom of God, which is life, were possessed by the body, it would happen that the life would be consumed by corruption. But now the life possesses what is dying, in order that "death may be swallowed up in victory"
source_title: Methodius From the Discourse on the Resurrection

author: Oecumenius
quote: This applies to Herod and Pilate. It does not apply in the same way to the high priests and scribes, because they knew that Jesus was the Christ. They were more like the workers in the vineyard who said: "This is the heir. Let us kill him, and the vineyard will be ours.".
source_title: PAULINE COMMENTARY FROM THE GREEK CHURCH

author: Oecumenius
quote: I think that by "spirit of the world" Paul means human wisdom and learning.
source_title: PAULINE COMMENTARY FROM THE GREEK CHURCH

author: Oecumenius
quote: The "mind of Christ" refers to the Father. Paul is saying that we have the Father of Christ in us.
source_title: PAULINE COMMENTARY FROM THE GREEK CHURCH

author: Oecumenius
quote: Paul did not write this because of Christ's resurrection, which had already taken place, but because of ours, so that we might believe and silence our opponents.
source_title: PAULINE COMMENTARY FROM THE GREEK CHURCH

author: Oecumenius
quote: Other sins like anger and greed come from the soul, but fornication has its roots in the flesh. Paul makes special mention of it here because it was the problem which he had to deal with at the time. Fornication is not self-evidently the worst sin of all.
source_title: PAULINE COMMENTARY FROM THE GREEK CHURCH

author: Oecumenius
quote: A man guilty of fornication and the impurity which comes from it insults his marriage and his wife. He sins against his own body and consequently against his wife, because the two are one flesh.
source_title: PAULINE COMMENTARY FROM THE GREEK CHURCH

author: Oecumenius
quote: Paul wants to show that slave and master are equal. We are all freedmen of Christ because he has set us free from the tyranny of Satan, and we are voluntary slaves of Christ because, having set us free, he led us into his own kingdom.
source_title: PAULINE COMMENTARY FROM THE GREEK CHURCH

author: Oecumenius
quote: Paul is coming here to a higher wisdom, but he is hesitant to impose it directly because that might show up the inadequacy of his hearers. Therefore he sets it out as an opinion rather than as a command.
source_title: PAULINE COMMENTARY FROM THE GREEK CHURCH

author: Oecumenius
quote: To be concerned about the things of the Lord is not anxiety but salvation. Paul has just told them that he wants them to be free of anxiety.
source_title: PAULINE COMMENTARY FROM THE GREEK CHURCH

author: Oecumenius
quote: It is clear from this that someone who has been overcome by apparent impropriety, even if married, is not yet firmly established in the work of the Lord.
source_title: PAULINE COMMENTARY FROM THE GREEK CHURCH

author: Oecumenius
quote: The question is not merely whether you are eating with a clear conscience. It is whether what you are doing is of benefit to your brother.
source_title: PAULINE COMMENTARY FROM THE GREEK CHURCH

author: Oecumenius
quote: By "received" Paul means that he was taught.
source_title: PAULINE COMMENTARY FROM THE GREEK CHURCH

author: Oecumenius
quote: If the gift is subject to the prophets, how can it not also be subject to you, so that you may keep quiet when you are meant to?
source_title: PAULINE COMMENTARY FROM THE GREEK CHURCH

author: Oecumenius
quote: Note that he does not say "to the eleven," and neither does John (Jn 20:24), who writes that Thomas was "one of the twelve." We should probably say that either he has included Matthias with the other apostles by anticipation or else that he is still thinking of Judas, even after his betrayal and hanging.
source_title: PAULINE COMMENTARY FROM THE GREEK CHURCH

author: Oecumenius
quote: The principalities and powers will be abolished and will be left powerless.
source_title: PAULINE COMMENTARY FROM THE GREEK CHURCH

author: Oecumenius
quote: Paul is writing to converted Greeks, because the Greeks worshiped Zeus, who revolted against his own father in order to seize his kingdom. He was concerned lest they should imagine something similar in the case of Christ and his Father.
source_title: PAULINE COMMENTARY FROM THE GREEK CHURCH

author: Oecumenius
quote: The things of the Son belong to God as Father, and everything which the Son can do is attributed to the Father, for he who begot him outside time is the source of the Son's power.
source_title: PAULINE COMMENTARY FROM THE GREEK CHURCH

author: Oecumenius
quote: Christ had a spiritual body, because he had received the full presence of the Holy Spirit when the dove rested on him. So the Lord had the power of the Paraclete in his humanity in a way distinguishable from his divinity, since he was himself the Spirit.
source_title: PAULINE COMMENTARY FROM THE GREEK CHURCH

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: If all were the church, what further need was there to add "with all who call upon"? If all alike were calling upon, what need was there to write not merely to all who call upon, but, beyond them, "to the church of God"? We have shown that only the praiseworthy are the ones who ought to be designated a church, whereas the blameworthy — not indeed apostates, but still wrestling with sin and yet still calling upon him — are not yet also a church. Let us hasten, therefore, from calling upon to ascend to the church that is spotless "and without blemish".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For just as not only fornication but also second marriages exclude a man from ecclesiastical dignities — for neither a bishop nor a presbyter nor a deacon nor a widow can be twice-married — so perhaps the twice-married man will also be cast out from the assembly of the "firstborn and undefiled", the "Church, which has no spot or wrinkle"; not that he is sent into the eternal fire, but that he has no part in the kingdom of God. I recall that, when I was interpreting that which is written to the Corinthians: "to the church of God which is at Corinth, with all who call upon him", I said that there is a distinction between the "church" and those "who call upon" the name of the Lord. For I think that the man of one marriage and the virgin and he who perseveres in chastity belong to the church of God, but that he who is twice-married, although he may have had a good manner of life and abound in the other virtues, nevertheless does not belong to the "church" and to that number which "has no wrinkle or spot, or any such thing", but belongs to a second rank and to those "who call upon" the name of the Lord, and who are indeed saved in the name of Jesus Christ, yet are by no means crowned by him: to whom be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 17

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Neither do these things suit sinners nor those things the righteous — I mean the words Now I exhort you, brethren, through the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same things and that there be no divisions among you and all such things. The church, then, was a mixed body, if indeed one ought to call "church" this whole thing compounded of the righteous and the unrighteous. At any rate, those who were gathered together were mixed; and for this reason the Apostle, being about to reprove for their sins those who were gathering together with wickedness, necessarily first makes his praises of those who well "come together unto the same place". I give thanks to my God always: it is fitting to give thanks for those things which he calls praiseworthy, and not to give thanks at one time and not at another, but to give thanks always. If I ever see someone at one time doing well and at another time sinning, I give thanks concerning him not always, but when he does well; and so also concerning myself. And in what will Paul, who gives thanks, give thanks? For his own hearers, of whom he has become father according to God. Just as, then, a father gives thanks over his sons whenever they are in health, whenever they do well, in the same manner whenever a teacher sees his hearers "fervent in spirit", rich in the word "of wisdom", worthy to be praised, he gives thanks always concerning them.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Let us behold, then, the grace of the praiseworthy ones in Corinth, that we may be zealous for it. That in everything you were enriched in him. Blessed are those who are rich in everything and come short in nothing of the things that are according to God, but who practice every virtue and enjoy the gifts from him ungrudgingly and richly, in all speech and all knowledge: so that they are at a loss for no scripture, but everywhere "seek and find", and, when it is necessary to expound a scripture, employ every kind of discourse — both the so-called discursive kind and that which proceeds by question and answer — and are prepared to speak also against every heresy, and to stand firm in the doctrine of the truth, and to fulfil what was said by the Apostle: "always ready for a defense to everyone who demands of you an account concerning the faith that is in you". So indeed also the phrase in all knowledge: not only according to the scriptures, but so that one may also say "for he himself gave me the unerring knowledge of the things that are" and what follows upon these things. For knowledge indicates only the knowing, but speech also interprets that which is known.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: even as the testimony of Christ was confirmed among you: Christ, that I may so name him, is the chief martyr, and, there being many martyrs unto Christ through their death, he is that ruler of the martyrs. This testimony of Christ, then, in some is firm, but in some it is not firm but is shaken. For if the faith concerning the testimony is such that one is able from a true disposition to say "I am persuaded" that "neither death nor life" and what follows "shall be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord", the testimony is firm in such a one; but if we are not such but are shaken by the things that befall us, the testimony of Christ has not yet been confirmed in us. And again we shall take the saying in another way: every scripture that testifies concerning Christ is a testimony of Christ; it is good, therefore, to be confirmed also in the testimony of Christ that comes from the scriptures. And in yet another way: behold the testimony of Christ, it being "borne joint witness to" "by signs and wonders and manifold powers and distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his own will"; and the testimony of Christ is firm in the saints.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: so that you come short in no spiritual gift: seeing that the spiritual gifts are many, he treats of them also in what follows in the epistle. awaiting the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ: the righteous man does not have his hopes in this age, but, suffering, being in danger, he awaits the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ — that is, the one which Christ Jesus reveals.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Who will also confirm you unto the end: who confirms? Christ Jesus, the Word, the Wisdom; and the testimony that is confirmed is not for days, but unto the end. blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ: until we come thither, we do not yet have blamelessness; for we do not know what the morrow will bring forth, even if someone seems to have blamelessness at the present time — in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Believe in him always; for you were called that we might simply be under Jesus. Great is what God bestows upon the saints: we were called into the fellowship of his Son; wherefore we are "heirs indeed of God, but joint-heirs with Christ".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He who in all things agrees with right reason and with the ecclesiastical teaching concerning both the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and further concerning the dispensation that touches us, and concerning "resurrection" and judgment, and who moreover follows the ecclesiastical canons, is not in a division.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: To preach the gospel is a greater thing than to baptize; and since Paul knew that certain men had been set apart for baptizing, he gives thanks that he has the better portion, above baptizing. In the Acts of the Apostles it appears which are the works of the apostles: for instance, Philip used to baptize, but Philip did not minister the Spirit to the one being baptized; rather Peter laid hands on those baptized by him, and the Spirit came upon them. And Philip baptized with water those "who were being regenerated out of water and" the Holy "Spirit", but Peter with the Spirit.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: There is need not so much of word as of power; wherefore it is written, "The Lord will give a word to those who preach the gospel with great power, the king of the powers of the beloved". So Christ sent me not to baptize but to preach the gospel, not in wisdom of word — not in polished diction; for if I do this and wish to deliver the word in that way, the power of Christ does not reach the soul of the hearers, and I empty out and pull down the grace of the power.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The name of Christ seems to be a stumbling-block; but if anyone lends his ears to the word of God and to his grace, he will see that "this too is a great mystery". Even the pagans have handed down that often, when great plagues occurred, or torrential rains, or droughts, these came to an end when a man gave himself up on behalf of the common good. What wonder, then, if, when the whole world was plague-stricken with error, it was necessary, for the sake of the true plague, that "one should die" in order to dissolve the plague of ignorance and of darkness and of destruction? And who was able to undertake this? Not a prophet, not an apostle, nor any other righteous man; but there had to come down from heaven a divine power able to undertake to die on behalf of "all" with a certain public display, so that through that death a trophy might be raised against the devil. For indeed those in the world who celebrate a triumph over their enemies are accustomed to set up their trophies against the vanquished in the form of a cross. The cross of Christ, therefore, is a trophy against Satan; for this reason I say, "But far be it from me to boast except in the cross"—I who have come to know what the power of the cross is; because I have been set free from evils through him who died in order to rescue me from death: "Except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world". A great good it is that to me "the world has been crucified"; through what has this good come to me? "Through the cross of Christ". A great good it is for me that I "am crucified to the world"; for if I have died to the world, I have been crucified to the world together with Christ; but if I live to my sins, I have not yet been counted worthy of the good that comes through the cross. And at the same time let us also prepare ourselves for trials, for martyrdoms, knowing that whoever denies has no salvation.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But if you wish to understand what I will destroy the wisdom of the wise and the understanding of the intelligent I will set aside means, consider for me someone quite formidable in heretical arguments—say, for instance, Marcion or Basilides—and one arguing on behalf of heretical doctrines with such power that no ordinary person could withstand him; then consider someone competent according to the truth, one who says "who also made us competent as ministers of a new covenant", and who shows that all those things in which the deceived man had put his trust are foolishness. It is the wisdom of those men, then, that he destroys, not that of the truly wise—of Isaiah, of Jeremiah, or of Solomon; it is the wisdom that seems to be wisdom that he destroys, not the true wisdom.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: To be wise and to be wise in this age are not the same thing; for the former, without any such addition, comprises the true wisdom. And you will understand foolishness in a like manner: to be foolish and to be foolish in this age are not the same; for the man who is such without the addition 'in this age' is truly foolish. And so we too, who believe the words of wisdom, are bidden to become foolish in this age; for such we seem to be to men — believing in Christ Jesus crucified, and believing in a resurrection of bodies, and believing that we shall live (not only we who are now upon the earth living afterward in the heavens), but also that, even if we sin, we shall be handed over to eternal fire. That we seem to men to be such . . . .

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And how too is it that In the wisdom of God the world did not know God through wisdom? The wisdom of God is in the law and the prophets; the world did not know Christ, who was proclaimed in the law and the prophets. For this reason, "at the consummation" of the ages he sent Jesus Christ, to be crucified on behalf of the race of men, so that those who came to believe in Jesus Christ crucified might believe through the foolishness of the preaching.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: We received power from believing in Jesus Christ crucified; and however much we fall short in this faith, by so much do we fall short in the power of having in ourselves the things that come from God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He added to the Not many wise the phrase according to the flesh, knowing that there are differences among the wise, and that some are wise according to the flesh, others according to the spirit; and wise according to the flesh are those who have practiced only petty turns of phrase (λεξείδια) and dress up whatever it may be as truth, though it is not truth. Nevertheless, not even so did he shut out the wise according to the flesh from the faith; for he did not say, No one wise according to the flesh comes to the word, but that very few do. And powerful according to the flesh are those who hold the offices of authority; but you will understand 'according to the spirit' if you observe the Savior—in what manner he was not powerful according to the flesh; for he was indeed betrayed and "was crucified out of weakness"; yet he was powerful according to the spirit, "healing every disease and every sickness among the people". So too consider the case of the apostles, in what manner they were powerful according to the spirit. He too is powerful according to the spirit who lives according to the spirit and "by the spirit puts to death the deeds of the body". Likewise you will understand in the case of the well-born; well-born according to the flesh are those descended from wealthy and illustrious fathers; but well-born according to the spirit are the sons of God, concerning whom it is written "But as many as received him, he gave them authority to become children of God".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
What, then, did God choose? Not simply the foolish things, but with the addition of of the world; we who believe are foolish as regards the world. So they laugh at us and call us foolish, saying, 'The Christians speak of a resurrection of the dead, and that we live after death, and that Jesus whom the Jews crucified was born of a virgin,' and all such things. Let those men, then, laugh at us and call us foolish; for "the natural man does not receive the things of the spirit; for they are foolishness to him".

The foolish things of the world, then, God chose, that he might shame the wise. Not simply the wise, but taking 'of the world' in common; so that he means the foolish things of the world God chose, that he might shame the wise of the world; for truly the wise of the world are shamed, when they themselves worship idols, while the unlettered and the untrained die rather than commit idolatry.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Only in the case of the Ephesians did we find set down the phrase to the saints who are; and we inquire whether the addition of who are to the saints is not superfluous, and what it can signify. Consider, then, whether — just as in Exodus he who gives the oracle to Moses says that his own name is "the one who is" — so those who partake of the One who Is come to be beings, being called, as it were, from not being into being. For God chose the "things that are not", says this same Paul, "that he might bring to nothing the things that are". And someone will inquire how he brings to nothing the things that are; but let us hear him adding "so that no flesh may boast before God". For if anyone who has partaken of being, forgetting his participation, grants to himself the cause of his being, and does not refer all thanksgiving to the one who out of not being graciously granted him being "in his likeness" and "according to his image", then that which is is brought to nothing.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
And the ignoble things of the world and the things despised God chose; again here with the addition of of the world. For what is more noble than a soul that abandons the idols and says "How false the idols our fathers acquired, and there is none among them that sends rain". The ignoble things of the world, then—but noble things of God—God chose; only let us live rightly, so that as a result we shall not be set at nought before God—concerning whom it is written "the evildoer is set at nought before him".

And the things that are not, that he might bring to nothing the things that are; by 'the things that are not' he named the foolish things of the world, the weak, the ignoble, the despised; by 'the things that are,' the well-born of the world; for in the world these are somebodies, whereas we are not, being worn down by all and despised. the things that are not God chose now, that he might bring to nothing the things that are, so that no flesh might boast and say, 'For this reason I was chosen, because I am well-born.'

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And from him you are in Christ Jesus, who became wisdom for us from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption; for on this account Christ is all these things for us, so that what is written might come to pass: Let him who boasts boast in the Lord. For if he who boasts must boast in wisdom, and Christ is wisdom, it is clear that he who boasts boasts in Christ; and likewise in the case of the rest—I mean of sanctification and of righteousness.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: If our Scriptures had persuaded people to believe because they had been written with rhetorical art or philosophical skill, there is no doubt that our faith would be said to depend on the art of words and on human wisdom rather than on the power of God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: When Paul talks about the wisdom of the rulers of this world he seems to be talking not about one wisdom common to them all but about different kinds of wisdom which are peculiar to each.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Lest anyone should say, "Then, since he brought forward the proofs of the faith in power and in the Spirit, did he have no wisdom at all, but is this alone "the mystery of godliness", merely to believe?" — and lest there be no promise of wisdom in him, he adds and says, But we speak wisdom among the perfect, a wisdom not of this age nor of the rulers of this age who are being brought to nothing. For it is one thing to lead certain people into the faith, and another to reveal the wisdom of God. We unfold, then, the wisdom of God not to those being introduced, nor to those just beginning, nor to those who have not yet given proof of a sound life; but whenever a man, having "exercised" in the way one ought "his faculties for the discernment of good and evil", becomes fit also for hearing wisdom, then we speak wisdom among the perfect; and I mean a wisdom not of this age, nor akin to the wisdom of the rulers of this age. And at the same time he has shown that the branches of learning current among the others are not, in their origin, of men, but of invisible powers who are being brought to nothing. And I would say that poetry is a wisdom of this age, and perhaps rhetoric also; and a wisdom too is that which professes to speak about heaven and earth and about the administration of the universe. We, therefore, if we speak wisdom and say that it is among the perfect, do not mean the wisdom of this age; for it is neither through poems nor through any such art.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Look also in another Scripture, and you will find that it was Christ's will that the devil should not know the coming of the Son of God. For the Apostle, affirming that the opposing powers did not know his passion, says: "we speak wisdom among the perfect, yet a wisdom not of this world, nor of the princes of this world, who are brought to nothing; but we speak the wisdom of God hidden in a mystery, which none of the princes of this world knew. For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory". The mystery of the Savior, therefore, was hidden from the princes of this world.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 6

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But we speak wisdom in a mystery, things which have not been known to the rulers of this age who work "the wisdom of the wise" of this world; and thus they did not know: they plotted against our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ and crucified him; for had they known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. We must therefore seek wisdom also in the word, but after the faith, after the manner of life, according to what is written: "You have desired wisdom, keep the commandments".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: From this we may gain an idea of how great the splendor, the beauty and the brightness of a spiritual body is.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Scripture knows a difference between those who love God and those who fear God, and it knows that those who love far surpass those who fear. Something, then, has indeed been prepared even for those who fear; yet he has prepared something greater for those who love than the things prepared for those who fear.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. There is a Spirit which is able to search all things; the soul of man cannot search all things, but a better spirit had to come to be in us, so that, when that one has come to be within us searching all things, even the depths of God, and has been commingled with us, we together with that one might search out all things, even the depths of God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The salvation of the human spirit is annulled — the spirit concerning which the Apostle speaks: "no one among men knows what is in man; only the spirit of man, which is in him." Since the Savior desired to save the spirit of man, concerning which the Apostle spoke in this manner, He took up also the spirit of man.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Let us consider the things that have been graciously given to us by God; for unless the Spirit that is from God comes to be in us, teaching us, we cannot say that we know the things that have been graciously given to us by God, for indeed no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Which things also we speak, he says, not in words taught by human wisdom, but in words taught by the Spirit, and what follows. All the forms of wisdom of this world are words taught by men, things which one learns in each of the rational arts; but they do not teach the things taught by the Spirit. Nor could you say that the teacher, having been taught by the Spirit concerning the things of which he speaks, taught them. For the Spirit, coming to be in the one who seeks and searches out the truth, illumines him, and thus he always, by the "renewal of the mind," finds the things he has not learned from men. For this reason the Savior says, "Do not seek a teacher upon the earth; for one is your teacher, the Father who is in the heavens, or one is your guide, the Christ." A man supplies a few small things—suppose, for instance, Paul teaching Timothy—and Timothy, having received his starting points, comes himself also to the spring to which Paul has come, and draws from it, and Timothy becomes equal to Paul.

But how one is taught by the Spirit must be considered from the apostolic words; for by comparing spiritual things with spiritual, by examining this expression together with that expression and gathering the like ones together, the mind, as it were, of the Scripture is uncovered. For thus do I understand the things of God and become taught by the Spirit; not only by having learned the things of the Spirit who moved Isaiah, but also by having had the same Spirit which shut and sealed the words of Isaiah. For unless the Spirit open the words of the prophets, the things that are shut cannot be opened.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
And since he said these things, he necessarily adds that there are some men who do not admit the things of the Spirit of God, not on account of their nature, as the heterodox suppose, but on account of not having prepared themselves. For the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit, for he was natural; but when he inclined toward the worship of God and admitted the Spirit, he became spiritual.

And the natural man cannot know that they are spiritually discerned; on this account he does not know that what he hears is spiritually discerned, and indeed the "power," when "tested," convicts the foolish—for instance, if I speak having been taught by the Spirit, and I speak with power, and the hearer, testing the power, may form an opinion and not give his assent, the "power," when "tested," convicts the foolish. And it is not so much that that man, having rejected what was said, has rejected what was said, as that what was said has rejected that man; for into a "malicious soul wisdom will not enter, nor will it dwell in a body enslaved to sin."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But the spiritual man discerns all things, yet he himself is discerned by no one. He who no longer walks "according to the flesh" but "according to the Spirit," and who by his diligence is always increasing it and "rekindling the gracious gift of God" to a greater degree, prepares for himself the becoming spiritual; and having become so, he is competent to discern all things—the things of the Greeks, the things of the barbarians, the things of the wise, the things of the foolish; but no one can discern him, on account of the greatness of his understanding and of his reasonings. But if you wish to recognize the spiritual man, "by their fruits you shall recognize them." And what are the fruits of the Spirit from which one must discern who the spiritual man is? Hear the Apostle saying, "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, long-suffering, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control"; where these are, there is the Spirit, that man is spiritual; but where any of these is lacking, that man is not yet spiritual.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Of those who hear, some are perfect, the spiritual, concerning whom we were speaking earlier; but those who are not spiritual, yet believe in Christ, are, as the Apostle says, babes in Christ and fleshly in Christ — for I take 'In Christ' as applying to both in common. There is need, therefore, of teachings for those who are not more perfect and not yet "exercised" in the sacred Scriptures, of the more elementary sort, which the Apostle named to be milk: for he says, I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able, but neither even now are you able. And I think there is a correspondence in the spiritual Scriptures of milk, of food, of "true eating", of "solid nourishment", of the "flesh" of the word, and of a spiritual "herb". And these things I dare to say, being persuaded by the Scriptures; for he did not say that all spiritual nourishment is true "eating", when he says "My flesh is true eating". What sort of things, then, are not "solid nourishment"? The more ethical matters, and whatever among the ethical matters is rather weak, spoken according to "concession" not according to "command", dispensed on account of the weakness of the hearers. But whatever teaching among ethical matters is more perfect, given among hearers who love learning and are diligent, these I would call, among ethical matters, "solid nourishment" — that concerning perfect purity, that concerning virginity or self-control, that concerning martyrdom; these are "solid nourishment". And there is "solid nourishment" in mystical matters, or concerning the Father and the Son. And so too the law, at one time delivers "solid nourishment", and at another more elementary fare. For instance, we come to the account concerning the serpents that destroyed the sons of Israel because of the murmuring; if we read it more simply, we say "Neither let us murmur, just as some of them murmured, and were destroyed by the serpents". But if the hearer is able to hear a mystical account, we say who the serpents are and who is the serpent that was hung upon the wood, and how one is saved by looking to that serpent, and so with each spiritual Scripture.

And who those are that are given milk to drink, Peter will make clear in his epistle when he says "as newborn babes, long for the reasonable, guileless milk"; and in the epistle to the Hebrews also "you have become such as have need of milk and not of solid nourishment"; "for everyone who partakes of milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, for he is a babe"; but "solid nourishment" belongs to the perfect, "to those who through habit have their faculties exercised for the discernment of both good and evil".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Among the sins in men the lesser are jealousy and strife. If someone is in fornication, such a one is no longer fleshly but worse than fleshly. But what such a one might be, let us see. I hold that there is a difference between the fleshly man and the earthy (χοϊκός): "As we have borne", he says, "the image of the earthy, let us bear also the image of the heavenly". If, then, you commit the sins that are unto death, you are not fleshly but earthy; but if you sin, yet not unto death, you are not wholly earthy nor fallen away from the grace of Christ, but then you are fleshly. And of our walks too, the one is according to man, the other according to God. If we walk as the many among men walk, we walk according to man; but if according to the "let your light shine before men", we differ from the many and do not walk according to man. Clear, then, to him who is able to see, is the life — of what sort is the one according to man and of what sort the one according to God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For whenever someone says, I am of Paul, and I of Apollos, and I of Cephas — let us attend to these things too — we shall see that we sometimes are not even men, but are worse than men. For he who then said, I am of Apollos, was speaking about a man of repute and holy and blessed; and he who says, I am of Paul, speaks about a man who is an apostle, sacred and blessed. But sometimes there arise attachments not like the attachment to Paul or Apollos, but someone attaches himself sometimes to a sinner and to a heterodox person. If, then, these are men and walk "according to the flesh" — those who say, I am of Apollos and I of Paul — whenever you say that you belong to someone more inferior, it is plain that you are no longer even a man, but even worse than a man; and perhaps it will be said to you, "Serpents, offspring of vipers".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: If Paul planted, he planted together with God who plants in the first place; if Apollos watered, he watered together with Christ who watered in the first place. For God plants; wherefore it is written, "Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up"; and again, "My Father is the husbandman". Let us therefore "bear fruit", lest we be cut down like the barren "fig tree". For "every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and cast into the fire". Let us take heed lest it be said concerning us, "I waited" that "it should produce a grape cluster, but it produced thorns". For if he says these things concerning us, he will also say what follows: Now therefore "I will declare what I will do to my vineyard. I will take away its hedge, and it shall be for plunder, and I will pull down its wall, and it shall be for trampling".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Since we are not only a field but also God's building, I inquire after the master-builder of the building and those who work together with him. For it is with this in mind that the Apostle says, according to the grace given to me, as a wise master-builder I have laid a foundation; for the church in Corinth, which in no way existed before the Apostle, Paul brought into being. And since there were divisions among them, he says that, grace having been given me by God, as a wise master-builder I laid the foundation, and another builds upon it; for if another has come along and builds upon the foundation of the church, that man is not the master-builder of the church but builds upon the church. If, then, you wish to see that Paul is a wise master-builder, hear him say: "From Jerusalem and as far round as Illyricum I have fulfilled the gospel of God, making it my ambition to preach the gospel not where Christ has been named, lest I should build upon another man's foundation." And not only did he lay a foundation as a wise master-builder, but he also wrote, as it were, master-builder's manuals — how the "master-builder must build" a house, "what sort the bishop must be," and presbyters and deacons and the remaining fullness of the church; for all these were, as it were, the laws of the master-builder's craft.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Another, then, he says, builds upon it; but let each one look how he builds upon it. For this he says to me too, that I may not build carelessly, knowing that the fire itself will test the work which I build upon it, of what sort it is, on that Day. And I take care lest, in building, I build wood, hay, straw. For if I bring paltry souls indiscriminately into the church, I have brought to the good foundation, Christ Jesus, wood, and others hay, and others straw; just as, again, if certain ones shine forth from the building, and shine forth to such a degree that some are found corresponding to what is written concerning Jerusalem and the temple — "chosen stones" and "stones of crystal" and stones of "sapphire" and all the stones he named there — it is plain that I have built upon the foundation precious stones. And since the temple of God and the building must have also gold, just as the temple which Solomon built was a symbol of a temple having gold and much silver, if some other person come who is built upon it, more precious than silver he would be found: gold. But I am wary lest through me there enter wood and hay and straw, and lest I, wretched man (even if in another respect I be judged worthy of salvation, since it is written but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire), be so saved as having become the cause — by not having made room for the grace nor having built well — of the building's having been filled with wood, hay, straw, which the word of God does not will; for the fire will test each one's work, of what sort it is.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But I wish to record in yet another way the saying For no one can lay another foundation besides the one that is laid, which is Jesus Christ, and what follows. From the time my Lord Jesus Christ sojourned here, he has been proclaimed as a foundation unto the world; and this foundation the apostles laid in Judaea, but among the nations it was the apostle of the nations and his fellow worker Barnabas: "For they gave to me and to Barnabas the right hands of fellowship, that we should go to the nations and they to the circumcision." Since, then, Jesus Christ the Word of God has been proclaimed, and this foundation has been laid, no one can lay another foundation besides Jesus Christ; and those who build upon it, if indeed they hold right doctrine through eternal teachings and divine conceptions and good words and holy deeds, build upon the foundation gold, silver, precious stone. For gold has often been observed to be taken in place of mind and conceptions; if I speak well, I build silver; if I expound fittingly and rightly urge my hearers toward the way of life, I build precious stones. Those, however, among the teachers of Jesus Christ who have swerved from the truth have built upon the foundation wood, hay, straw; and I would say that of all those from the heresies, the more blasphemous are wood, those who have erred less in doctrine hay, and those whose faults are slight and, so to name them, of lesser account straw.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But come, let us look also according to the literal sense. What is now to be said touches each single one of us. Each of us, having received the word of the gospel, received Jesus Christ as a foundation, so that in all he does and says and thinks he might build upon this foundation. If, then, we think and consider good things, we build gold; if, speaking purely, we speak every word that is spoken in a holy manner, we build as silver; if every deed we do is good, we build as precious stone — but the value of the stones and their quality God judges. If, however, I sin after the foundation, the great of my sins will be wood for me, the lesser hay, and those still lesser straw. And I inquire whether perhaps the roots and the conceptions, whenever they are erroneous, are wood; for the conceptions are the fount of evils; and the words are hay, and the deed straw; for the worth of the deed is lesser than that of the reasoning; but he who plants and he who waters are one.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: We can still add also this, that the nature of sin is like the material which is consumed by fire, which the Apostle Paul says is built up by sinners, who "upon the foundation" of Christ "build wood, hay, stubble." In which it is manifestly shown that there are certain sins so slight that they are compared to "stubble," over which, when fire is brought, it cannot tarry long; but others are like "hay," which the fire likewise consumes not with difficulty, yet tarries somewhat longer than upon "stubble"; but others there are which are compared to "wood," in which, according to the quality of the crimes, the fire finds lasting and great fuel. Thus, then, each sin, according to its quality or quantity, pays its just penalties. Nevertheless, what need is there for the faithful and for those who have known God to think about the qualities of penalties? What need to place "wood," what "hay," what even "stubble" itself "upon the foundation" of Christ? Why do we not rather place "gold" or "silver" or "precious stones" upon the precious "foundation," where, when the fire comes, it may find nothing that it may consume? For if it comes to "stubble," from "stubble" it will render embers and ashes; but if it comes to "gold," it will render "gold" purer.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But that this house can sometimes be sold, that is, that a building of this kind may fall into sin, hear how the Apostle Paul speaks concerning such: "as a wise architect I laid the foundation", he says, "another builds upon it, but let each one see how he builds upon it. For no one can lay another foundation besides that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus. But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble". You see, then, that there can be "built upon the foundation of Christ wood, hay, stubble", that is, works of sin; and whoever "builds" these has without doubt "sold his house" to the worst buyer, the devil, from whom each of those who sin obtains the price of sin, the satisfaction of his desire. If perchance anyone should incur this—which God forbid—let him quickly redeem it, quickly repair it, while there is time for repairing, while there is place for repentance, praying in common that we be not defrauded of the habitation of the eternal house, but be held worthy "to be received into the eternal tabernacles", through Christ our Lord, "to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
If you wish to learn what the true temple of God is, seek "living stones", pure and hewn out, laid by the word, and standing four-square, having nothing unstable nor rolling; for even if "holy stones roll upon the earth", yet the stone-cutters do not allow them to roll to the end. You therefore, as "living stones, are built up a spiritual house for a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ". And in the Apostle too it is said that "we are a temple", all of us one, each of us being some stone of the temple. And he says thus in the epistle to the Ephesians: "So then you are not strangers and sojourners, but fellow-citizens with the saints and members of the household of God; built upon the foundation of the apostles and the prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the cornerstone; in whom the whole building, fitly framed together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord; in whom you also are built together for a habitation of God in the Spirit". It is necessary, therefore, that no stone be unfitted to the building; for "if", he says, "two of you agree on earth concerning anything that they shall ask, it shall be done for them by my Father who is in heaven". How much more, then, if all the stones agree into one harmony and the heart and soul of all become one, will their prayer be able and have power? It is good, therefore, that we all say the same thing, that we may be "perfected in the same mind and the same judgment"; for thus you are "a building fitly framed together into a holy temple in the Lord".

But each of us can also be a temple by himself in another sense; for if a temple is that which has the glory of God, everyone who has in himself the glory of God is in this respect a temple of God. And he has more or less glory who causes the name of the Father in heaven to be glorified through his deeds; wherefore it is written, "Those who glorify me I will glorify".

Then, therefore, shall we most be a temple of God, if we prepare ourselves capable of the Spirit of God. One who has a spirit of some sin cannot, however, be a temple of God, since the Spirit of God dwells only in that in which it judges to dwell.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: If anyone corrupts the temple of God, God will corrupt this man. So far as in him lies, each one, even if he be a stone, corrupts the temple of God by sinning, and he who provides some stumbling-block to the Church corrupts the temple of God; but more properly he who commits fornication corrupts the temple of God, since "your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit which is in you, which you have from God". Therefore he who is pure is called incorrupt, but she who is no longer a virgin is called corrupted, since indeed this deed alone corrupts. If, then, this is a deed of corruption, let us guard against this most of all. Since also the Lord "is with all those who love God in incorruption".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And these things have had their own delimitation; but since the Corinthians thought highly of themselves on account of the wisdom of the world, therefore he says to them If anyone among you thinks he is wise (not 'if anyone is wise' but 'thinks he is wise among you'), let him become a fool in this age; he did not say simply 'a fool', but 'in this age', for it is with regard to this age that they call us fools. Let him therefore become a fool in this age, that from having become a fool with regard to this age he may become truly wise; for the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For how is he not a fool who says there is no providence, or that all things are composed of atoms and void, or that pleasure is the end of goods, and who says all the other things that are the nonsense and trifles of the external and seeming wisdom? For this man is truly a fool, and these doctrines are foolishness. And, quite simply, examining every Greek and barbarian philosophy you will say that in whatever points it disagrees with the teaching of Christ it is foolishness.

author: Origen of Alexandria
