quote: I say that it is no great matter if God, as God, catches the wise in their craftiness, but rather in Paul who says "for though living in the flesh we do not wage war according to the flesh; for the weapons of our warfare are not fleshly but powerful for God to the pulling down of strongholds; casting down reasonings and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God". And that you may understand this more clearly, look for me at Paul, when he had come to Athens and was disputing with those he met, so that even some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers engaged with him; for then by the grace of Christ he grasped them all around and exposed their sophisms; and here I think the wise are named the sophists, all who speak entangled sophisms but do not teach the truth.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And again "The Lord knows the reasonings of the wise, that they are vain". It is not marvelous if the Lord knows in himself the reasonings of the wise, that they are vain; but I wish the Lord, having come to be in me, to know the reasonings of the wise, that they are vain. For if Christ comes to be in me, he can demonstrate to me how the reasonings of the wise of the world are vain, and how the wisdom of God alone shines, conquering and trampling down every seeming wisdom.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He who is able to renounce all men and to become wholly worthy of the boasting that is in Christ, this man does not boast in man.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But how is death mine? That I may die to sin; that I may say "If we also died together, we shall also live together". For the other death, according to which "the soul that sins, it shall itself die", is not mine. And things present too are ours: because we are gathered together in the present age, because we hear the sacred scriptures, because we pray. And things to come: "for when that which is perfect comes, then that which is in part shall be done away". And it is not possible to come to things to come unless things present first become mine. all things are yours: a certain saying spoken among the Greeks is admired, of this kind: 'All things belong to the wise man and nothing to the base man'; but these things the word of God taught first, that All things belong to the holy man. To the believer, then, he says, belongs the whole world of goods, but to the unbeliever not even an obol; for the unbeliever has what he has as a robber does; for since he does not know how to use them, nor knows the God who created these things, nor listens to him who says "Mine is the silver and mine is the gold", he does not have those things as his own. But we see that all things are ours; and to the believer belongs the whole world of goods, but to the unbeliever not even an obol.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He who has not advanced in the word to the comprehension of the mysteries hidden in Scripture can indeed be a servant of Christ, but cannot be a steward of the mysteries of God; for he who is a steward possesses the things stewarded and knows the "mysteries" of God. Perhaps, then, the servant of Christ is understood as one set over the more common ministry, while the steward of the mysteries of God is understood according to the administration concerning the mysteries that have been made known, so that he may not cast these things aside at random nor deliver them without examination; but having first purified, first prepared, first withdrawn from the world the one who is about to hear supramundane teachings, then he speaks them. We, he says, are servants of Christ; and the Apostle served for the most part rather in the service of Christ than in the stewardship of the mysteries of God; but he stewards the mysteries of God, for example, toward Luke, that he might be able to write the Gospel; toward Timothy, that he might become able to rule over those in Ephesus who had received more, and to steward the mysteries of God. And I dare even to say that in Corinth he became a servant of Christ, but in Ephesus a steward of the mysteries of God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And Paul, having learned from the words of the Saviour, "Who then is the faithful and prudent steward, whom the lord will set over his household, to give the measure of grain in due season to his fellow-servants", says, But what is further sought in stewards is that a man be found faithful. For neither does knowing suffice, nor ought the one who has come to know to speak at random, but, understanding the "giving of the measure of grain in due season" to his fellow-servants, he must see which of the fellow-servants ought to receive a greater "measure of grain" of the mysteries of God or a lesser one, and when; for if he administers the stewardship well and blamelessly, what promise has he? "Over all" he says "his possessions the master of the house will set him". But if Paul is afraid and says these things concerning himself and concerning Cephas and Apollos, how much more must the stewards among us fear, that they may be found faithful stewards.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Then concerning himself he says, But to me it is a very small thing that I should be examined by you or by man's day. Those in Corinth were examining, so far as in them lay, though not examining truly. For it belonged to one examining to say that Paul is superior to Cephas and Apollos, and to another to say, Peter far surpasses Paul; for in the Gospel Paul is not called an apostle. So Paul says, To me it is a very small thing that I should be examined by you. He was conscious in himself of the noblest things, and that he was not subject to the Corinthians as though they were able to examine him, for the "spiritual man examines all things, but he himself is examined by no one"; just as elsewhere he says, "I have become a fool; you compelled me"; having some such thing in mind here too, he speaks. There is a certain human day, and there is a certain divine day, concerning which countless things are written, including this: "Behold, the incurable day of the Lord comes". My examination, therefore, he says, cannot take place in a human day, for a human day does not contain my examination; if I am to be examined, I shall be examined in the day of the Lord.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Then, conscious in himself of something more paradoxical, he says, Nay, neither do I examine myself; for I am conscious of nothing against myself. Here the conscience of the Apostle appears to have become greatly pure, so that he dared to write not only to those then living but also that the generations up to the consummation might read what is said. Paul, then, is truthful when he says, "Become imitators of me, as I also am of Christ"; and how Paul imitated Christ, hear: "The ruler of this world comes, and in me he has nothing"; and Paul says, I am conscious of nothing against myself; and he did not say, I am conscious in myself of no evil deed; for if he had said this, we might say that he had been cleansed in his deeds but not yet in his words; or again, that he had been cleansed in these but his heart was sinning. But as it is, he seems to be conscious in himself of purity to an extraordinary degree—not formerly, when he was persecuting, or when he came to the faith, but now, when he was saying these things.

Then, that he may not seem to have spoken beyond man, he adds and says, Yet I am not thereby justified; for I, he says, am conscious of nothing against myself, yet I am not thereby justified. For it is possible that I be conscious of nothing against myself, yet that something sinned by me escape my notice; for many such things occur in human nature, so that one sins not according to reason, not with comprehension or by consent, not with the observing that we have sinned. That man, then, who in all things is conscious of nothing against himself, says, Yet I am not thereby justified, but he that examines me is the Lord.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
For as one who has passed beyond the examination of the angels and of the other powers, he says this: Until the Lord come. Since, then, a judgment is at hand, and that alone is true—the judgment of the Lord, who knows both how to weigh the reasonings and to set the words in the balance and to search out all the deeds and to render to each of us what is due—for this reason, even if we find fault with someone, let us not condemn; for we do not know by what measure he sinned, nor do we know with what disposition he sinned, and whether he has good things counterbalancing his sin. For if we become cautious, we shall not judge anything before the time, but shall refer all things to the judgment of God through our Saviour Jesus Christ.

Here it is said, Judge nothing before the time, and what follows; but in another place of the epistle, "Do you not judge those within, while those outside God judges?". Do the Scriptures, then, contain contradictions, and must we both judge and not judge according to the same signification of judgment? If you who are entrusted with judging those within do not judge those within, the Church is about to become, instead of a Church of God, a "synagogue of evildoers"; then, if those within are being judged, how is it true, "Judge not, that you be not judged"? We say, then: Those entrusted with judging those within are not so foolish as, when judging those within, to say, We judge the judgment of God, but they make their judgment with a view to the administration of what is beneficial to the Church. If it is beneficial that such a one be put out of the assembly, having so judged, they do it; and again, with a view to what is beneficial they will reinstate him, not judging the judgment of God but the one given to them; for it is impossible for us to judge the judgment which God will judge in Christ; for we neither search hearts nor know with what reasonings the deeds done by each have been done. For "the hidden things" the judges according to the Gospel yield "to the Lord God", but "the manifest things", as it is said, "to you and to your children"; whatever has reached them and is known among them, these things they judge. Let us therefore never, anticipating the judgment of God, say, So-and-so is perishing, nor, blessing him, say, So-and-so is being saved; for we do not know how to measure and compare deeds against deeds, or reasonings, or thoughts. Judge nothing, then, before the time, until the Lord come, who will both illuminate the hidden things of darkness and make manifest the counsels of the hearts.

Since two things are mentioned, there ought to be some difference between them; for some he named hidden things of darkness, and others counsels of hearts. Consider, then, whether our sins are the hidden things of darkness, and our brave good deeds the counsels of the hearts; for whatever we do well, we do with counsel, but whatever we sin, we sin being in darkness. Since, then, some have either these or those, and a man does not know these things, let us not judge anything before the time, until the Lord come, who will both illuminate the hidden things of darkness and will reveal the counsels of the hearts; "For we must all be made manifest before the judgment-seat of Christ, that each may receive the things done through the body according to what he did, whether good or evil". I have found a Gospel saying to expound similarly to this: "There is nothing hidden that shall not be made manifest, and nothing covered that shall not be revealed"; you see the Saviour giving a distinction between hidden things being made manifest and covered things being revealed. What, then, are the hidden things that are made manifest, but the good things? And what are the covered things that are revealed, but the evil things?

One of those who search out everything might say: Why did he not say, And then the praise shall come—or the blame—to each from God, but only the praise? Now one person will explain it thus: that he attached the more auspicious thing to God, passing over in silence the rest as not fitting for Him; but I will dare and would say that God praises and accepts our good things, while the father of evils, the devil, [claims] our evil things; and the praise comes from God to the saints, but the blame to those who have done things worthy of blame comes from the devil. For this reason it is said to you by the Apostle, "that the one on the opposing side may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say about us".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
These things, he says, are written in a figure adapted to the affairs of that time, not that we should learn these things about Paul and Apollos only, but that in each generation, looking upon the things that happen as analogous to these, we may rightly take heed lest we too fall into such things, and lest, as in theatres where men are split into factions over the entertainments, we too be split into factions over our teachers.

But let us look at that in us you may learn the lesson, Not beyond what is written. If anyone, having an inferior condition, wishes, before he has fulfilled the things that are written, to ascend to the things beyond what is written, he will not even understand the things that are written. For just as it is impossible for anyone to climb a ladder unless he ascends by the way from the lower rungs so far as he is able, in the same manner it is with the divine teachings. Not understanding this well, those from the heresies proclaim traditions and say, These are beyond the things that are written; for these our Saviour delivered to the apostles in secret, and the apostles to this or that man; and thus "by this mythology they deceive the hearts of the guileless". But the rest say, It is written, "Why do you behold the mote that is in your brother's eye, but the beam that is in your own eye you do not consider"; and "Judge not, that you be not judged". For if we are one and are bound together with one another, we ought not to rise up against one another. For "He that humbles himself shall be exalted", and "Whoever wishes to be first among you, let him be last of all", and "Let each one remain in that in which he was called".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
These and such things are the things that are written, that you be not puffed up on behalf of the one against the other; for those who divided themselves up, some wishing to be called after this man and some after that, fought with one another, each side contending to set their own teachers above the others, and then, further, against the teachers themselves. For who distinguishes you? Who appointed you over a part? Why are you not called the teacher of all alike? And what have you that you did not receive? And on what do you pride yourself? On eloquence? But God has granted you this. But on knowledge? This too is a divine gift. But on works of wonder? This too is the working of the Spirit. But if you also received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it? No one prides himself on deposits belonging to another, but keeps vigilant watch over them so as to guard them for the one who gave them.

It will be necessary to gather from the Scriptures what to distinguish signifies, that we may thus fit it to what is now being said. "God stood", he says, "in the assembly of gods, and in the midst he will distinguish gods"; in this it appears that to distinguish is a work of God; for, judging being another matter, which happens concerning those worthy of judgment, it is a good thing to be found a god in the "assembly" of gods, so that one may no longer be judged but be distinguished and, as it were, entrusted with some one rank of those with which the gods in the "assembly" are entrusted. But also in the passage "Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others distinguish", to distinguish there seems to be taken in the sense of articulating, as it were, "Let them make clear" the things spoken and distinguish them and understand them. But in the passage "He that distinguishes, if he eat, is condemned, because it is not of faith", distinguishes appears to be said in a sense of blame. And again, "Receive" one another, "not sinning unto the distinguishing of thoughts"; the word was thus found from Scripture set at one time upon the better things and at another upon their opposites. Here, then, to distinguish is said in place of: No one of those in Corinth distinguishes you nor judges you; but you distinguish "stewards of the mysteries of God", and you say, I am of Paul, and you assert, I am of Cephas, or you say, I am of Apollos. It is a work of God to distinguish the apostles, not yours. As, then, you ought not to judge, neither ought you to distinguish the servants of the gospel; for in the distinguishing by which you distinguish the apostles, you yourself distinguish and separate yourself, sinning. For Christ came to unite the things that had been distinguished, that we might no longer be divided. If we are perfected so that the "flesh" no longer "lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh", by the mortifying of "the members that are upon the earth", we shall no longer be in distinction but, as it were, in a fusion and in our gathering together into one. But let it also be understood more simply, with reference to the various divisions.

But let us look also at And what have you that you did not receive? For the phrase is ambiguous; for it can be understood that every possession we have, we have received from God and so have it; and again, Why do you pretend to have what you did not receive? as, for instance, if someone who has not received a gift from above from God pretends to be in possession of a gift, it is said to such a one who has not received, And what have you that you did not receive? But if you also received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Already you are filled full; already you have grown rich; without us you have come to reign? "He that hungers and thirsts after the righteousness" that comes of the oracles of truth is not satisfied with one teacher, but if he finds a second he makes use of him too, for he is insatiable for good things; and if he is well supplied with a third, he comes to the third also; he does not, cutting off one for himself, say, I am of Paul, or of Cephas, or of Apollos. Since, then, being filled full signifies — when there are several teachers, both Paul teaching and Cephas and Apollos — that the one who inclines to a single one gains no benefit from all of them, for this reason he says to the Corinthians, Are you already filled full? And consequent upon this is Have you already grown rich? as, for instance, Have you gathered together the wealth that comes from the teachings from Paul, and no longer have need of the things from Apollos or the things from Cephas? Or do you despise them all, as being sated and rich "in all utterance and in all knowledge"? And consequently also Without us you have come to reign; for, so far as in you lay, you have separated me from the kingdom, and yourselves too, having inclined to some single one apart from the rest; and he does not say without me but without us, that he may include others and make it common.

And would that you had indeed come to reign, that we too might reign together with you. And at the same time perhaps he also intimates a certain mystery at this point. For the inferior come more quickly into the promise, while the more perfect receive the promises more slowly; and this I shall show from Scripture. Those who received their inheritance under Moses received the promise first, while those who receive their inheritance under Joshua received it later; but also concerning all the righteous it is said, "These all, having obtained witness through faith, did not receive the promise, God having foreseen some better thing concerning us, that they should not be made perfect without us". Is it for this reason that he says without us you have come to reign? And would that you had indeed come to reign, that we too might reign together with you. For when you, the disciples and hearers, reign, then it is necessary that we too attain to the perfect kingdom of God and of the Lord Jesus.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
In proportion as anyone lays claim to the true and heavenly primacy, so much the more, out of humility, does he become last of all men. And I think the Apostle too had something of this sort in mind when he said, "To me, who am less than the least of all saints, this grace was given"—not that in respect of sanctification he was less than all the saints, for this he neither thought, nor, if he had said it, would he have been speaking the truth; but he made himself more humble than all who believe, becoming "gentle in the midst of all, as when a nurse cherishes her own children". Since, then, the apostles made it their endeavor by their own choice to be last, and since for every good endeavor, unless God bears witness and fulfills the will of the one endeavoring, the good end does not follow through the one endeavoring—for this reason perhaps the Apostle has said, For I think that God has set forth us the apostles last, as men doomed to death. For even if I too, he says, and the apostles have acted so that we might become last, yet we needed the demonstration and the grace from God, so that we might be perfected in being last to the world. And the I think is as elsewhere he said, "But I think that I too have the Spirit of God".

And it is fitting that those set forth as last by God should become first with God; for it is true that the last become first. And it is fitting for them also to be doomed to death. For in proportion as one lives out Christianity more perfectly, so much the more is he doomed to death. For when is he not in danger—reproving the sinner who is often more powerful in life and able to punish, sojourning in places "where Christ has not been named", and laying a foundation that is strange and disturbing to those who hear? For truly Paul said, "I die daily, by your boasting which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord". But it appears to me, as I examine the passage, that the one doomed to death can be taken in two ways: in one, the manner already stated, according to which one must "always carry about the dying of Jesus in the body"; in the other, the righteous man is doomed to death as being conformed to the death of Christ, ever dying to the world. And thus it is fitting that God should set forth the apostles of Christ as being both last and doomed to death.

Then it is necessary to see the meaning of we have become a spectacle to the world, and to angels, and to men. If Paul contends, and Peter, the angels of God hasten to this new spectacle, that they may see a man clothed with flesh wrestling "against the principalities, against the powers, against the world-rulers of this world, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places"; and men too came to see a new sight, a herald and teacher of a new word. Thus Paul was a spectacle of all those on earth and of the angels who rejoice "over one sinner who repents".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Then, so great a man, as last in the world, rebukes those who are "puffed up", and says to them, We are fools for Christ's sake. For Paul, who gives me a commandment and says, "If anyone among you thinks himself to be wise in this age, let him become a fool, that he may become wise", much more did he himself keep to becoming a fool in this world. For how was he not a fool in this world, proclaiming the "crucified one" and "the resurrection of the dead" and the things concerning the age to come, and persuading men to despise the present life?

Then with irony he says, You are wise in Christ; for they were not truly wise in Christ, but in saying these things ironically he was urging them to become wise in Christ. You are honorable, but we are despised: he no longer added You are honorable, in Christ. For if you see many of those who seem to believe possessing worldly dignities, say to them, if you are lowly in the world, You are honorable, but we are despised; we are weak, but you are strong: for nothing is weaker than a true Christian as regards this world.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For in this place I think three things can be assigned from the Scriptures, in which he says that the sinner stands against him, and speaks in his ears the things by which he can be irritated and exasperated to retaliate. And if indeed I am small, I seek the like, and an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, and I repay curses for curses. But if I have already advanced somewhat, yet am not yet perfect, I both keep silence and bear the reproaches patiently, and answer nothing at all. But if I am perfect, I do not keep silence, but when I am cursed, I bless, just as Paul also said: "We are cursed and we bless, we suffer persecution and we endure it, being blasphemed we entreat". And since those who do these things, that is, who render blessings for curses, who for blasphemies entreat, seem to men to be as it were cattle and refuse, as those who have no sense of injury, therefore he added, saying: "We are made as it were the refuse of this world, the offscouring of all". But we are unwilling to become with the apostles the refuse of this world, but wish not to be despised by men, nay rather even to be feared, and we do enough to repay those who harm us, and to anticipate the vengeance which the Lord reserved for himself, saying: "Vengeance is mine, I will repay, saith the Lord". But if we cannot advance so far, and ascend to that summit of truth, so as to say with Paul: "We are cursed and we bless, we suffer persecution and we endure it, being blasphemed we entreat", let us at least say this which we are still taught through the Prophet: "While the sinner stood against me, I was dumb and was humbled, and I kept silence from good things".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: These things seem to be perfectly simple and to require no exposition; yet they hold hidden meanings. No grown man is placed under a tutor, but only one who is an infant and immature; and he would not have written this to the Ephesians but to the Corinthians, to whom he says, "I gave you milk to drink, not solid food; for you were not yet able. But neither even now are you able, for you are still fleshly. And I was not able to speak to you as to spiritual men but as to fleshly, as to infants in Christ." And this too must be considered: even if we do have need of a tutor, at all events let the one who has been entrusted with this give a pattern — his word, his life — to our good ordering. The father, then, is the one who first sowed Christianity in the soul; while the tutor is the one who after him takes over the child and leads him along.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: That is: As I practice moderation, practice moderation; as I suffer, suffer; take your pride in the sufferings, not in the spiritual gifts.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Both his disposition toward them he showed by sending Timothy, and his affection toward Timothy by naming him a beloved child; and his further excellence he has made clear by calling him faithful in the Lord. This man, he says, will narrate my deeds; for by ways he means the deeds. And of these he did not say He will teach, but that He will remind. Now the word charges them with forgetfulness; for they had been eyewitnesses of the apostolic excellence. And he has added that to all the churches too he is accustomed to bring forward this same teaching.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Having accused all of them in common with these things, he now proceeds to bring forth the verdict against the one who had committed fornication.

Foreseeing his repentance, the divinely-inspired Paul does not set down the name, so that the man might not become manifest to all people, but he said indefinitely, some.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: By speech he means eloquence, as also elsewhere: "even if I am unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge"; and by power the power that is from God. For whenever the word is from God, it has power; wherefore it is written: "The Lord will give a word to those who preach the good tidings with much power". And the apostles, trusting in power rather than in speech, took up residence among the churches and the cities. For it is not that, if someone expresses himself finely, he on that account has the kingdom of God; but where there is power in words, there is the kingdom of God, which both banishes the "sin that reigns" in souls and makes ready for the "kingdom of God to come to be within us".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Neither God nor his inspired disciples always use kindly words toward those who hear, nor always severe ones, but sometimes the one and sometimes the other. Since, then, Paul's word had a rod, but had also a spirit of gentleness and of kindliness, he inquires of the Corinthians, not wishing too rashly and too quickly to employ the more severe course; not that the rod comes to be apart from love, but that the love is hidden in the one who holds the rod, and he does not display the love in the severity of the rebuke.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Then he adds the reason for such an inquiry, saying, It is actually reported that there is fornication among you, such as is not even among the Gentiles. We learn that we need to have a charm chanted over us concerning fornication so that we may not fall; and we must learn another thing as well, that even those who are not conscious in themselves of fornication, but who are aware that those gathering with them commit fornication, should not be puffed up, knowing that they too are sinners in that he who gathers with them is a sinner. For he brings a charge against the whole Church on account of one man who has committed fornication, and he charges their being puffed up as something occurring not according to reason, especially because there was still a fornicator among them. And thirdly we learn that there are also differences of fornications, so that there is a certain most grievous fornication, and another lesser, and another still lesser. Therefore in the judgment of God the fornicators are not judged without distinction, nor will they receive the same condemnation for having committed fornication, but both the quantity and the quality increase the punishment, and so too the deliberate choice and the time. In Corinth, then, a certain man contracted an unlawful marriage; for he took his stepmother to wife; but such a marriage the Apostle calls fornication, and such as is not even to be heard of among the Gentiles, in order to teach us that, if ever we marry unlawfully, what is supposed to be a marriage is not reckoned to us as a marriage but as fornication.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Then, leaving this man aside, he brings his accusation against this man's company: And you are puffed up, and did not rather mourn, that he who has done this deed might be taken away from among you. He rebukes them all as having wrongly received him. For whenever, while the one who has sinned is in our midst, we who think we are conscious in ourselves of better things are puffed up, then the words are spoken, And you are puffed up.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: To be absent in body and to be present in spirit belongs to Paul and to those like him; for he said also elsewhere: "For though I am absent in the flesh, yet I am with you in the spirit, rejoicing and beholding the firmness of your faith in Christ." But none of us is able to say, I am present and I behold the excellences of the Church, or "the order and the firmness of the faith in Christ." Such was Elisha; for even though he was not present in body, in spirit he went along with Gehazi and says to him: "Was not my heart with you when you took the two talents of silver and took the garments from Naaman the Syrian?" Was it, then, that Elisha had this grace, while Paul the apostle of Christ, who "is zealous for the greater gifts, but rather that he may prophesy," did not have such a grace? No — I declare, and say confidently, that Paul was not only an apostle but also a prophet. Such was he when he says: "Men shall be lovers of self, lovers of money, boasters, haughty, blasphemers, disobedient to parents"; for he said these things not as an apostle but as a prophet. And "The Spirit," he says, "says expressly that in the last times some shall depart from the faith." And what Spirit? As if he were saying, The Spirit that is in me. Having, then, this grace, even if he was absent in body, he was present in spirit wherever he wished; for it was not he alone who was present in spirit, but also the power of Jesus.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Hear, then, himself saying of him who had sinned: "I have delivered", he says, "such a man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved". You see, then, that even now not only through his Apostles does God "deliver" transgressors "into the hands of enemies", but also through those who preside over the church and have the power not only of loosing, but also of binding, sinners "are delivered into the destruction of the flesh", when for their offenses they are separated from the body of Christ. And, as it seems to me, even now men are delivered from the church into the power of the devil in two ways: in this manner which we spoke of above, when his offense becomes manifest to the church and he is driven from the church by the priests, so that, marked out by men, he may blush, and being converted there may befall him that which follows: "that the spirit may be saved in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ"; but in another way one is "delivered to the devil" when his sin does not become manifest to men, yet God, "who sees in secret", perceiving his mind and his soul serving vices and passions, and that in his heart it is not he who is worshipped, but either avarice or lust or vainglory or other such things — such a one the Lord himself "delivers to Satan".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And therefore, knowing these things to be expedient for the faithful, the Apostle Paul says of him who had sinned: "whom I have handed over," he says, "to Satan for the destruction of the flesh," that is, to have punished him with death. But what the fruit of this death is, he shows in what follows, saying: "that the spirit may be saved in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ." You see, then, how openly the Apostle has set forth the usefulness of this death. For what he says, "I have handed over for the destruction of the flesh," that is, for the affliction of the body, which is wont to be paid out by penitents, and he named it a destruction of the flesh which nevertheless confers life on the spirit. Whence now too, if perhaps any of us recalls in himself the consciousness of some sin, if anyone knows himself to be liable to an offense, let him take refuge in penitence and take upon himself a voluntary destruction of the flesh, that, purged in the present life, our spirit may proceed clean and pure to Christ our Lord.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Concerning the man who had sinned at Corinth, the Apostle declared, saying: "To deliver such a man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh." Is it to be supposed that he wished the man whom he said ought to be delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh to become wicked? Rather, on the contrary, it is apparent that for the man's salvation he delivered his flesh to destruction. Indeed, he adds, saying: "I have delivered such a man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord," showing that the spirit cannot be saved unless the flesh be delivered to destruction. What, then, the destruction of the flesh is, hear. For what has been destroyed is without doubt dead. But the flesh lives in the sinner; the flesh is dead in the righteous man. On account of which the righteous also say: "Always carrying about the mortification of Jesus Christ in our body, that the life of Jesus Christ also may be made manifest in our mortal flesh." And again we have received a command, saying: "Mortify your members which are upon the earth." And blessed is he who has died to sin, according to what has been said: "The body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit lives as life because of justification." To be delivered, then, to the destruction of the flesh is such that the carnal sense may die in us, and the desire of the flesh may not live in it. For from the fact that the sense of the flesh dies, so that we may not be wise according to the flesh, the spirit is made safe. Otherwise, while the sense of the flesh lives in us, and the flesh lives, we cannot be wise about spiritual things. In this way, then, the Apostle delivered to the destruction of the flesh the man who had lived according to the flesh, so that, the sense of the flesh being dead, the spirit might be saved in the day of the Lord.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Not for the destruction of the soul, not for the destruction of the spirit, but for the destruction of the flesh; for he is delivered over that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord. For Paul cast out such a man, not knowing that "he will repent and turn back," but wishing to discipline him. For it is one thing to cut someone off as incapable of repentance and conversion, and another to set him aside for the present and to expel him from the flock, as a shepherd expels a sheep that has the scab, so that the spread of that wound may not be grazed abroad over the whole flock.

Let those, then, who are living badly, having been put outside the flock, be healed, confessing and mourning their own sins, offering the things of repentance in fastings and mournings and weepings and the like. For they are delivered over that they may be disciplined, so that their flesh may be destroyed — that is, the "mind of the flesh"; not that he may touch their soul, not that he may drive them out of their senses, not that he may do anything else, but that he may receive authority over their flesh alone — I not giving the authority, but the power of Jesus which is in me.

From its better part he named the whole salvation, so that he does not say Both the spirit and the soul and the body may be saved in the day of the Lord, but that the spirit may be saved, naming the salvation of the whole man from the better part. For he commands, as of one who is to be saved, that he be received back into the Church in the second epistle.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Since the people of the Hebrews once came out of Egypt, a legislation pertaining to this feast is fittingly assigned to them. This is the prescription: "In each house the individual members, having chosen a lamb, male, perfect, and without blemish, are to sacrifice it and eat it in the evening, roasted with fire, neither raw nor boiled in water, so that in this way the destroyer of the firstborn of the Egyptians, on seeing the doorposts of their gates anointed with blood, may not touch them." This done, the people come out of Egypt, the firstborn of the Egyptians perish, and Pharaoh, after the departure of the Hebrews, repents and sets out in pursuit of them, accompanied by his army and his chariots. In this way he sinks into the Red Sea, while Moses with the people passes through the sea.

The Apostle too teaches us that even to this day the Passover is celebrated, the lamb is immolated, and the people depart from Egypt, when he says: "Christ our Passover has been immolated, that we may keep the feast not with the old leaven of impiety and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of purity and truth." If, then, Christ our Passover has been immolated, those who sacrifice Christ come out of Egypt, pass through the sea, and shall see Pharaoh drowned in the sea. But if some of them wish to return to Egypt, they shall not enter the holy land.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
The lamb is offered in sacrifice by the saints or by the Nazirites, whereas the Savior is offered in sacrifice by the transgressors of the Law and by sinners. And since the paschal lamb is sacrificed by the saints, the Apostle says: "Christ our Passover has been sacrificed," that is, Christ is offered in sacrifice according to the typology of the Passover, but He is not offered in sacrifice by the saints; the Passover is a type of Christ, not, however, of His passion.

For we must offer the true lamb, if we have been consecrated or offer as equals to the priests, roast it and eat its flesh. If this did not come about with the passion of the Savior, then certainly His passion is not a type of the Passover, but the Passover becomes a type of Christ in Himself, when He is offered in sacrifice by us. Each of us first takes the lamb, then consecrates it with an invocation, next offers it in sacrifice, and so, after roasting it, eats it and, having fed upon it, leaves no remainder of it until dawn, and then celebrates the unleavened bread, because he has by now come out of Egypt.

Let us consider, then, whether the words uttered by the Savior are connected with those reported concerning the Passover. As in that passage it was said that whoever did not eat the Passover would be cut off from the midst of his people, so now too the true lamb says that whoever does not eat of His flesh has no life. As there the destroyer cannot strike the one who has fed upon the lamb, so now too the one who has eaten of the true lamb escapes the destroyer.

Perhaps Christ is offered in sacrifice, and is crucified not for all, but for those who can affirm: "For me the world has been crucified, and I to the world," and for those who can declare: "Having stripped the principalities and the powers, He made a spectacle of them in His triumph on the cross," and for those who can say: "There could be for me no boasting, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified for me, and I to the world."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
He who has put off "the old man with his deeds" and has nothing of the old leaven in himself, but has made a new lump according to Christ Jesus, this man has kept the feast of unleavened bread; then, after the feast of unleavened bread, the new leaven appears. Jesus the Christ is the new leaven. Let us therefore first eat unleavened bread, abstaining from all malice and wickedness. Teaching about these things the Apostle says, Purge out therefore the old leaven, that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened: just as happens among the Jews — if the day of unleavened bread is dawning, they purge out all old leaven, searching around every place of the house lest leaven be found anywhere there — so also do you examine the storerooms within you, lest leaven be anywhere there, that you may be a new lump.

As you are unleavened. Since in Corinth there were some who were holy and some who were not such but sinners, as we said earlier in the opening of the epistle, on account of the praiseworthy ones he says as you are unleavened.

For indeed our Passover, Christ, was sacrificed. Seeing that according to the law of Moses the Passover comes first and the lamb is sacrificed, and then after the lamb they eat unleavened bread, for this reason he said Already the Passover, Christ, has been sacrificed.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. Of sincerity, in respect of conduct; of truth, in respect of knowledge; for in both of these the true unleavened bread is characterized.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Some have supposed from this saying that before the former letter to the Corinthians another letter had been written by the Apostle, one which is now not preserved; and that he wrote to them not to mix with fornicators so far as concerns the present wording, but that, having heard that the Corinthians were troubled, supposing it was said not to mix with fornicators nor with those of the world—which is impossible, that a man living in this life should not associate with heathen fellow-workers, tradesmen, and certain other such people—he clarifies, they say, what had then been left unsaid: I do not speak, he says, about the fornicators of this world, but about those who are indeed named brothers yet are not respectable. But those who do not wish there to have been another letter before this one will say that this wording refers to this very letter, namely, that "in this letter I wrote you not to mix with fornicators, and by fornicators I mean these, not those."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The carcass of a man, as we said above, we can say to be that which the Apostle says to the Corinthians: "I wrote", he says, "to you in the epistle that you should not mingle with fornicators; not indeed with the fornicators of this world, or the covetous, or the rapacious, or those serving idols; otherwise you would have had to go out of this world. But now I have written to you that you should not mingle, if anyone named a brother is a fornicator, or covetous, or serving idols, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or rapacious — with such a one not even to take food". This, therefore, is to touch the "carcass" of a man: for one to offer himself as a companion, even in food, to one who, having been made a man in Christ, has again died in his sins.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And not at all with the fornicators of this world or the covetous or robbers or idolaters. As there are fornicators of the world and fornicators who have been called to Christ, so also there are the covetous, some of this world and some of the Church. Let us therefore guard, down to the very least degree, against covetousness; for it too is yoked together with the sin of fornication. And thirdly he names certain robbers, when they seize what belongs to their neighbors. And there are also certain idolaters among us alongside the idolaters of this world, those who wish to teach that to commit idolatry is a matter of indifference; and this sin is found especially among those in military service: "Necessity," they say to me, "lies upon me"; the army demands this; I risk my head if I do not sacrifice, or if I do not, robed in white, place the incense according to the customs of the army of the world; and besides all this, such a man calls himself a Christian—with such a one, he says, not even to eat. There is also the God-denier in time of persecution, an idolater among us. I wrote therefore, he says, to such a one, who is not yet gone out of the world, not to mix, since then you would have to go out of the world. But now I wrote to you not to mix, if anyone is named a brother. Well did he say that such a one is no longer indeed a brother, but a brother only as far as the name.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The Apostle seems, by a comparison of fornicators, to say that the fornicators among us are far worse; for he who fornicates from outside does not corrupt the "temple of God", does not, taking away the "members of Christ", make them "members of a harlot", does not leaven the whole lump; and that one, when he wills, repents and has forgiveness of sins, but he who has fornicated after the faith, even if he afterward repents again, does not have forgiveness of sins, yet is able to cover over the sin. For "Blessed", he says, "are those whose sins were forgiven"—those who came from the nations; "and those whose sins were covered over"—those who sin after the faith but cover them over with good works, as for instance intemperance by much self-control.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But these things most of us can recognize in ourselves, that we do not have these evils; yet regarding what follows I fear even for myself, lest somehow I am liable to the other sins. For he says or a reviler or a drunkard or a robber—with such a one not even to eat. With how great evils did he number the reviler—with the fornicator, with the covetous, with the idolater; therefore the reviler too is already an enemy of the Church. For this reason we hear the Lord saying "Bless those who curse you", and the Apostle saying "Being reviled, we bless"; for a reviler "does not inherit the kingdom of God". One must therefore keep the mouth pure; for what is it to me to judge those outside? Let the drunkards be outside; shall I eat with fornicators and spend my time with them? Does their "little leaven" not harm me? Does it not "leaven this whole lump"?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Jesus alone was empowered to distinguish among the hearers His own from the outsiders, so as to speak to the outsiders in parables, but to explain the parables to those who entered with Him into the house. The outsiders and those who entered into the house have a mystical meaning. For "why should I judge outsiders?" Every sinner is an outsider. This is why the outsiders are addressed in parables: so that they might be able to leave the outer and enter the inner. Entering the house has a mysterious meaning: he who enters the house of Jesus becomes His true disciple.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He has permitted all of us to judge those within who sin. We ourselves refer the sin to the bishop, so that such a one may be lawfully cast out from the Church.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And from among these too put away the evil one; but consider, lest, while wishing to put away the evil one from outside, you have the evil one within yourself. Therefore do everything so that you may put away the evil one from yourself; for when he has gone out, Christ Jesus will dwell in you.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He shames those in Corinth who are sinning and busying themselves about law-courts and the affairs and hardships of this life, and he says: You were called for this purpose, that being made perfect you might judge angels; and shall you not rather be able, if ever a brother goes to law with a brother, to judge the things of this life of the brethren?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Truly, sometimes the matters of those going to law are such that they have no need of a wise man to judge them, but rather you set those who are least esteemed in the Church to judge; yet there might sometimes be matters of those at law such as to need even a wise judge. And what I mean will become clear in this way: if those at law have need of worldly laws and experienced judges — not of Scripture nor of the law that is in Scripture, but as it were of those who seem to be "more prudent sons of this age" — then those who are least esteemed in the Church will be trustworthy judges; and it will be a reproach to those at law when they have need even of the least esteemed rather than of the wise. For he who follows reason, even if he needs a judge, needs rather a wise one, so that he may be admonished by the wisdom of the wise man who brings to him words that build up.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He brings a charge against the Church of the Corinthians, that although they were seated in the midst of Greece they had no true wise men, and this though he had said before that many among them profess wisdom — on whose account also he said, "He who catches the wise in their craftiness". But some are wise men of this age, and others are wise according to God. And Paul knew those first ones; therefore he says, Is it so, that there is not among you a wise man who shall be able to give judgment between his brother?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: We have rulers of the Church to whom we ought to refer our judgments, that we may not be laughed at in the courts of the nations.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: not being mindful of the words Why do you not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded? Let us stand aloof from the judgments of the tribunals of the nations, from having lawsuits and disputes. For he who has lawsuits with a brother is already defeated, and he who is wronged has conquered; he who is struck and reviled and yet does not requite the one who does these things has conquered, for he keeps the commandment which says, Why do you not rather suffer wrong? Why do you not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Now everyone who does these things sins; but by so much as the person wronged is more honorable, by so much the graver is the sin. For indeed, if someone wrongs the blessed one, in effect he wrongs Christ and defrauds Christ.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: If the kingdom of God is in Christ, and Christ is "Righteousness", then the righteous man inherits the kingdom of God in Christ, who is "Righteousness"; and accordingly he who is in the opposite condition, this man does not inherit the kingdom of God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "Let no one deceive you" with plausible words: ‘God is merciful, kind, loving to men; he forgives sins.’ "We must all be made manifest before the judgment-seat of Christ, that each one may receive the things done through the body according to what he has done, whether good or evil". Let no one make the excuse: I was young, I was unmarried, before taking a wife I committed fornication. And why did you not take a wife? Do you not believe that "If anyone corrupts the temple of God, him will God corrupt"? But do you take the "members of Christ" and make them "members of a harlot"? He who commits fornication acts impiously against the God of all.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He who commits fornication corrupts the "temple of God"; but he who commits adultery, besides this, also offends against the husband. So neither adulterers; but neither the effeminate. We exhort you also, O children, to keep your own prime of life pure and not to be "defiled" with such womanish defilement. Neither shall those who lie with males inherit the kingdom of God; but far be it that even one such be found in the Church.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The Apostle set alongside these vile, dishonorable, and criminal deeds those transgressions which we most often acknowledge as insignificant. What then does he say? "Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor adulterers, nor effeminate men, nor sodomites, nor thieves, nor drunkards, nor revilers — shall inherit the Kingdom of God." You see that together with such grave malefactors as the sodomite, the effeminate man, the adulterer, the fornicator, he lists the drunkard and the reviler — sins which we all acknowledge to be insignificant — in order to teach us that it is not on account of grave sins alone that we are deprived of the Kingdom of God, but also on account of those which we customarily regard as less serious.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Then he descends also to the sins that seem to be lesser, saying Nor thieves; and this sin of theft nearly all who serve as soldiers commit, not "being content with their wages", as the Gospel taught, but "extorting by intimidation and bringing false accusation". But also those who are liars in their business dealings are thieves, not inheriting the kingdom of God; and so too those who take advantage in their business dealings are the covetous; and others are drunkards; but he says also that revilers do not inherit the kingdom of God. Let sin therefore "reign" over no one; for the kingdom of God must be pure from all sins and faults, that God may reign.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For the "reviler," not only against God but also against his neighbor, is by the sentence of the Apostle Paul excluded from the kingdom of God. For see how the Apostle says: "Do not err: neither fornicators nor adulterers nor the effeminate nor abusers of themselves with men nor thieves nor the covetous nor revilers shall possess the kingdom of God." See among what crimes—among "adulterers," among "abusers of themselves with men," among "the covetous," whom elsewhere he calls "servants of idols"—he has also placed "revilers" and has excluded them together with those from the kingdom of God. Let them see, then, if there are any who by an almost daily habit accustom their mouth to this vice, what peril hangs over them. For thinking this to be a slight and easy sin, they do not easily guard against it; but let them consider how the Apostle excludes the "reviler" from the kingdom of God, and how God through Moses commands the "reviler" to be punished.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: One must be above the things over which one has received authority; and even in doing these we shall not sin. For this is how those who conduct their lives more ambitiously conduct themselves. For, says the Apostle, "have we not authority to eat and to drink? have we not authority to take about with us a sister as wife, as also the rest of the apostles and the brethren of the Lord and Cephas? or is it I alone and Barnabas who have not authority to refrain from working?" But we did not use this authority. Therefore all these things were lawful for the Apostle in the passages I have cited; but examining them alongside his own profit and the stewardship of the Church, he saw that it is lawful—if he does it, he will not sin—yet he does better by not using the authority. And again: for every virgin it is lawful to be married; but the fair and good woman abstains from marrying, not as though marrying were not lawful, but having raised the authority higher and wishing to be pure both in "body and in spirit", she keeps her virginity. But also, when a husband has died, a second marriage is not altogether forbidden; for, he says, "If the husband die, she is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord". Yet the good woman, having heard the "she is more blessed if she so remain, according to my judgement", does not use the authority.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: All things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of anything: the saying has something more exalted in it. For if "our wrestling is not against blood and flesh but against the principalities or against the powers", then when the power prevails, I have been brought under the power of it; but if I conquer every power, I shall not be brought under the power of anything.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Do not think that, just as the belly came to be for foods and foods for the belly, so too the body came to be for the sake of sexual intercourse. If you wish to learn the primary purpose for which it came to be, listen: that it may be a temple for the Lord, and that the soul, being holy and blessed, ministering as it were to the Holy Spirit, may become a priest of the Holy Spirit that is within you. For Adam too had a body in paradise, yet even so, while in paradise itself, Adam did not know "Eve his wife", but only when he had been cast out after the disobedience. But I say these things not to circumscribe marriage; for I know that if anyone "does not exercise self-control", he ought to marry; for "it is better to marry than to burn". But even if the thing is conceded, it is not as a primary matter but on account of weakness. For the primary thing is to be chaste and pure and to "devote oneself to prayer".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For the body of one who has already been raised with Christ and has "become conformed to his resurrection and to the newness of life" ought to belong to none other than the Lord.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The bodies of human beings are instruments of the soul; and, the soul being the ruler, the body serves and is used by it for whatever it wishes. But in the proper sense the argument intends that our bodies should no longer be actuated by our own soul, but by Christ himself; therefore Paul says, "And it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me". They then become members of Christ when we move all things according to his word.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The soul of Jesus clung to God from the beginning of the creation in a union inseparable and indissoluble, as the soul of the wisdom and word of God, and of the truth and the true light. Receiving him wholly and itself entering into his light and splendor, it was made one spirit with him in a preeminent degree. This is what the apostle promises to those who imitate Jesus.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The Apostle says that the righteous man is one with Christ, but he is distinct from Christ: "And he who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit with Him." Is it not true that one of them has a lower nature, transient and fleeting, while the nature of Christ is more divine and glorious and blessed? And notwithstanding this, are they no longer two? Yes, for man and woman are no longer two, but one flesh, and the righteous man and Christ are one spirit. … When the righteous man cleaves to Christ, the fitting word is spirit. But when Christ is one with the Father, the fitting word is neither flesh nor spirit, but the more worthy one — God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "He who cleaves to the Lord becomes one spirit" with him. If, then, "he who is joined to the Lord", though he was natural, is by that very thing turned into a spiritual man and "is one spirit", let us too lose our soul, so that, cleaving to the Lord, we may be transformed into one spirit.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 36

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Someone will inquire whether every sin is outside the body. For someone will say: To be drunk is a sin; it is a sin to take oneself out of life by hanging, by a precipice — is then this sin also outside the body? But one must hear in a fair-minded way how this is said; and we shall take a starting-point for understanding the matters concerning this passage from Leviticus, for there it is said that "his body is composed out of the flux". Since, then, the composition of the body is from seeds, for this reason he who sins with respect to the flowing-forth of the seeds sins against his own body; and this sin is the one that comes about from those same things from which is also the beginning of the composition of the body.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Well did he, foreseeing an objection and guarding against it in advance, say You are not your own. For someone will say, I sin against my own body; I have authority over my own body. Then he says, Or do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit that is in you, which you have from God? We act impiously against the Holy Spirit, and through him against the Father and the Son — into whom we have been baptized — if we commit fornication: against Christ, when "taking the members of Christ I make them members of a harlot"; against the Holy Spirit, when one corrupts the temple of the Holy Spirit that is in us; against the Father, when I corrupt the "temple of God". Besides these things, then, however much we may sin — even if we commit murders, yet remain uncorrupted (ἄφθοροι), not having tasted the corruption (φθορά) that comes through intercourse — we are not said to have been corrupted from having committed murder. But since both incorruption (ἀφθαρσία) and corruption have to do with the nature that has not tasted the intercourse pertaining to sexual acts — for we say, 'The virgin has been corrupted,' and again, 'The young man is uncorrupted,' or 'has been corrupted' — every sin that a man may commit is outside the body. Since, then, the blood of Christ was given as a ransom for you and took you from the authority of the devil, glorify God in your body, so that your body may become worthy of blessedness, as belonging to those who have loved incorruption, as the Apostle also says: "the grace of God be with all those who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Human beings, when they sin, generally speaking sin in two ways: by falling short of the commandments or by overstepping them. For when we do not order our lives from knowledge, and go astray without knowing the measures of righteousness, and sometimes even by overstepping the rule, in the imagination of doing something better, we fall away from what is set before us. A "weight," then — which is neither "great" nor "small" but well-proportioned — is to know how one ought to live. You are bound together with a wife; you make one great weight, you take no thought for the wife but say, I am able to practice self-control and to live more purely; but see that your wife "perishes," being unable to bear your purity — she for whom "Christ died."

Something of this sort happened in Corinth, and there was disorder in the households of the brethren, in some cases the men and in others the women attempting to practice self-control and rising up against one another. So those in Corinth wrote a letter about this to the Apostle, and in reply to this letter the Apostle writes back the words set out above; and he neither pressed the teaching about chastity so as to do away with that about marriage, nor, preferring that about marriage, did he do away with that about virginity, being "a good steward," but throughout the whole discourse he keeps his purpose in a certain way and exhorts to be pure; and having conceded to make allowance, he exhorts again to practice chastity; and having exhorted to practice chastity, again he brings the matter round to the necessity of making allowance for the weakness of the weaker. And he began not from the inferior matters — for that would not have been fitting — but from the more perfect matters, saying Now concerning the things about which you wrote to me, it is good for a man not to touch a woman; as if to say: I praise you insofar as those who have withdrawn from intercourse with a wife have willed to be chaste, but consider "not your own" only, but also that of the wife; for "love does not seek its own"; therefore, because of the fornications, let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband. Let the stronger one have his own wife not because of his own fornication, but lest somehow the wife commit fornication through the self-control of the husband, or the husband through the self-control of the wife. For it is more desirable that the two be saved, being found in the works of marriage, than that, on the pretext of the one, the other should fall away from the hope that is in Christ; for how shall he even be saved, being guilty of the death of his wife? The dignity of the husband, then, is not pure when the discipline is not undertaken by both from the agreement of the wife, for the sake of devoting themselves to prayers according to God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Let the husband render to the wife the debt owed, and likewise also the wife to the husband. He took forethought both to heal human weakness and to arrange most decorously the matter concerning the local circumstances; wherefore he said that a debt is owed by the husband, and to the husband by the wife.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Then, so that he might not shame those in marriage, as being one another's slaves, he says that they should not come to the discipline of purity apart from agreement: The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; likewise also the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does. The husband, then, has authority over the body of the wife, and, having authority, if he wishes, let him not use the authority; but "we did not use this authority," says the Apostle, teaching this, I think, by saying, "Have we not authority to lead about a sister as a wife", as also the rest of the apostles and the brethren of the Lord and "Cephas"? Does the wife, then, have authority over the body of the husband, and yet cannot refrain from using the authority?

The word likewise, placed twice, gives us to understand that the husband must not think that in the matters concerning marriage he is superior to the wife; there is likeness and equality for those who are married toward one another.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The mysteries of marriage ought to be performed with holiness, deliberately and without disorderly passions.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For you both ought to know that the prayer which comes from the purity of a husband and wife is not the same as the prayer which comes from intercourse. For if even in the case of their idols the Greeks sometimes keep themselves chaste, how much more should you, who pray to the God of all things? It is good, then, to make allowance on account of weakness, but to abstain on account of prayers. And Moses too purifies the people and says, "For three days do not approach a woman," so that from having purified themselves beforehand they might be able to become hearers of God. And in the Books of Kingdoms, Abiathar — or Abimelech — the priest wishes to set "holy loaves" before David as he was fleeing the plot of Saul, and, wishing to set out the "holy loaves," what does he say except, "Are the young men pure from a woman?" — not, that is, from a strange woman, but from a wife. So then, in order that one may receive "loaves of the presentation", one ought to be pure from "a woman"; but in order that one may receive the loaves greater than those of the presentation, over which the name of God and of Christ and of the Holy Spirit has been invoked, ought one not to be far more pure, so that he may truly receive the loaves unto salvation and not "unto judgment"?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Most people suppose that to deprive is said only with reference to gold or silver or something of that kind; but the Apostle clearly named it deprivation also in the case of those who are in marriage and who practice chastity unseasonably and without agreement. And, quite simply, whoever does not render back what is owed deprives the one to whom he owes it, by not rendering what is owed. But sometimes a person is hemmed in so that he cannot render two debts at the same time; therefore it is written that he should render the necessary debt. And what I say will become clear thus: it is not possible for the married man both to render his prayers to God as he ought and to render the debt to his wife; therefore, if the debt toward God presses upon him, he must deprive the other. For listen to him saying, Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer, and again be together in the same place — inasmuch as the prayer sent up by those who have come together is not pure, even if they have come together lawfully. But one must abstain from a woman also at the time of her menstruation, and it is reckoned a great charge to come together with a woman who is in her menstruation. At any rate, in the catalogue of good deeds and in the catalogue of sins in Ezekiel it is recorded that "he shall not approach a woman in" her separation. And one must be altogether pure, even from one's own wife, at the time of prayer and fasting.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Everywhere he relaxes the word on account of weakness, and again he tightens it, in order to turn back those who hear the word.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Marriage breathes of a spiritual gift when the measures are kept — the gift that comes from agreement. And truly it may be said of certain people that for this one marriage is a spiritual gift, when there is no disorder, when there is all peace, all agreement. But to say that the marriage of a believer to a heathen woman, or of a heathen man to a believing woman, is a spiritual gift from God — this I would not say. For the spiritual gift of God cannot reach as far as the heathen; if she believes, if she is saved, then she will receive the beginning of the spiritual gift.

The followers of Marcion also use this saying, and senselessly they forbid marriage, saying that chastity is a command of the other god whom they have fabricated alongside the Creator. Yet from the saying itself one can bring them to admit that they wrongly forbid marriage, and wrongly too divide the Godhead. For if it is a spiritual gift to the one in this way and to the other in that, then marriage too is a spiritual gift; and if marriage too is a spiritual gift, then wrongly is the spiritual gift, marriage, forbidden; and if the one in this way and the other in that are from God, it is clear that one God is he who has given chastity and he who has given marriage, and one is the God of the Law and of the Gospel, whom the prophets proclaimed formerly and Christ Jesus later.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Some among us teach "beyond the things that are written"; and thinking that they are doing something—whereas they ought to exhort to monogamy without laying a "noose" upon those who are not able—this they do not do, but they impose a compulsion and wish not to gather in the twice-married nor to have fellowship with them, as with transgressors, having no shame even before the words of the Apostle. For he who says to the unmarried and to the widows, if they do not have self-control let them marry, plainly permitted, after the first marriage, after a woman has been widowed, that she marry—yet with a reproach of the man who marries, with a reproach of the woman who is married; for he said If they do not have self-control, let them marry; for consider whether the not having self-control is not already an accusation, such as it is for Christian people to be told It is better to marry than to burn, since he named as burning "the desire of the flesh" not quenched by the word but prevailing over the soul of the sinner.

We, therefore, having been taught by the Apostle, do not forbid the twice-married state, for in comparison with burning the twice-married state is the more choiceworthy; but when a thing that is compared with evils is reckoned to be better, that thing plainly is not good. The second marriage is not chastity; it is not according to nature as with Adam the first-formed, for it cannot be said to the second wife "This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh." Abraham had Hagar as well, and he was also with Keturah; but when he died, none was laid with him but the wife by nature; for Abraham and Sarah were in the tomb. And Jacob too, though he was with Rachel and with Leah and was also with the maidservants, yet in the tomb Leah alone was with him.

With the being of a mystical dispensation of the fathers; yet surely not even now does the man who takes a second wife say that "I am accomplishing a mystical dispensation." For Paul will come saying "tell me, you who read the law, do you not hear the law?" for it is written "Such-and-such a one had two sons", and what follows; is it not going to be said of him too "Which things are allegorized", and "for these are two covenants"; "for these things happened to them figuratively, and were written" for our sake "upon whom the ends of the ages have arrived."

But I say to the widows and to the unmarried, it is good for them if they remain as I also am. This is a second good; for there is another good prior to this: it is good for a man not to touch a woman. What is the second good? It is good for them if they remain as I also am; but if they do not have self-control, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn. For this reason let those who are in first marriages and have not yet made trial of second ones practice purity, so that, if anything human should happen, they may not, being caught untrained, behave disgracefully. It is better, then, to marry a second marriage—for he does not speak here of the first, as is clear from the word to burn.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
From here he passes over to another legislation: But to those who have married I charge—not I, but the Lord: the legislation directed to those who have married is not from me, but from the Lord. And at the same time he keeps a necessary observation, that he named as "those who have married" the case when both are believers, both the husband and the wife. And that he did not name among "those who have married" the others, as many as "are unequally yoked", is clear from his adding But to the rest I say, not the Lord. Are the rest, then, not married? For he does not count them as married; for in their case a wife is not joined to a husband by God; but in the case of believers, when both share both in prayers and in holy begetting of children and in all things in which Christians must share, he says that marriage is not alien to God.

I charge, then—not I, but the Lord—that a wife not be separated from her husband. The chief point is this: that a conjugal union already formed, "being bound, is not to be loosed".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But if she is indeed separated: for many things might become causes even of being separated; for instance, if fornication should occur in the wife, it is a sin to retain the wife who has committed fornication. If, then, she is indeed separated and some cause of separation should occur, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband. And likewise I wish the husband too to be such a one, that he not put away his wife.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But to the rest I say, not the Lord. To those who have married it is not I who legislate, but the Lord; but to those who have not married but "are unequally yoked" with unbelievers I have no law to give from God; for they are not even worthy of the laws of God; but let them hear us. And I will make use, for the understanding of the matters relating to this place, of things written in the law. The laws according to Moses—some are God's, and some are Moses'. And knowing this, the Lord, in marking a difference between laws of God and laws of Moses, said, concerning the things legislated by God, "For God" he said "Honor your father and your mother", but concerning the things by Moses, "Moses, because of your hardness of heart, permitted you to put away your wives." At any rate, if you attend to the matters of the "book" of "divorcement", you will find the law written not from a command of the Lord. Moses, then, serving God, gave secondary laws beside the laws of God; and Paul, serving the gospel, gave secondary laws to the men of the Church after the laws that are from God through Jesus Christ. And it is good to hear laws from the Lord rather than to hear laws of Paul the apostle. For even if he is holy, yet he has laws far inferior to the laws of the Lord.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: As a kind of mixture comes to be of the two, husband and wife, "into one flesh," just as of wine and water; and just as the believer imparts sanctification to the Gentile spouse, or conversely the believing wife to the unbelieving husband, so also the unbeliever imparts defilement to the believing wife, or the unbelieving wife to the believing husband. For why does he say The unbelieving wife or the unbelieving husband has been sanctified by receiving something from the believer, whether man or woman, and is not profaned by receiving something from the unbelieving party? For each one, conversing with the other out of "the abundance of the heart," either imparts or receives, and in time altogether the one prevails over the other. And what need is there, he says, of such a struggle and such danger? For either he will succeed or he will fail, and either he will lose his own soul besides, or, after much labor, he will scarcely be able to gain.
