For this reason it is good, before a person is caught unawares, carefully to consider not only this present matter but also what is to come, and, having considered, either not to marry or, if marrying, to marry "in the Lord." For "a wife is bound for as long a time as the husband lives; but if" the husband "dies, she is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord." We do not hear the "only in the Lord," but we read the "she is free to be married to whom she wishes," while we no longer join to it the "only in the Lord." And yet there too, when he had said "only in the Lord," he again checked the statement by saying "but she is more blessed if she so remains, according to my judgment." Therefore the Apostle, having spoken the more auspicious word, the For she is sanctified, left it to us to understand the other.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
It will seem that he has inserted this out of season into the discourse concerning marriage and chastity, since no inquiry had arisen about the fact that believers from circumcision ought not to remove the marks of circumcision, and again that those in uncircumcision ought not to be circumcised, together with the matter concerning "Wast thou called a slave?" "Let it not concern thee", and what follows. Perhaps, then, he took slavery and freedom as an illustration of the married and the unmarried, calling circumcised the man who has cast off his wife, and uncircumcised the man who has married? For as "the two shall be one flesh" and the woman and the man are one flesh, and the circumcised man has cast off what belongs to the flesh, so too the man who has cast off his wife has, as it were, circumcised his own flesh; so also he calls him a slave. For since he says also in other places "the brother or the sister is not enslaved in such cases", as though the married were slaves, for this reason here too he names a slave the one called after marriage, and free the unmarried.

So then the things said upon this passage are spoken as concerning circumcision and concerning slaves. Nevertheless it is not out of place at times to use the text against those who think that after coming to faith one ought to be circumcised out of scrupulousness—a scrupulousness that is "not according to knowledge"—because of the things written in the Old Testament concerning circumcision. Again, is it not fitting, on account of certain believers from circumcision who think that circumcision brings shame upon them and who wish to draw uncircumcision over themselves, to use the text which says Was anyone called circumcised? Let him not remove the marks of circumcision? And indeed it stands to reason to say to such people that, taken in itself, circumcision is an indifferent matter. So the present passage is neither about circumcision nor about uncircumcision, but about the unmarried and the married man. Was anyone called circumcised? Let him not remove the marks of circumcision—as though he said, Let him not draw a wife to himself; he has already been circumcised, he has cast off a wife; let him not marry another. Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised—that is: Wast thou called in marriage? Do not cast off thy wife. Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing. Since some think that the unmarried man has in this respect something more than the married, and that the married has something less than the unmarried by the very fact of being married, we wish, he says, to teach that in its own account celibacy is indifferent, and in its own account marriage is indifferent. For it is possible that a man who is unmarried and truly keeps himself pure from all intercourse, but who otherwise lives badly, should derive no benefit from his celibacy; and it is possible that someone, though in marriage and doing the things of marriage, yet doing them in due order and in due season, and preserving the rest of his manner of life, should be no less than the unmarried. For that celibacy, and purity itself, are indifferent, we shall demonstrate thus. If only those of the Church practiced celibacy, one might say that celibacy in its own account is something pure and divine; but as it is, one can find people unmarried even with a wicked purpose. The followers of Marcion, at any rate, themselves also practice celibacy and purity, but not as those of the Church do; for the latter do so in order to please the God who created the world, whereas the former do so in order not to cooperate with the God of the world. But celibacy is adorned by a churchly life and doctrine, by pure knowledge and by truth. So too the unmarried man is indifferent in his own account; and it is possible, even while being in marriage, to be blameless, as we have already shown above. Circumcision therefore is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, both according to the literal text and according to the matters set before us. But what is it that saves? The keeping of God's commandments. For everyone "who shall loose one of these least commandments and shall teach men so"—he did not say "He shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven", but "he shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven." And if the one who has loosed "one of the least commandments shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven", where shall the one who has loosed two commandments be found? Let each one, therefore, in the calling in which he was called, in this remain. Wast thou called in marriage? Do not envy the unmarried. Wast thou called unmarried? By no means draw a wife to thyself, if thou art able to live more purely.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: I am a slave of that affair and care to which I am bound. For I know that it is written that whatever one is conquered by, to that he is delivered as a slave.… Who will free me from this most unseemly slavery except him who said, "If the Son shall make you free, you shall be free indeed".?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He necessarily called the married man a slave; for the husband is a slave of the wife, not having authority "over his own body", and the wife of the husband; for "she does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does". Were you then called as a slave? Let it not concern you; but even if you can become free, rather make use of it; that is, if you do not transgress the law according to reason, you can be free; how? "by agreement", so that "you may devote yourselves to prayer" with all concord.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For the one who was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord's freedman; as, for instance: Were you called as a slave? Know this, that not only are you not a slave, but you also have something of freedom through the Lord. For the freedman is neither purely free nor any longer a slave, so that the pure man is in every way free, but the man in marriage is a slave; yet when he is a slave in the Lord, then we say that he is the Lord's freedman. And the one called as free is a slave — not of a wife, but of the word of God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And it is certain, they say, that each one buys that which is not his own; for the Apostle says: "you were bought with a price." But hear what the prophet says: "By your sins you were sold, and for your iniquities I dismissed your mother." You see, then, that we are indeed all the creature of God, but each one is sold by his own sins and for his own iniquities departs from his own creator. We are, therefore, God's, according as we were created by him; but we became slaves of the devil, according as we were sold by our sins. But Christ, coming, "redeemed us," while we were serving that lord to whom we had sold our very selves by sinning. And so he seems to have received back as his own those whom he had created, but to have acquired as aliens those who by sinning had sought for themselves an alien lord.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men. As far as your power allows, understand the Word of God who "bought us out"; let us propitiate "the blood that was poured out" for us. We were saying, in the discourse concerning the unmarried and the married, that he tightens and slackens his argument. So here too he has done, saying Do not become slaves of men; for, as it were, he tightens and makes his argument more vehement, urging on those who are able, so far as possible, to keep themselves pure, and urging each one to keep himself pure in the calling in which he was called.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: It should be known that the rest of the interpreters have rendered the sense concerning uncircumcision and circumcision according to the literal wording; for customarily, they say, he passes over from the subject at hand to other matters, laying down for all what is fitting.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Of the commandments, some are enjoined, but others are not enjoined but are left to free choice and entrusted by God to the will. For some of them, without which one cannot be saved, are the ones that are ordained; but those that are greater than the ordained ones, which even if we do not perform them we are saved, are not a command of God. For hear, he says, the gospel of Jesus Christ teaching in him and saying, "When you have done all the things ordained for you, you ought to say, We are unprofitable servants, we have done what we ought to do." And if, when I have done all the things ordained, I am an unprofitable servant, when shall I escape being an unprofitable servant? If, being more zealous for honor, you ascend beyond the things ordained; for example: If I keep the "you shall not commit adultery" and the not looking "at a woman so as to desire her," I have done what I ought to do. But if I remain a virgin, not being ordered nor ordained to do so, I no longer say, concerning the right achievement of virginity, "We are unprofitable servants, we have done what we ought to do." So also with the rest of the commandments: if I do not steal or defraud, we ought to say, "we are unprofitable servants." But if I sell all my possessions and give to the poor, I no longer say, "I am unprofitable," I have done what I ought to do. Therefore the Apostle says, Now concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give my opinion as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord to be faithful. For when the Lord says to the disciples, "Not all receive this saying, but those to whom it has been given," he also adds, "Let him who is able to receive it receive it"; he did not command, but left it to free choice. Therefore, says the Apostle, I give my opinion, and in order to establish that the Lord speaks in him, he said, as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord to be faithful.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: By necessity he means the sojourn in the body, as also elsewhere he says, "but to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake." Four times in this passage the Apostle named the "good": for first he says, "it is good for a man not to touch a woman;" second, "it is good for them if they remain as I also am;" third, I think therefore that this is good because of the present necessity; fourth, It is good for a man to be so. You see, whatever has been said concerning chastity, these things have been named together with the good; but whatever concerns marriage, together with the one who marries not sinning.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Throughout the whole passage, as has been said, he tightens and relaxes, so that the hearer, taking it into his own authority, may judge whether he is able to do anything and to what discipline he may be able to give himself. So then here also he turned him away from dissolving the marriage, but again exhorts him to be pure. Accordingly he called the man who has married bound; and if to be bound is a circumstance, one must also flee such circumstances as far as one is able. And the being bound to a woman—do not seek to dissolve it; but he who is not bound ought to guard himself lest he be bound; for truly you will find them bound by the marital love-charm. It is not permitted, therefore, for one who has been caught beforehand in marriage to seek untimely freedom, but to remain in the servitude; and if one is released, not to seek a woman.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But if you also marry, he says, you have not sinned. He did not say, If you marry, it is good; but, If you marry, you have not sinned; observe the difference. And if the virgin marries, she has not sinned; again he did not say, Good, but, she has not sinned.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For how will they not have tribulation when the things said to the woman come upon her who has married: "In pains you shall bear children, and toward your husband shall be your turning, and he shall rule over you." But from all these the virgin is free, freed by purity, awaiting the bridegroom of blessing. Every marriage takes place in darkness, wherefore not "in chamberings and licentiousness"; but the marriage of Christ, when he receives back his Church for himself, takes place in the light. For why do the virgins enter into the marriage with lamps and oil that lasts? Because that marriage is one of seemliness. He who "cleaves" to flesh "is one body"; but he who "cleaves" to spirit "is one spirit." And what is more seemly than a soul cleaving to the spirit and being united to it, and no longer being a soul but becoming that which the spirit is? For concerning marriage it is said, "the two shall be one flesh;" but concerning the other, "he who cleaves to the Lord shall be one spirit."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But that man has made an "idol" who, according to the Apostle who says that "an idol is nothing", makes what is not. And what is it that is not? A shape which the eye has not seen, but which the mind itself fashions for itself. For example's sake: as if one should form, upon human limbs, the head of a dog or of a ram, or again should fashion two faces on one human form, or join to a human breast the hinder parts of a horse or of a fish. He who makes these things and things like them makes not a likeness, but an idol. For he makes what is not, nor has it anything like itself. And therefore, knowing this, the Apostle says: "for an idol is nothing in the world"; for the shape is not taken from any of the things that exist, but is what the idle and curious mind has itself devised for itself.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: From this, I think, the Apostle Paul also took what he writes to the Corinthians, saying: "for even if there are those that are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth". And he adds: "as indeed there are many gods and many lords, but for us there is one God the Father, from whom are all things and we unto him, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
As a God-fearing soldier the Apostle says Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense?; but as one entrusted with God's "tillage" and tilling the Church, Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit?; and as a disciple of the good shepherd, who also laid down "his life for the sheep," Who tends a flock and does not eat of the milk of the flock? And as a soldier he teaches us too to serve as soldiers, saying, "No one serving as a soldier entangles himself in the affairs of this life, that he may please the one who enlisted him"; and as a farmer he teaches us too to farm: "I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase." And concerning shepherds the prophets have taught us, recounting the rewards of the good ones and announcing the punishments of those who shepherd otherwise.

And it will seem, to one who does not attend to the Scripture, that the Apostle has through these things forgotten the matter before him; but the truth is not so — rather, he keeps to his argument. It is set before him to teach concerning things sacrificed to idols, so that even if someone who professes to have knowledge should assert that he takes no harm from the use of things sacrificed to idols, yet becomes the cause of harm to others, he ought to have taken thought for his neighbor, lest through his pretext others perish; to this end he takes up the examples and says: Not necessarily, if we have authority over something, "ought we to make full use of the authority." For if he is a soldier, he does not serve as a soldier so as to gain nothing for himself from the wages; if a farmer, he is not content with his wage but eats of the cluster; if a shepherd, along with his wage he partakes of the milk. So I too ought, besides the promises laid up for me from having served well as a soldier or farmed or shepherded, to partake in this world of the things needful from the soldiers under me, from those farmed, from those shepherded. But nevertheless, even if I have authority over the things needful, looking to the edification of men I do not make full use of the authority, taking care not to give any hindrance "to the gospel of Christ," or even to give a pretext to those "who walk disorderly and do nothing but are busybodies." As therefore I do not use the authority which I received from the word, in the same manner you also who claim to be wise ought not to use the authority but to provide for the edification of your neighbors. And if the argument is thought by some to be without witness and to be spoken according to human reasoning, let him hear the law saying, "You shall not muzzle an ox that treads out the grain," and what follows.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: God's care was not only for the oxen but moreso for the apostles, for whose sake he uttered these words.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Therefore these things have been said for our sake, who have received the new covenant, and it is written concerning men, the letter being understood spiritually according to the divine Apostle. But what is the sense? That the plower ought to plow in hope, and the thresher to partake in hope. Paul the farmer plows the soul of a catechumen, making "new-broken ground" in his soul according to the divine Jeremiah, who declares to them, "Break up for yourselves fresh ground" — with a view, clearly, to the reception of seeds, concerning which it is written, "The sower went out to sow." And after sowing the new-broken ground, I watch over, he says, the seeds, lest "the birds" of heaven, "coming," carry off the seed; and when it bears fruit and produces fruits of righteousness, and when it is "already white for harvest," then at last it is permitted to me to take. For he will not be made to stumble whenever he remembers all that I have toiled, that I might plow his soul, that I might sow, how I persevered until his crop came, brought to completion, upon the threshing floor. And for this reason it is permitted to me to receive food from him. But I do not by all means make use of the authority; rather, I do this in hope, to present the produce to the master of the house — for I am a farmer — not that I may take into my own storehouses the things that are owed to be rendered to God. Then the Apostle, teaching something concerning the same matter, says, If we sowed spiritual things for you, is it a great matter? and what follows.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "For it is better for me to die" than that they should snatch and plunder any of my brothers and, by the clever theft of words, lead away captive "the little ones" and those still nursing in Christ.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
But if, on account of that which is written, that such a one is sent "into the outer darkness", what is said displeases you — if on account of the fact that someone did not teach he is judged as one who did not use the capacity given to him for the profiting of souls — recall the apostolic saying which says: "for woe is me if I shall not have preached the Gospel".

For not on account of any other blameworthy conduct of his, but on account of this alone, if he shall not have preached the Gospel, does he confess that woe will be to him. For it manifestly appears that that man expected to hear: "wicked and slothful servant", and the rest, unless he had preached the Gospel, although the other things of his life had been upright.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: We are taught that whatever we do out of necessity has no boasting; but whatever we do by choice, when no necessity is laid upon us, this has boasting. For example: the one who does not commit adultery or murder does not have boasting, but the one who keeps virginity does; for he came to virginity not out of necessity but from choice. But where the Woe lies alongside it if I do not act, I have no boasting. For this reason he says, If I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship. Again we are taught a general point. Some things we do willingly, with the whole soul; but some things we do indeed, yet not willingly, nor even with the whole soul, but out of grief or out of necessity. For of the things done by us voluntarily there is a reward; but of the things that are done indeed, yet as out of grief, there is neither reward nor punishment. For example: I give alms; if willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I am not charged along with those who hear, "I was hungry and you did not give me to eat" and what follows. This, then, is the reward: that where I have the liberty [to act], I should not do it.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: What then shall I do, to whom the dispensation of the word has been entrusted? Though I am an "unprofitable servant," I have nevertheless received from the Lord "the measure of wheat to be distributed to the Lord's household."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: To be free from all things belongs to a perfect apostle. For someone can be free from fornication but a slave to anger, free from love of money but a slave to vainglory; he can be free from one sin, but a slave to another sin. But to say Being free from all belongs to a perfect apostle; such as Paul was.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And according to the passage before us it has this sense: I became to the Jews as a Jew, that I might gain Jews. For being free from Judaism, I enslaved myself to Jews, that I might gain Jews; being free from being under the law I made myself as under the law, that I might gain those under the law. For Paul condescended to go into the synagogues of the Jews, he entered in among them, he acted according to their customs without harm, not playing the hypocrite along with them but hunting for some of them.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Some have inquired what the difference is between those under the law and the Jews; we say, then, that those under the law are others than the Jews, like the Samaritans.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: To those without the law as without the law: he came to Athens; he found philosophers there; he used neither prophetic words nor legal ones, but if anywhere there was some Greek learning from his prior education, being reminded of this he would say to the Athenians; for he says, "As also some of the poets among you have said, For we too are his offspring." There to those without the law he became as without the law, that he might gain those without the law. And again he says, "Passing through and observing your objects of worship, I found also an altar on which was inscribed, To an Unknown God. Whom therefore you worship in ignorance, this one I proclaim to you." And through these words he begins to hand down reverence for God. To those without the law, then, as without the law, not being without law to God. Not by condescending to them did I commit any lawlessness, but I kept myself under the law of Christ, that I might gain those without the law. And at the same time he also preserves his precision: I became to the Jews as a Jew; he did not say here, Not being a Jew. For he was a Jew in secret, no longer in the open. And again, To those under the law as under the law, not being myself under the law; necessarily here he placed the Not being under the law; "For Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us;" as if he had said, Not being a Samaritan.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But to those without the law as without the law, not being without law to God. But someone will suppose that I have become an apostate from the law and lawless to God; but I say that even if I do not keep the law according to the letter, I am not lawless to God, but I am under the law of Christ, keeping the way of life that is according to the gospel, that I might gain those without the law.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: I became to the weak as weak; he did not say here, Not being myself weak; for that would have been boastful, it would have been arrogant, it was not for the apostle to say, Not being myself weak—he who had heard from the Lord that "my power is perfected in weakness" and on account of this "boasted in weaknesses". But how weak to the weak? When he permits those who burn to marry, when he suffers together with the women who have lost their husbands, when he says, "But because of fornications let each man have his own wife and let each woman have her own husband" and the rest. In these things he became weak to the weak, that he might gain the weak.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Then after these things he says, To all I have become all things, that I might save all or some. Whatever man you take, he is one of five; for either he is a Jew, or under the law, or without the law, or weak, or he is all things. The perfect man is all things; to all, then—that is, to the perfect—I became perfect, that I might gain all. For "We speak wisdom" he says "among the perfect" and what follows. This man can say, "To Greeks and to barbarians, to the wise and to the foolish, I am a debtor."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Only the perfect man can speak the utterance of the perfect apostle in the Lord, the I do all things for the sake of the gospel. For the one who sins cannot say this. And if the one who does all things for the sake of the gospel is a partner of the gospel, while the one who commits fornication is a partner of the fornication of the spirit, likewise also with the other passions. Each one, then, becomes a partner of that in which he has partaken. But one of the hearers will say, My life is mixed; I neither do all things for the sake of the gospel, nor do all things on account of sin and pleasure. To this we will say, These things God has as his judgments; according to the many judgments he renders varied things.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Do we then all run, and one receives the prize, while the rest of us perish? For he said that the one receiving the prize is one, though many run. All who are being saved "are one, and one body;" for "we all are one bread and partake of the same bread, and you all are the body of Christ." Therefore, of all who are being saved, the one receiving the prize is one. In the stadium, then, all run, as many as order their life toward a doctrine; and those from the heresies order their life toward a doctrine, and perhaps the Jews too, and those who, philosophizing in the manner of the Greeks, order their life toward a doctrine. And all these are those who run in the stadium; the Church also runs; but one receives the prize, the one man, concerning whom the Apostle says "Until we attain to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ." And every judgment of God must be found concerning all who run in the stadium, so that one may receive the first place, and thereafter each according to his own worth.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But he who is not yet perfect doubts concerning himself, as though he too could fall; according to which human weakness Paul, writing to the Corinthians, said: "but I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, having preached to others, I myself be made reprobate". And see: what he says, "lest perhaps, having preached to others, I myself be made reprobate", he so pronounces as one fearing, lest perhaps he too could both fall and become reprobate; but what he said, "I am confident that neither death nor life" and the rest, is of a confident and firm man on account of his perfection, since a thousand contrary things have not the strength to separate him "from the love of Christ". And to such as these it is not unfitting to say always: "do not glory in the Lord, for you do not know what the coming day may bring forth". But recalling all these things, that we do not know "what the coming day may bring forth" for us, we shall not be puffed up, nor be proud, nor ever glory, although we know that we have many good things.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "The teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth," the Apostle Paul, handed down to the Church which he gathered from among the Gentiles how it ought to attend to the books of the Law, which it had received from others and which had formerly been unknown to it and altogether foreign, lest, in taking up institutions foreign to it and being ignorant of the rule of those institutions, it should tremble amid an alien instrument. Therefore he himself, in a number of passages, hands down examples of the understanding, so that we too may observe things similar in the rest, lest perchance, on account of the likeness of the reading and of the instrument of the Jews, we should believe that we have been made their disciples. This, then, is what he wishes to distinguish between the disciples of Christ and the disciples of the synagogue: that the Law which they, by understanding it badly, did not receive Christ, we, by understanding it spiritually, may show to have been rightly given for the instruction of the Church. The Jews, then, understand only this: that "the children of Israel departed" from Egypt, and that their first departure was "from Rameses," and that departing thence they came "to Succoth," and that "departing from Succoth" they came "to Othon" by Epauleum near the sea; then, further, that there the cloud went before them and that "the rock" followed, from which they drank water, and that they also passed through the Red Sea and came into the desert of Sinai. But let us see what rule of understanding concerning these things Paul the Apostle has handed down to us. Writing to the Corinthians, he says in a certain place thus: "For we know that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank of the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ." You see how much Paul's tradition differs from the historical reading: what the Jews think a crossing of the sea, Paul calls baptism; what they reckon a cloud, Paul sets down as the Holy Spirit; and he wishes that to be understood as like this which the Lord commanded in the Gospels, saying: "unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdoms of heaven." And again the manna, which the Jews reckon food for the belly and satiety for the gullet, Paul names "spiritual food." And not only Paul, but the Lord Himself in the Gospel says concerning the same thing: "your fathers ate manna in the desert, and they died. But whoever shall eat of the bread which I give him shall not die for ever." And after this He says: "I am the bread which came down from heaven." Then, further, concerning "the rock that followed" Paul openly declares and says: "and the rock was Christ." What, then, must we do, who have received from Paul, the teacher of the Church, institutions of understanding of this kind? Does it not seem just that we should keep the rule of this kind handed down to us by a like example in the rest? Or shall we, as certain people wish, forsaking these things which so great and such an Apostle handed down, turn back again to "Jewish fables"? For my part, if I should expound these things otherwise than as they seem to Paul, I think this is to give a hand to the enemies of Christ, and this is what the prophet says: "Woe to him who gives his neighbor to drink with turbulent overthrow!" Having therefore received from the blessed Apostle Paul the seeds of spiritual understanding, let us cultivate them, insofar as the Lord shall deign to enlighten us through your prayers.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The Apostle wishes to set before us that it is not the mere obtaining of a gift of God that saves the one who has obtained it, but, along with the obtaining of the gift, to abide in it, having become worthy of it. For indeed the sons of Israel, though they had received so many benefits, since they did not become worthy of the benefaction of God, were not saved. For God was not well pleased with the greater part of them; "for they were laid low in the wilderness." For indeed, since the sinners were the more numerous and the righteous the fewer, on that account God was not well pleased with the greater part, the sinners, over against the few righteous.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Now these things, he says, became types of us, that we should not be desirers of evil things, as they also desired. Those things were written figuratively for us, so that we, reading of the sins on account of which those people suffered these things, may guard ourselves against falling into the same desires as they did.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Many do not bear it but are conquered by temptation. What God gives us is not the certainty that we shall bear it but the possibility that we may be made able to bear it.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: In the Apostle also it is written: "Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?" And where we have "we provoke the Lord to jealousy", in certain copies it is written "we provoke the Lord". In that passage he said these things where he disputes about sacrifices and about the things offered to idols. "Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy", he says, that is, do we rouse him to zeal by eating the things offered to idols, just as the Jews stirred his zeal in their idols? Do we too wish to act in a like manner? Therefore he says: "Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?" This is what he means. If indeed we rouse to jealousy someone who is inferior to us in strength, we can easily despise him; but if we rouse a strong one to jealousy, are we not contriving these things unto our own ruin? If therefore we feed on things offered to idols, and rouse the Lord's zeal against us, we provoke a stronger wrath against us, that is, unto our own destruction.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But the eyes of the wise man, of which it is said that they are enlightened by the commandments of God, are in his head, in Christ, because "the head of the man is Christ," says the Apostle. The capacity to think proceeds from Christ.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "He shall not" it says "take the mitre from his head". We have already said before that the "mitre" is a kind of covering which, set upon the head, affords adornment to the high priest. This "great high priest" of mine therefore never lays aside the adornment of his sacred head. But what the "head of Christ" is, learn from the Apostle, who says: "but the head of Christ is God". Rightly therefore he never lays aside this adornment of his head, which is "God", because "the Father is" always "in the Son, as the Son" is always "in the Father".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Here then we see the just judgment of God's providence, that diversity of conduct is taken into account and that each is treated according to the deserts of his departure and defection from goodness.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: When your soul is sick, and is pressed by the sicknesses of sins, are you untroubled, do you make little of Gehenna, and despise and mock the punishments of eternal fire? Do you make light of the judgment of God, and despise the Church that admonishes you? Do you not fear to communicate the body of Christ, approaching to the Eucharist as though clean and pure, as though there were nothing in you unworthy, and in all these things think that you escape the judgment of God? Do you not recall that which is written, that "For this cause many among you are weak, and sick, and many sleep"? Why are many weak? Because they do not judge themselves, nor examine themselves, nor understand what it is to communicate with the Church, or what it is to approach to such and so exceptional sacraments. They suffer that which the feverish are wont to suffer, when they take beforehand the foods of the healthy, bringing destruction upon themselves.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
There are many differences among spirits, which no one will know with precision unless he has the gift of the discernment of the spirit. And so that we may not too rashly either reject the spirits that are in those who speak, or approve them, John says in his epistle: "Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are from God; every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ having come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God." And he teaches us, whenever we hear people speaking, neither to assent haphazardly nor rashly to deny the things spoken as though they were not from a divine spirit, but so that each of the hearers, knowing that he stands in danger in the very act of approving or rejecting, may attend carefully neither to believe the false nor to disbelieve the true.

Concerning this the Apostle also adds, next after these words: "If anyone among you is a prophet or spiritual, let him recognize that the things I write are of God; but if anyone is ignorant, he is ignored." Not only, then, is the one who is ignorant of the Apostle's words ignored by God, but also, if anyone is ignorant—speaking by a divine spirit and yet saying that he does not speak by a divine spirit—he is ignored by God. And through these words the Apostle seems to teach that there is no man who does not have another spirit in him besides the spirit of the man that is in him. For whether he is a stranger to the faith or belongs to it, he has a spirit of his own from God. But how we who hear the divine word need to learn that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says "Anathema to Jesus," let us see. Some can be a matter of doubt, to those who do not accurately know the facts, as to whether they speak in the Spirit of God or not, while anathematizing Jesus. If ever you should behold some Jew expounding the divine scriptures and setting forth prophetic sayings to the multitude in no contemptible fashion, perhaps one would doubt whether perhaps the Spirit of God is also in that man. Therefore, so that you may not be thrown into perplexity over such a person, whether the Holy Spirit is in him or not, he teaches that, since every Jew says "Anathema" to Jesus, and no one speaking in the Spirit of God says "Anathema to Jesus," the one who claims to know the law and the prophets but anathematizes Jesus does not have the Spirit of God. There is a certain heresy which does not receive the one who approaches unless he anathematizes Jesus. And that heresy is worthy of the name which it has loved; for it is the heresy of those called Ophians, who say unlawful things in praise of the serpent, which is "accursed" by God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: There he has rather kept the discourse in order, but here he proceeds as if at random and mentions the spiritual gifts according to what has come to his mind; nevertheless even so, from the second saying he declares that the gifts effected among the powers are less than the gift that is according to apostleship and prophecy and teaching — unless indeed someone should grant two kinds of prophecy, so that here too he may keep the order preserved, so that there is a certain prophecy that has surpassed and a certain prophecy that has risen up. For the more universal one, which imitates the prophecies of Isaiah and Jeremiah, he will call the second rank after apostleship, but this other one, ranked in the last place after the gifts that have been mentioned, is of such a kind: "And if" you should prophesy, "and there come in someone unbelieving or unlearned, he is reproved by all, he is examined by all, the hidden things of his heart become manifest, and thus, falling upon his face, he will worship God and declare that God is truly among you". For this is not far from the "working of powers" and the "gift of healings" which come to pass for the astonishment of those who behold, so that the one prophesying may say: This you have in your heart; From this sin you have come to the Church. And this prophecy itself can be later in rank than the former things, while that more divine and greater one is second, concerning which he says: God appointed in the Church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers. For the establishing of the point that two things are signified by the name of prophecy, I set forth beforehand the things aforesaid which I stated. See whether I am still able to set out more clearly what is said: God appointed in the Church first apostles; but not all are apostles, for if all are apostles, to whom is the apostleship ministered? Second prophets; not all are prophets; but according to the other prophecy, "if all" you should prophesy, "and there come in an unbeliever or an unlearned person", not as though it were impossible but as being possible for all to prophesy in this way. There are, therefore, two things signified by the name of prophecy. Wherefore here too the order has been preserved by the Apostle, which says first apostles, second prophets and what follows. These things, then, are said concerning the order, since the phrase and to another prophecy, ranked last in another passage, seemed to press upon us.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Whence it seems to me to be no small grace to discern the mouth which the devil opens. It is not without the grace of the Holy Spirit to distinguish a mouth of this kind and its words; and therefore in the distribution of spiritual graces this too is added, that to some is given "the discernment of spirits". It is therefore a spiritual grace by which the spirit is discerned, as also elsewhere the Apostle says: "test the spirits, whether they be of God".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For there is "one body" which is awaited to be justified; there is "one body" which is said to rise again in the judgment. "For although there are many members, yet one body; the eye cannot say to the hand: I have no need of you". Even if the eye be sound and not troubled, as far as pertains to seeing, if the remaining members are lacking to it, what gladness will there be for the eye? Or what perfection will it be seen to have, if it has not a hand, if the feet are lacking or the remaining members are not present? For even if there is some surpassing glory of the eye, it is chiefly in this, that either it itself be the guide of the body, or it not be forsaken by the offices of the other members.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: There he has rather kept the discourse in order, but here he proceeds as if at random and mentions the spiritual gifts according to what has come to his mind; nevertheless even so, from the second saying he declares that the gifts effected among the powers are less than the gift that is according to apostleship and prophecy and teaching — unless indeed someone should grant two kinds of prophecy, so that here too he may keep the order preserved, so that there is a certain prophecy that has surpassed and a certain prophecy that has risen up. For the more universal one, which imitates the prophecies of Isaiah and Jeremiah, he will call the second rank after apostleship, but this other one, ranked in the last place after the gifts that have been mentioned, is of such a kind: "And if" you should prophesy, "and there come in someone unbelieving or unlearned, he is reproved by all, he is examined by all, the hidden things of his heart become manifest, and thus, falling upon his face, he will worship God and declare that God is truly among you". For this is not far from the "working of powers" and the "gift of healings" which come to pass for the astonishment of those who behold, so that the one prophesying may say: This you have in your heart; From this sin you have come to the Church. And this prophecy itself can be later in rank than the former things, while that more divine and greater one is second, concerning which he says: God appointed in the Church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers. For the establishing of the point that two things are signified by the name of prophecy, I set forth beforehand the things aforesaid which I stated. See whether I am still able to set out more clearly what is said: God appointed in the Church first apostles; but not all are apostles, for if all are apostles, to whom is the apostleship ministered? Second prophets; not all are prophets; but according to the other prophecy, "if all" you should prophesy, "and there come in an unbeliever or an unlearned person", not as though it were impossible but as being possible for all to prophesy in this way. There are, therefore, two things signified by the name of prophecy. Wherefore here too the order has been preserved by the Apostle, which says first apostles, second prophets and what follows. These things, then, are said concerning the order, since the phrase and to another prophecy, ranked last in another passage, seemed to press upon us.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Now do angels, when they converse with one another, converse in these same tongues in which men also do, so that some of the angels are perhaps Greeks and some Hebrews and others Egyptians? Or is it absurd to say this about the higher angelic orders? May it not be, then, that just as among men there are many languages, so there are also among the angels? And if God grants us to be ranked from the human nature into the angelic — my Lord Jesus Christ declaring the promise when he says, "They shall be equal to the angels and sons of God of the resurrection" — being sons thereof, shall we no longer use the language of men but the angelic language? And just as the language of little children is one thing and that of those whose speech is articulate is another, so is every language among men, as it were, a language of little children; while the angelic is, as it were, that of grown and articulate men? And perhaps there too, according to the analogy of the condition, there are also languages. If then I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I have become sounding brass or a clanging cymbal. Just as the sounding brass gives an indistinct sound, just as the clanging cymbal gives nothing clear, in the same way, apart from love, a tongue — even if it be, by supposition, the tongue of angels among men — is inarticulate; for nothing makes the things of men, or indeed of angels, articulate and clear as love does; and when love is not present, that which is spoken is nothing.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: We inquire here whether anyone in this life can both have prophecy and know all the mysteries apart from love, and in general whether it is given to anyone to know all the mysteries; for Paul says, "If anyone thinks he has known something, he has not yet known as he ought to know"; and again he says, "In part we know and in part we prophesy; but when the perfect comes, that which is in part shall be done away". And his saying these things about himself and the apostles who were like him makes clear that it is not possible to know all the mysteries and all knowledge. How then does he say these things as though it were possible to know all knowledge and to understand all the mysteries? If we look at the preface of his words, in which he says And still I show you a way beyond all measure (kath' hyperbolēn, "by way of excess"), and understand what hyperbolē ("excess," an overstatement) is, all these things will be made clear. Hyperbolē, then, is, as the Greeks too have defined it, a manner of speech that for the sake of emphasis exceeds the truth; and they use an example, that certain persons are said to be whiter than snow — not that anything can be whiter than snow, but it is said by way of excess (kath' hyperbolēn). And again: certain horses run like the wind — not that such a thing is possible, but for the sake of emphasis, that the swiftness of the horses may be set forth, such a thing is said about them. And in the scripture of the Psalms too it is said concerning the sea, "Its waves go up to the heavens and go down to the depths"; which is impossible, but is said for the sake of emphasis. And in the law also you will find written this manner of hyperbolē, where it is written, "We saw cities great and walled up to the heaven". But how can this be? It is said hyperbolically, the statement not at all setting forth the very thing indicated, but in order to make clear the greatness of the waves or their lowness, and the greatness of the walls, or something similar to these. So here too the Apostle takes a supposition for the sake of examining the nature of spiritual gifts, the nature of love — not that it is possible for there to be a spiritual gift, and one so great, apart from love; nor that it is possible in this life for anyone to know all knowledge apart from love, or to have faith so great as to remove mountains; but wishing to set forth that, if love be placed on the scale, the statement is made by way of supposition. He says, then, that one must above all "be zealous for" love.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
But what is the difference between knowledge and the knowing of the mysteries? For the Apostle speaks about two things. I consider, then, that to know about the manifest things is knowledge, being more generic than the mysteries; for the understanding is in a part of knowledge or of the mysteries; while to know about the more ineffable and more divine things, this is to know the mystery, so that there is a generic account of knowledge, but the apprehension of mysteries no longer belongs to all knowledge — those mysteries concerning which it has been said, "But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, the hidden wisdom, which God foreordained before the ages unto our glory". For when I know these things, then I have the knowledge of the mysteries.

Even if I have all faith so as to remove mountains. It is written in the Gospel, "If you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, Be lifted up and cast into the sea, and it will pass over, and nothing will be impossible for you". For he who has faith as a grain of mustard seed has the whole of faith.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And though I dole out all my goods in food — not for love's sake; and though I hand over my body that I may boast — inasmuch as it is possible for someone to dole out his goods in food not for love's sake but out of vainglory, and inasmuch as it is possible for someone even to bear witness as a martyr for the sake of boasting and of the glory with which the martyrs are glorified in the churches.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He goes through the praises of love, which surpasses the spiritual gifts. For he had to teach both what love is and what sort of person the one who has love is. Love is patient: if you have "patience", which is "a fruit of the Spirit", you have it because of love. Is kind: what is contrary to kindness? Wickedness. If you act wickedly against someone, you do not have love. If you are kind and sweet toward all people, you have love. Love is not jealous: if there is in you jealousy such as was in Cain toward Abel, or such as was in the brothers of Joseph toward Joseph, you do not have love. Loving and being jealous are things at war with each other. Love is not boastful: when someone is rash, professing to know either about an art or about a science or about knowledge, this is the one who is boastful, from not having love.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Does not behave unseemly: no one who has love does anything unseemly; if therefore at some time our brethren, a man and a woman, claiming to love one another according to God, should through weakness fall under the pretext of love, let us tell them that they do not have love; for love does not behave unseemly. Does not seek its own: no one who has love seeks his own things; for example a mother in loving her son, or a father, does not seek her own as she does the son's; for to have love is not self-loving. If the Savior, "being in the form of God" and being "equal to God", had sought his own, he would have remained in that form; but as it is, wishing to save a perishing world, he "emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; and being found in fashion as a man he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross". Come also to the saints; see the love of Moses: "If you will forgive them the sin, forgive it; but if not, blot me also out of your book which you have written". And the Apostle also says, "Even as I too please all in all things, not seeking my own profit but that of the many, that they may be saved", and "I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for the sake of my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh". He prays to be accursed from Christ for the salvation of others.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Tongues shall cease, when I shall converse with the mind with which I wish to hold discourse.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But just as among "children" some are more eager than others and more quickly attain the things handed down to them, so, I say, Moses and the prophets, and also the Apostles of the Lord Jesus Christ, were made like gifted "children." Therefore, being aware of themselves — that, even if they made progress, they made the progress of "children" — they said: "We know in part and we prophesy in part." For they did not yet behold the realities of truth, but the shadows of the realities, nor the full light, but a dim image; and so they repeated, saying: "For now we see through a glass and in a riddle, but then face to face." Who then, reading and understanding these things, will be puffed up and exalt himself over his knowledge, or over any of the gifts? For since the things which have come to "children" are far inferior to those which are reserved for grown men, those who seem among the "children" to be of keener and quicker wit ought not to be lifted up and grow proud.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He who seems to be making progress here makes progress as among little children; but when that which is perfect comes "and we attain to a perfect man", then we shall have room for the things of grown men—both knowledge and prophecy and the vision of God, which the "blessed" "shall see", those blessed on account of the purity of the heart.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: There is, then, a certain childish age according to the inner man, and there is also a youthful age, and there is an aged age, according to what the Apostle said: "When I was a little one, I spoke as a little one, I was wise as a little one, I thought as a little one; but when I became a man, I did away with the things that were of a little one". I understand these things to be said by the Apostle not of bodily age, but because, when in the beginning he had believed, he was a little one lately born, desiring the reasonable and guileless milk; then he understood the Scriptures as a little one, was wise concerning the Gospel as a little one, thought as a little one; but after this, advancing in age after the likeness of Christ — of whom it is written that "He advanced in age and wisdom and grace with God and with men" — he laid aside the things that were of a little one: and therefore he said, "When I became a man, I laid aside the things that were of a little one".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: If the knowledge manifested to those worthy of it comes through a mirror and is an enigma in the present age and will be fully revealed only "then," it is foolish to suppose that it will not be the same for the other virtues as well.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The one who has the edifying gift is greater than the one who does not have such a gift, inasmuch as he who has the edifying gift is more beneficial to the community; but if one who speaks in tongues should also have the gift to interpret, for the building up of the Church, then he who prophesies is no longer greater. For there are times when he speaks lofty things, and he speaks to himself and to God, so that the Church is unable to "hear".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Prophecy is the knowledge that signifies, through speech, the things unseen — the awareness of the constitution of the world and of the working of the elements and the times. Teaching is the instructive word distributed among the many. Revelation is when the mind comes to be outside earthly things and puts away every fleshly activity by the power of God; the one who has attained this has come to be in revelation. And perhaps the knowledge concerning things to come can also be called revelation; but he who has grasped the strict meaning of each term is permitted to use the names in a looser, more extended way.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He wishes to shame those who speak with a tongue into "keeping silence in the church", if there be no "interpreter", and he says The things without soul, flute and harp, for the musicians. And giving no distinction to the notes, it is not known in what rhythm one has played; and the soldier does not arm himself for war, unless the trumpet sends forth the rousing sound for war; and those who speak with a tongue and do not interpret ought not to speak, inasmuch as they give no distinction to their words so that they may be understood. The doctrines of contemplation, then, he called flute and harp, as displaying nothing ethical, but the teachings that exhort toward virtue a trumpet; and by this it is possible to say that the obscure parts of Scripture, such as those concerning the sacrifices in Leviticus and the tabernacle in Exodus, ought not to be read aloud, unless someone makes clear their meaning by exposition.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Thence one comes to Mount Shepher, which is called "trumpet-blowing." The trumpet is the sign of war. Therefore, where it perceives itself armed with such and so great virtues, of necessity it advances to war, which is for it against the principalities and powers, and against the rulers of this world; or else certainly it sounds the trumpet in the word of God, that is, of preaching and of doctrine, that it may "give a distinct sound by the trumpet," so that he who hears it may be able to prepare himself for war.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He who speaks in a tongue speaks in God; and even if human beings do not understand, still the powers about the air do hear.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "Even things without soul," then, "give forth a voice" — some of them with this distinction of notes, and others again with a different one; for every body has its own peculiar sound, when it is struck against another body.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Everyone who speaks to someone things which the other does not understand — the hearer seems to him to be a barbarian, and he in turn to the hearer.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Abounding comes about through the excellence of spiritual gifts, from seeking the things that are for the building up of the Church, in the sense that he does not abound in spiritual gifts who does not seek the common good. For it is likely that the working of a spiritual gift lies idle whenever it does not shine "before men". Therefore, if we wish to increase our spiritual gifts, we will give ourselves to the benefit of the greater number.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: If the one who speaks in a tongue does not have the gift of interpreting, then, even if the others do not understand, he himself nonetheless understands the things put into him by the Spirit so as to be moved to speak. But whenever what is spoken should be understood by others, then this is held to be a fruit of the speaker toward those who understand.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: You see that everywhere the things which pertain to the praises of God — for this is "the sacrifice of praise" — ought to be "new and fresh", lest perchance, when you bring forth old things in the Church, your lips speak and your "mind be without fruit". But hear what the Apostle says: "if," he says, "I speak with tongues, my spirit prays, but my mind is without fruit. What then is it? I will pray," he says, "with the spirit, I will pray also with the mind, I will say a psalm with the spirit, I will say a psalm also with the mind". So therefore you too, if not out of spiritual learning, out of the doctrine of the grace of God, you bring forth a present and fresh discourse in the praises of God, your mouth indeed offers "a sacrifice of praise", but your mind is convicted for the barrenness of yesterday's flesh.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For our mind would not even be able to pray unless the Spirit prayed for it as if obeying it, so that we cannot even sing and hymn the Father in Christ with proper rhythm, melody, measure and harmony unless the Spirit who searches everything, even the depths of God, first praises and hymns him whose depths he has searched out and has understood as far as he is able.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And through these words we are taught to seek what is of common benefit to the Church.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And to speak the perceptible words spiritually — the five senses — is to seek what is of common benefit; but the word of instruction, which comes through the five senses, is appointed for those who hear in the Church, since they too are instructed by the five words. For those who do not know the distinctness of the things spoken, but attend only to the bare resounding of the Scriptures, are designated as those under instruction; whereas those who hear from the Scripture the "distinction of the sounds" — these are not under instruction, but are the faithful.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Since the things He commands are possible, it is possible for us to become mature in our understanding. And this very nearly interprets the saying "Unless you turn and become as the little children"; for the one who is an infant in evil, by turning, becomes as a little child.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He gave the name law to the prophetic word as well; and these words we found in Aquila and the remaining editions, though not indeed in the Seventy.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Since the prophetic gift makes one "to know" the hidden things of the heart of the unbeliever and of the uninstructed man and of the one who draws near to them, it is clear that "when that which is perfect is come" they will know perfectly the hidden things of every uninstructed and unbelieving man; and it is likely that then also the hidden things of the holy man become manifest to the prophets—perhaps the things of the lesser to the greater. And the one who is benefited "is afraid to look upon the face of God"; wherefore, when he pictures God to himself, he falls upon his face, giving to Him both preeminence and glory, and thus he "worships" God. And the convicting and examining of the hidden things of the heart—which is to make them manifest—marks out that God is in the spirit of such men. But if the remaining spiritual gifts also are signs that God truly exists, in what is it to be sought?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: When we come together, all who have spiritual gifts must be permitted to speak — that is, those who are able to teach.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: By others he means those who have the gift of making clear the spiritual words of the prophets, if indeed the prophesiers themselves did not possess the gift of discernment; for insofar as they do not have this, it is likely that they have been deceived by some evil spirit that "transforms himself into an angel of light", as though they had attained prophetic rank.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Therefore the prophets were not out of their senses; for it lay within their power to fall silent and to hold in check the spirit that was upon them.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: There is danger for those who read in making pronouncements carelessly, and likewise for those who hear. Hear, then, Paul saying: "If anyone among you thinks himself to be a prophet or spiritual, let him recognize that the things I write are God's"—implying that not everyone recognizes the things of God unless he be "a prophet or spiritual". And the Apostle delineated the spiritual man when he said: "But the spiritual man discerns all things, yet he himself is discerned by no one". And who is the one who discerns all things but he who is able to examine and judge every argument? And this man is discerned by no one, not being comprehended because of the depth of his thoughts. For the spiritual man has "the mind" "of the Lord". As, then, a small child cannot discern the mind of a man and examine his thoughts—for the little boy does not even begin to follow the thoughts of the man—in the same way neither "can the natural man" know which things are "of God" and which are not; but this work belongs to the spiritual man alone. I have often inquired within myself why ever it was that, when there were both prophets of God and false prophets, the false prophets were held in higher esteem by their kings than the prophets; and the books of the false prophets were neither written down nor preserved among the people, whereas those of the prophets—who were condemned, hated, and suffered what we know—came forth into public view and have been honored. What was the origin of these things, I state, taking my starting points from the Apostle: that there was a spiritual gift among the people, just as to prophesy, so also to discern prophets. For you can all prophesy one by one; there was then an abundance of those who spoke and of those who were permitted to speak. For on this account the Apostle permitted all to speak in the Church; he all but permitted even the women to speak, had he not said what follows.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For this reason he shows, judiciously and through silence, the matter of subjection: that the spirits are subject to the prophets, yet it is the souls of the prophets that prophesy.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
For as though all were speaking and able to speak, if a revelation should come to them, he says, Let the women keep silence in the churches. But of this commandment those women's disciples were not observers — those who were made disciples of Priscilla and Maximilla, and not of Christ, the husband of the bride. Yet let us nonetheless be fair, and meet even their plausible arguments. Philip the evangelist, they say, had four daughters, and they prophesied. And if they prophesied, what is out of place in our own women too — as those people say — prophesying, being prophetesses? These things we shall resolve. First, saying: 'Our women prophesied — then show the signs of prophecy in them'; second, even if the daughters of Philip did prophesy, still they did not speak in the churches — for we do not have this in the Acts of the Apostles. But neither in the Old Testament: Deborah is attested to be a prophetess, and "Miriam the sister of Aaron, taking the timbrel," took the lead of the women. But you will not find that Deborah delivered a public address to the people as Jeremiah and Isaiah did; you will not find that Huldah, being a prophetess, spoke to the people, but to some one man who came to her. And in the Gospel too it is written, "Anna a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher"; but she did not speak in the church. So that even if it be granted, from a prophetic sign, that a woman is a prophetess, still she is not permitted to speak in the church. When Miriam the prophetess spoke, she was leading certain women; for it is shameful for a woman to speak in the church, and "I do not permit a woman to teach" — not merely that, but "neither to have authority over a man".

And from elsewhere too I shall establish this — even though that other passage is more securely stated concerning the woman not becoming a leader of the man by speech: "aged women in demeanor reverent, teachers of what is good, that they may train the young women to be sober-minded," not simply that they may teach. For let women too be teachers of what is good, yet not so that men should sit and listen to women, as though there were a lack of men able to serve as ambassadors of the word of God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Since the men had authority from the beginning to speak and to benefit those who heard, while the women asked questions about the things they were puzzled over. And by the Law he means what is said in Genesis: "Your turning shall be to your husband".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And if they wish to learn anything, let them ask their own husbands at home; for it is shameful for women to speak in the church. It seems to me that their own husbands does not refer to the wedded husbands only; for the virgins will either speak in the church or will not have those who teach them, and the widowed women likewise. But perhaps their own husbands means, for instance, the brother too, and the household member, and the son? Once for all, let a woman simply inquire of a man of her own, according to the generic name of "man" as distinguished from "woman"; for it is shameful for a woman to speak in the church — whatever she may speak, even if she should speak marvelous things, even if holy things, if only they come forth from a woman's mouth. A woman in the church is spoken of, clearly, according to what is shameful, to the reproach of the whole church.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: As though this disorder existed in Corinth along with the other sins as well. This, then, is what he says: that God sent his word into the world. Did then the truth and the ecclesiastical rule reach to you only, the Corinthians?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Concerning this the Apostle also adds, next after these words: "If anyone among you is a prophet or spiritual, let him recognize that the things I write are of God; but if anyone is ignorant, he is ignored." Not only, then, is the one who is ignorant of the Apostle's words ignored by God, but also, if anyone is ignorant—speaking by a divine spirit and yet saying that he does not speak by a divine spirit—he is ignored by God. And through these words the Apostle seems to teach that there is no man who does not have another spirit in him besides the spirit of the man that is in him. For whether he is a stranger to the faith or belongs to it, he has a spirit of his own from God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: A spiritual man is one able to test every word and every meaning, even one that, through the great depth of meaning, is so hard to discern that it cannot be examined. Now it does not belong to any chance person to know that the things written by Paul are the Lord's, but to a prophet or a spiritual man; therefore he who does not know that they are the Lord's is neither a prophet nor a spiritual man. And it is one thing to believe and another to know; therefore he who is ignorant that they are the Lord's is ignorant, since he has not yet attained to being properly God's. For the one who is known is, in a certain manner, blended together with the one who knows him.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: In order, then, that we may recognize the things of God, let us entreat the one who gives gifts of grace, that he may give us a prophetic gift and make us spiritual by the Spirit that governs; and so we may be equipped to judge which things are God's or which are not his. For he who has been deprived of this grace cannot comprehend; whence he added But if anyone is ignorant, let him be ignorant.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He seeks also "onyx", with which as with a kind of shield his animal is covered and remains unharmed. So he wishes you too to be protected with "the shield of faith, with which you may extinguish all the fiery darts of the evil one". Yet all these things he wishes to be composed by you, nothing disordered, nothing restless, nothing unseemly, but he wishes this, "that all our things be done in a composed and honorable manner". Therefore even now our true "high priest" Christ stands and wishes "his hands" to be filled "with the fine composed incense", and from each church which is under heaven he considers what is offered, how wholly and diligently it composes its "incense", how "fine" it makes it, that is, how each one of us orders his works and how he examines the sense and words of the Scriptures with spiritual explanation.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He calls gospel what he proclaims as good news, for this is also what he handed down; and that man stands in the gospel who has his own soul mounted upon it, as upon a boat, upon that very thing through which also he is saved. And he says that the one has "believed" in vain who does not "hold fast the word" of the gospel, but has heard it irrationally and by chance and without examination.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The Jews do not stand in the gospel, since they have not received Jesus; those from the heresies stand ill, since they do not understand the gospel but interpret it in their own private way; those who sin do not stand, since they do not live according to the gospel. Who, then, stand in the gospel but those who have received it and accepted it and live according to it? But if With what word I preached to you, if you hold it fast be understood, and if what is reasonably appended to these words be understood—unless you believed in vain—we shall know that it is impossible for the one who has believed in vain to have thus believed something false; rather, to have believed, and that indeed a truth, is no achievement—but to believe with discernment is. "Those who believe for a time and in a time of trial fall away" believe in vain; and yet they have not believed something false but the truth, but since they have not believed firmly, for this reason "in a time of trial they fall away." For one who believes rightly will not fall.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After these points, Celsus proceeds to bring against the Gospel narrative a charge which is not to be lightly passed over, saying that "if Jesus desired to show that his power was really divine, he ought to have appeared to those who had ill-treated him, and to him who had condemned him, and to all men universally." For it appears to us also to be true, according to the Gospel account, that He was not seen after His resurrection in the same manner as He used formerly to show Himself — publicly, and to all men. But it is recorded in the Acts, that "being seen during forty days," He expounded to His disciples "the things pertaining to the kingdom of God." [Acts 1:3] And in the Gospels it is not stated that He was always with them; but that on one occasion He appeared in their midst, after eight days, when the doors were shut [John 20:26], and on another in some similar fashion. And Paul also, in the concluding portions of the first Epistle to the Corinthians, in reference to His not having publicly appeared as He did in the period before He suffered, writes as follows: "For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures; and that He was seen of Cephas, then of the twelve: after that He was seen of above five hundred brethren at once, of whom the greater part remain unto the present time, but some are fallen asleep. After that He was seen of James, then of all the apostles. And last of all He was seen of me also, as of one born out of due time." [1 Corinthians 15:3-8] I am of opinion now that the statements in this passage contain some great and wonderful mysteries, which are beyond the grasp not merely of the great multitude of ordinary believers, but even of those who are far advanced (in Christian knowledge), and that in them the reason would be explained why He did not show Himself, after His resurrection from the dead, in the same manner as before that event.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: By He appeared to the twelve he means the Lord after the resurrection; for it was likely that Matthias too was present, who had been appointed an apostle in place of Judas.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The divine dispensation raised him up and made not only two or three to be witnesses of his resurrection, but far more. For "he was seen by Cephas, then by the eleven, then he appeared to more than five hundred brethren at once", "and last of all" by Paul. And it was no small sign of his resurrection, that he was seen by so many — by those who took up the danger of proclaiming him alive among the peoples who had demanded him for the cross.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Being conscious to himself of the sins from which he had been set free, he says, I am not fit to be called an apostle.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: When he said that his grace was not in vain toward me, he taught that those who live unworthily of the grace have obtained it in vain. Yet it is not the grace that labors; rather it is to be understood thus: It is not I who have done these things, but the grace that is with me.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Since all the apostles have been fully assured concerning the resurrection of Christ from the dead, the demonstration is firm; and therefore we say the same things. For you too so believed.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: From the text before us the resurrection of Christ is clear, having come about together with the flesh which he had; but they, the heterodox, wish to allegorize the resurrection of human beings. Then let them allegorize the Savior's resurrection also, wickedly annulling the text by their own [device].

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Since neither is the preaching empty nor is the faith empty, it is clear that Christ has been raised. And we have noted these points to show that, even though Paul was acquainted with dialectical argumentation, he nevertheless used it naturally; for it is from nature and common usage that the art of dialectic was given its bodily form by those who practice philosophy.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: If he testifies falsely against God — the one who says that Christ has risen — then so too does everyone who says that there is a resurrection of the dead; but if Christ has risen as "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep," it is clear that the dead too are raised.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Since those from the heresies, while professing the faith of the Church and yet sneering at it as the faith of fools, reject it in deed, even if not in word, saying that the resurrection does not come to pass as the Church believes—see how they must be answered from this apostolic text and from countless others.
