Did Christ rise from the dead, or not? On this point every heresy has agreed. If Christ rose from the dead, and he is "the firstborn from the dead", and no one is "firstborn" of another kind, then his resurrection must be of the same kind as the resurrection of those who rise. For example: Reuben is firstborn, being a son of Jacob, his brothers being of the same kind; for Reuben is not of one nature and Simeon or Levi and the rest of another nature. And the same holds for the other firstborn. If therefore Jesus too is firstborn from the dead, the resurrection of those who rise must be of the same kind. But if he wore a body, and his resurrection was with a body—so that he even ate, as is written in the Gospel according to John—whereas those of the believers in Christ who rise are raised in another manner, as those from the heresies suppose, then they cannot show how Jesus is "the firstborn from the dead". For if we "have become conformed" to the death of Christ, we shall be conformed "also to his resurrection"; and consider how Paul teaches, saying, "Who will transform the body of our humiliation into conformity with the body of the glory" of Christ.

Shamelessly, then, do certain people accept that "Christ has been raised from the dead, yet say that there is no resurrection of the dead". Therefore the Apostle says, "But if Christ is preached as raised from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?" Even if a man does not say it with his mouth, but says in his heart "There is no resurrection of the dead", he in effect rejects also the resurrection of Jesus Christ. For if the universal statement is false, it is clear that the one who rose from the dead is also included in the universal. For if "the dead are not raised", and Jesus too was among the dead, then "neither has" Jesus "been raised"; but if he has been raised, through him the resurrection of the dead is made manifest—unless we disbelieve because of the impossibility of the matter in itself, forgetting who it is that has promised. For what, among things impossible—so to speak—is more impossible: that the body be made alive, or that heaven come to be out of things that are not, or the sun, or the rest of created things?

Come now to the very beginning of man; go back over his origin. There is shown to you the seed of a man. If someone said, 'This seed will become a man, it will be formed, there will be bones, from it flesh, sinews, veins; it will walk about; from this small, paltry seed a man raised upright upon the earth will make use of his organs'—would we not have called the one proclaiming these things to us a fool, had we not had experience of it? So then, let me be bold and set before you the resurrection, that you may the more accept it, having put your trust in the perfection of God. As that seed stood in relation to this present body—the body that now stands present, the generative one, the one that sows, that has become the instrument of words and deeds done according to righteousness—so this body comes to stand in relation to that one: "The grain of wheat, unless it falls into the ground and dies, remains alone by itself"; but if it falls into the ground and dies and rots away, out of the rotting of the grain of wheat an ear grows a hundredfold. For that your body is the seed of that which is to rise, hear Paul saying: "It is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption; it is sown in dishonor, it is raised in glory; it is sown in weakness, it is raised in power; it is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body". You see how there, in the case of the seed, something paltry and of no account was sown, and there has risen a comely and beautiful man; in the same way this dead thing is a grain of wheat to God, as that which is to rise up beforehand. So then, just as God found the means to make an ear from the grain of wheat—not from resources apart from those in the small seed; for from that seed he raised the ear, and from each seed he raises what is present potentially in the seed—so from the seed of a man, at the beginning, this man came to be. But if his body dies, it becomes the seed of that which is to rise from the dead "in glory" in Christ Jesus. And the Apostle reckoned disbelief in the resurrection from the dead to be equivalent to not believing that we shall exist at all after our departure. Therefore, to those who do not believe that there will be a resurrection of the dead—since according to them there is no other life beyond the present one—he says, "If in this life only we have hoped in Christ, we are of all men most to be pitied". And in what follows too, as against those who say there is no resurrection of the dead, there being no life beyond this present existence, he says, "Why do we too endanger ourselves every hour? I die daily, by your boasting, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord", and so on. The sect of the Sadducees too, who reject the resurrection of the dead, makes clear that it follows for them that you do not even live after the present life. Wherefore the Savior, in answering them, takes an example from the Law alone concerning the existence of the resurrection from the dead, quoting the express text, saying: "But concerning" the "resurrection of the dead, have you not read" that "God said at" the "Bush, saying, I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob? God is not the God of the dead but of the living".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But now Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. The firstfruits are the firstfruits of many. And as we have seen by way of the example of the things in the Law: a firstfruit of grain is offered up by those who have reaped grain; and, say, of wine by those who have harvested wine; and of oil from those who have pressed the olive; so, if our Lord Jesus Christ is the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, there must be many of whom he is the firstfruits; and we inquire whether he is the firstfruits of all or of many. For he says, Christ the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. If, then, we did not have the wording from the outset, we might indeed have said—thinking it something ill-omened in this passage to say that he is the firstfruits of all—that he is the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, of the righteous only and not of the rest. But now the Apostle himself says, For since through a man came death, through a man also comes the resurrection of the dead; how could he be speaking of some, when he speaks of all? For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ—he did not say The righteous shall be made alive, but all shall be made alive. Then, lest you be troubled and say, 'Has, then, all this great toil been drained out by me in vain, if indeed Christ, risen from the dead, is the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep of all, and in Christ all shall be made alive?'—he says, But each in his own order. All, then, died in Adam, and all shall be made alive in Christ; but even if all died in Adam, none the less Abraham was righteous, Isaac was a patriarch, Jacob—who begot the twelve patriarchs—was Israel; and thus you will proceed to the rest of the righteous as well. I make bold to say that, whereas the Apostle said that Christ Jesus is the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, I, alongside him, would put it thus: This one is the firstfruits unto life of those who are to live, while Adam has become the firstfruits of the death of men; for in Adam all die, since he received the firstfruits of death; but the Savior, wishing to take up the firstfruits of life, first took up the death of those who have died, so that, having abolished death, he might become the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep and are alive.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But since the merit of all is not one, nor is the advancement in faith one, therefore the ark too does not furnish one and the same dwelling to all these, but the lower parts are double-chambered and the upper parts triple-chambered, and nests are distinguished in it, so as to show that in the Church also, although all are contained within one faith and are washed by one baptism, nevertheless the advancement is not one and the same for all, "but each in his own order."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: When Christ shall have delivered up the kingdom to God, even the Father, then those living beings, because they have before this been made part of Christ's kingdom, shall also be delivered up along with the whole of that kingdom to the rule of the Father, so that, when "God shall be all in all," they also, since they are a part of all, may have God even in themselves, as he is in all things.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For the destruction of the last enemy must be understood in this way: not that its substance which was made by God shall perish, but that the hostile purpose and will which proceeded not from God but from itself will come to an end. It will be destroyed, therefore, not in the sense of ceasing to exist but of being no longer an enemy and no longer death.… We must not think, however, that it will happen all of a sudden, but gradually and by degrees, during the lapse of infinite and immeasurable ages, seeing that the improvement and correction will be realized slowly and separately in each individual person.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Christ the Lord himself will instruct those who are able to receive him in his character of wisdom, after their preliminary training in his holy virtues, and will reign with them until such time as he subjects them to the Father who subjected all things to him. When they have been rendered capable of receiving God, then God will be to them "all in all."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: In short, so long as I am not subject to the Father, neither is he himself said to be "subject" to the Father. Not that he himself needs subjection with the Father, but on my behalf, in whom he has not yet consummated his work, he himself is said not to be subject; for thus we read, that "we are the body of Christ and members in part".… But when he shall have "consummated" his "work" and shall have brought his whole creation to the summit of perfection, then he himself is said to be "subject" in those whom he has subjected to the Father, and in whom he has "consummated the work which the Father had given him", "that God may be all in all".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But the heretics, not understanding (I cannot tell why) the apostle's meaning contained in these words, deprecate using the term subjection in regard to the Son.… Such men do not understand that the subjection of Christ to the Father reveals the blessedness of our perfection and announces the crowning glory of the work undertaken by him.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: God will be all things in each person in such a way that everything which the reasoning mind can feel or understand or think will be all God. When purified from all the dregs of its vices and utterly cleared from every cloud of wickedness, the mind will no longer be conscious of anything besides or other than God. That mind will think of God and see God and hold God. God will be the mode and measure of its every movement. In this way God will be all in all.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
But of that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son, but the Father alone.

These words seem to refute those who promise that they can comprehend the consummation and destruction of the world and who declare "as though the day of the Lord were at hand" — such as certain people are said to have been at Thessalonica in the time of the Apostle, of whom he writes: "Now we beseech you, brethren, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together unto him, that you be not soon moved from your mind, nor be troubled, neither by spirit nor by word nor by letter as though from us, as though the day of the Lord were at hand." Perhaps because among the Jews there were certain persons professing, whether through the scriptures, that they knew of the times of the consummation or of hidden things, therefore he writes these things, teaching his disciples that they should believe no one who professes such things. And the Savior, according to this passage, joins himself to those who are ignorant of that day and hour. And it must reasonably be asked how he who is confident that he knows the Father, saying: "No one knows the Father but the Son and he to whom the Son shall will to reveal him", knows the Father indeed, yet does not know the day and hour of the consummation, and why the Father hid this from the Son. For there must certainly be some reason why the time of the consummation is hidden even from the Savior and why he is ignorant concerning it.

But someone will dare to say that the man who exists according to the Savior is understood to be advancing "in wisdom and stature and grace before God and men", who in advancing did indeed advance above all in knowledge and wisdom, yet not so that there had already come to him that which was perfect, before he fulfilled his own dispensation. It is therefore no wonder if this alone he did not know out of all things, that is, the day and hour of the consummation.

But perhaps also, when he said that he did not know the day and hour of the consummation, he said this before his dispensation, because no one knows, neither the angels nor the Son, but the Father alone; but after his dispensation was fulfilled he by no means said this, after "God highly exalted him and gave him a name which is above every name".

For afterward the Son too came to know it, receiving knowledge from the Father even concerning the day of the consummation and the hour, so that now not only the Father might know concerning it but also the Son. And indeed in the Acts of the Apostles the apostles "coming together questioned him, saying: Lord, wilt thou at this time restore the kingdom of Israel? But he said to them: It is not for you to know the times or the moments which the Father hath set in his own power". And since he "set in his own power the times and moments" of the consummation of the world and of the restitution of the kingdom of Israel, therefore what had not yet been predefined by God no one could know. But each of the things which he predefines, he does not predefine from anything inexperienced (for this is impossible); but what he predefines, he predefines by making a beginning of predefining. And if this is so, he predefined indeed to bring about the consummation of the world, but he did not also predefine the "times and moments which he set in his own power", so that, if he wished to increase them, judging thus he might increase them, but if to shorten them, he might shorten them, no one knowing it. And therefore he set the times and moments of the consummation of the world in his own power, so that accordingly he might determine the due judgment for the human race (established in its own free will) acting in this way or that. Many things too are to be found in the prophets, written for the benefit of the hearers, in precepts and denunciations, as though God were not predefining anything about them, but punishing indeed if they should sin, and saving if they should keep the precepts. And just as in those cases the scripture did not introduce God as predefining, but as speaking forth according to the benefit of the hearers, so is it to be understood also concerning the day of the consummation and the hour.

Another explanation (which is more famous than those which have already been set forth) says something else about that which is written neither the Son, but the Father alone.

The Apostle, it says, speaks somewhere concerning the Savior and concerning the matters to be ordered at the end of the age in this manner: "But when all things shall be subjected to him, then shall the Son himself also be subject to him who subjected all things to himself, that God may be all in all."

By these words he seems to show that, before he subjected all things to him, he was not subject "to him who subjected all things to himself": which is demonstrated from this, that unless the Son had been subject to the Father, who subjected all things to himself, the Father would never have subjected all things to him.

And through these words he seems to say that the subjection of the Son becomes the subjection of all who were to be subjected to him, and their coming through the Son to God and to perfection.

If, then, this is rightly said concerning the future subjection of the Son to the Father — that then those who are to be Christ's and shall have cleaved to him may, together with Christ himself, be subjected to the Father — why shall we not likewise expound also that no one knows of that day and hour, neither the Son?

For as long as the Church, which is the body of Christ, does not know that day and hour, so long is the Son himself also said not to know that day and hour, so that he is understood to know then, when all his members shall have come to know it. And it is rightly said "to know" according to its proper signification, as is the custom of the scriptures. What is it to know? That he shall come to know that day and hour who shall arrive at the end and shortening of that day and hour.

But that "to know" and "to recognize" have some such signification in the scriptures is manifest from that which is said in Ecclesiastes in this manner: "He who keeps the commandment shall not know an evil word", that is, shall not experience an evil word. And in the Apostle it is said concerning the Savior himself: "Him who knew not sin, he made sin for us".

And he called the Savior one not knowing sin, as though he were to say one who did not sin nor was in the nature of sin.

It signifies something of this kind, that also which it says: "Adam knew Eve his wife".

For as long as she had not been joined to him, he did not know her.

And therefore no one knows, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son of God, the day of such a consummation and destruction of the age, since God provides better for the saints, that they may come to be together in the blessedness which is to be after the day and hour of that consummation. And just as it is written among the Hebrews concerning those who have testimony in faith, that "all these, having been attested through faith, did not receive the promise of God, God providing some better thing concerning us, that they should not be perfected without us", so is it to be known also in this matter, that, since God foresaw some better thing concerning those who were to be saved, they have not yet received the promise, who did not come to know concerning that day and hour, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son. For the Son prepares the knowledge of that day and hour for the coheirs of that promise, from the time that "he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant", working out the way that leads to the restitution of all things, for whose sake he took "the form of a servant"; that all may together know (that is, may in the very reality experience) that hour and day, for "what eye hath not seen nor ear heard, and hath not ascended upon the heart of man, God hath prepared for those who love him" training and preparing in the knowledge of prior things every one whom he wills to know that day and hour together with the holy angels and with our Lord Jesus Christ himself. And the consummation of each single one, which is to be in these certain things aforesaid, and concerning individuals, the Father alone knows: since the Son, accompanying and going before those who follow after, and calling (so to speak), is to come, and delays. So that those who strive to follow him may be able to follow him, and, following him, may be found with him in that day and hour.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But the Apostle too signifies things great and mystical concerning subjection when he says: "But when all things shall be made subject to him, then shall the Son himself also be made subject to him who subjected all things to himself". Hear then what he says, that it is necessary that all things be subject to Christ, and that then he himself is subject, by that subjection, namely, which it is fitting to understand of the spirit. Meanwhile it is necessary that all things be subject to Christ, so that then at last, when all things are fulfilled and made perfect through subjection, he himself, as it were bearing back this palm of his victory to the Father, is said to be about to be made subject. And unless this be understood mystically, it is believed without doubt to indicate something impious to those who do not attend. For it is not to be supposed that the Son of God is now indeed in no way subject to the Father, but that in the last times, when all things shall have been made subject to him, then he too shall be made subject; but rather, because he takes up into himself all that is ours, and says that it is he who hungers in us, and he who thirsts in us, and is naked and sick, and a guest and thrust into prison, and testifies that whatever has been done to one of his least ones has been done to himself; consequently and deservedly, when each one of us is fully and perfectly made subject to God, so that in nothing at all does he show himself disobedient, he protests that he himself is made subject. But in yet another way what we say is more fully understood. If we suffer pain in some member of the body, although our soul be sound, and all our remaining members be healthy, nevertheless, because by the pain of one member the whole man is afflicted, we do not say that we are well, but that we are ill. For example, we say: That man is not well. Why? Because his feet pain him, or his loins, or his stomach. And no one says that he is well if his stomach pains him, but he is not well because his stomach pains him. If you have understood the example, let us now return to what was proposed. The Apostle says that we are the body of Christ, and members in part. Christ, therefore, whose body is the whole race of men — nay, perhaps the whole universe of all creation — and each one of us is a member in part: if some one of us who are called his members is sick, and labors under some disease of sin, that is, if he is branded with the stain of some sin, and is not subject to God, rightly is that one said not yet to be subject, whose members are those who are not subject to God. But when he shall have all those who are called his body and members sound, so that they have labored under no disease of disobedience, all the members being sound and subject to God, deservedly does he say that he is subject to him, we, his members, obeying God in all things.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: It must be inquired whether he did not transgress the evangelical command that says "Do not swear at all".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: There are also intelligible wild beasts.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: We see quiet and respectable men who, when they have become associated with turbulent and shameless people, have their good manners corrupted by evil conversations. They are turned into men of the same sort as those who are steeped in every kind of witness. This sometimes happens to men of mature age, who prove that they have lived more chastely in youth than when advanced years had granted them the opportunity of a freer life.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Is then the seed of man, alone of all those bodies, useless to the Creator — so that one may hope there is a resurrection of the dead, if one may so speak, in the manner of the olive and of the vine and of the wheat? And from the tiny seed-kernel of the fig there rises so great a fig tree, and you do not laugh at this which you behold in actual experience? And if someone tells you that from this little thing there rises up a fig tree bearing fruit, having learned it by experience you do not laugh it to scorn. But since the season has not yet come for that which is to rise from the human body — in the resurrection from the dead — to spring up, are you unwilling to wait, that you may see this too? Or do you not know that in the case of all the other seeds as well, not every season is suitable for the seeds to spring up? Rather, a grain of wheat rises up at this season of the year; the grape-stone rises up at this hour of the year; the stone of the olive in this month, not at every time. But do you wish, in the case of the body of man — so that you may believe — that the dead should rise year by year, like the grape-stone, like the olive, and will you not behold one extraordinary season, that you may know the resurrection of the dead? What is the one season? At the consummation of the age. So that after the resurrection from the dead you may no longer be in the present evil age. For Jesus Christ suffered "that he might deliver us out of the present evil age"; and "redeeming the time, because the days are evil". Well, then, did God dispense this too, together with the rest.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The power which exists in a grain of wheat refashions and restores the grain, after its corruption and death, into a body with stalk and ear.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Even among earthly bodies there are no small differences. Take the human race, for example. Some are Greeks and some are barbarians, and among the barbarians, some are wilder than others. Some have higher laws. Some lower ones, and some follow savage customs which are not laws at all.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: In regard to our bodily nature we must understand that there is not one body which we now use in lowliness and corruption and weakness and a different one which we are to use hereafter in incorruption and power and glory. Rather this same body, having cast off the weaknesses of its present existence, will be transformed into a thing of glory and made spiritual, with the result that what was a vessel of dishonor shall itself be purified and become a vessel of honor and a habitation of blessedness.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The quality of a spiritual body is something such as will make a fitting habitation not only for all saints and perfected souls but also for that "whole creation" which is to be "delivered from the bondage of corruption."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: It is from the natural body that the power and grace of the resurrection calls forth the spiritual body, when it changes it from dishonor to glory.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Since our Savior and Lord took on a body, let us investigate what this body was. … Since the firstfruits was raised from the dead, the dead too must be raised. The firstfruits is Christ; therefore His body became a corpse. For if His body had not become a corpse, it would not have become capable of being wrapped in a shroud, of being anointed with myrrh and all that is used in the burial of the dead, of being buried in a tomb — all those things which a spiritual body could not have undergone. For it is absolutely impossible for the spiritual to become dead, just as it is impossible for the spiritual to be deprived of sensation. For if it were indeed possible for the spiritual to become dead, it would be necessary to fear that after the resurrection, when our body has been raised, as the Apostle says, "the natural is sown, the spiritual rises," — we should all die.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: You see what he shows, that, if you remain in that which is first, which is of the earth, you will be reprobated, unless you change yourself, unless you are converted, unless, having been made "heavenly," you receive "the image of the heavenly."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But you indeed then bore "the image of the earthly"; now, however, having heard these things, cleansed by the Word of God from all that earthly mass and oppression, make "the image of the heavenly" shine forth in you.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For just as a coin or denarius bears the image of the emperors of the world, so he who does the works of "the ruler of these darknesses" bears the image of him whose works he has: which image Jesus here commanded to be rendered back and cast off from our face, and that image to be taken up according to which from the beginning we were fashioned to the likeness of God. The logical sequence of these things Paul too has expressed, saying: "as we have borne the image of the earthy, let us also bear the image of the heavenly". So then, what he says: "render what is Caesar's to Caesar", this he means: lay aside the person of the earthy, cast off the earthly image, so that, putting upon yourselves the person of the heavenly, you may be able to render "what is God's to God".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 39

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Paul, in the first Epistle to the Thessalonians, calls all those like himself "the living"; for the "God of the living" is the God both of Paul and of those like him.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Toward the beginning of the epistle he said, "I hear that there are divisions "among you""; for "each one "of you"," he says, ""says, I indeed am of Paul, and I of Apollos""—this being the Apollos concerning whom he speaks, when such faction and disturbance existed in the Church of the Corinthians. This admirable Apollos, being bishop of the people of that time, took refuge with the Apostle as with a judge. Paul was doing the work of his apostolate; the affairs pressing upon him while he was then staying in Asia did not permit him to leave the affairs in Asia and go to Corinth; but in his own stead he chose Timothy and sent him to set right the affairs in Corinth, and necessarily, in sending him with the letter, to commend him to the Church. For when the saints visited a place and benefited those who heard them, they came neither ""in weakness"" nor ""in fear"" nor ""in trembling""; but when they came to those who were weaker, they visited ""in weakness and in fear and in trembling""; such were the Corinthians, so that it was not Paul the great who visited them, but the weak one, according as he said, ""I became to the weak as weak, that I might gain the weak"." And for this reason he said, ""And I was with you in weakness""; for this reason too he came to be ""in fear and in much trembling"," so that he might prevail over his hearers. Since, then, to visit in fear and in trembling belongs to the one who is going to be of benefit to his hearers, he now exhorts the Corinthians that Timothy may be with them without fear; for he is doing the work of the Lord, as I also am; that is, what I would have done had I visited you, this Timothy does for you. Let no one, then, despise him; for if you despise him, you despise me also; for he is doing the work of the Lord, as I also am. Send him on his way in peace, that he may come to me; now indeed he comes to you to make peace. For he finds faction among you in the Church; but when you have come to concord and have been set right by the things spoken by him, and have taken up peace, send him on his way in your concord and peace, that he may come to me. For I am awaiting him along with the brethren; what brethren? Those concerning whom he said before, ""Whomever you approve, these I will send by letter"." I await him, then, hearing that he will return, reporting to me your affairs.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Now concerning Apollos the brother, I urged him to come to you; and it was by no means willed that he come now. He was, as is likely, a holy man, a friend of peace, and, seeing faction and disturbance in the Church under his charge, he did not lay claim to the place but yielded. Then the Apostle urges him, after showing patience, to return to his own community. But this man had not so much as seen Corinth, not because he disobeyed the Apostle; for he would not otherwise have thus commended his own judgment, as though it were not subordinate; for he says, It was by no means willed that he come now; as if to say: it was not without the will of God that he acted in not coming to you; but he will come whenever he has opportunity. And when does he have opportunity? If you are at peace, if you do not despise Timothy.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For there is a certain sleep of the soul, and a wakefulness; and therefore, turning the soul away from slumbering, the word through Solomon says, "Give not sleep to your eyes, nor drowsiness to your eyelids, that you may be saved like a gazelle from the snares and like a bird from the trap." And the Savior says, "Watch at every season and pray that you may be able to escape the trials that are about to come." Stand fast: be not shaken, but become steadfast. The double-minded man does not stand in the faith, nor does he who is in doubt about the matters pertaining to the faith. Be courageous: he speaks as to soldiers; for he says, "put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil." Be strong: as if to say, "Take up strength," that, having been strengthened, you may be able to say, "I can do all things in Christ Jesus who strengthens me."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Let all your affairs be done in love: for beginners it belongs to act in fear, but for the perfect to act in love.

author: Papias of Hierapolis
quote: As the presbyters say, then those who are deemed worthy of an abode in heaven shall go there, others shall enjoy the delights of Paradise, and others shall possess the splendour of the city; for everywhere the Saviour will be seen, according as they shall be worthy who see Him. But that there is this distinction between the habitation of those who produce an hundred-fold, and that of those who produce sixty-fold, and that of those who produce thirty-fold; for the first will be taken up into the heavens, the second class will dwell in Paradise, and the last will inhabit the city; and that on this account the Lord said, "In my Father's house are many mansions:" for all things belong to God, who supplies all with a suitable dwelling-place, even as His word says, that a share is given to all by the Father, according as each one is or shall be worthy. And this is the couch in which they shall recline who feast, being invited to the wedding. The presbyters, the disciples of the apostles, say that this is the gradation and arrangement of those who are saved, and that they advance through steps of this nature; and that, moreover, they ascend through the Spirit to the Son, and through the Son to the Father; and that in due time the Son will yield up His work to the Father, even as it is said by the apostle, "For He must reign till He hath put all enemies under His feet. The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death." For in the times of the kingdom the just man who is on the earth shall forget to die. "But when He saith all things are put under Him, it is manifest that He is excepted which did put all things under Him. And when all things shall be subdued unto Him, then shall the Son also Himself be subject unto Him that put all things under Him, that God may be all in all."

author: Papias of Hierapolis
quote: As the presbyters say, then those who are deemed worthy of an abode in heaven shall go there, others shall enjoy the delights of Paradise, and others shall possess the splendour of the city; for everywhere the Saviour will be seen, according as they shall be worthy who see Him. The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death." For in the times of the kingdom the just man who is on the earth shall forget to die. "But when He saith all things are put under Him, it is manifest that He is excepted which did put all things under Him. And when all things shall be subdued unto Him, then shall the Son also Himself be subject unto Him that put all things under Him, that God may be all in all."

author: Peter of Alexandria
quote: Whence it follows that those who, contending in prison, have fallen from their ministry, and have again taken up the struggle, are plainly wanting in perception. For how else is it that they seek for that which they have left, when in this present time they can be useful to the brethren? For as long as they remained firm and stable, of that which they had done contrary to reason, of this indulgence was accorded them. But when they lapsed, as having carried themselves with ostentation, and brought reproach upon themselves, they can no longer discharge their sacred ministry; and, therefore, let them the rather take heed to pass their life in humility, ceasing from vainglory.

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: Although faith hath been implanted in our construction by God our Creator, yet hath it been corrupted and changed from faith to error, and after the manner of that natural wisdom which hath also been given to us in our construction we have changed it, and instead of the wisdom of God we have gathered together the wisdom of [this] world with it. And something else which is external to God through the wisdom of God have we changed, even as Paul saith, "Through the wisdom of God the world knew not the wisdom of God." And thus also hath the natural faith which is in us been turned into error, and these things which have been given to us by the Creator for [our] advantage have been found by us to be a loss, for we have changed their profitable orderings, and we have made use of them in a manner other than that for which they were designed. Our faith hath believed in what is unseemly, and our wisdom hath made acquaintance with what is not befitting; for where faith was unnecessary there have we made use of faith.

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: "Because, by the wisdom of God, the world knew not the wisdom of God, God willed that by the simplicity of preaching, He might make to live those that believed." And it is well known that the Apostles were the simplest of men, and it was for this reason Jesus chose them, that by their simplicity He might mock at the wisdom of the world, and that by their ignorance He might make manifest the emptiness of the learning of the wise and learned.
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 4 -- On Faith: First Discourse on Simplicity

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: The Apostle Paul considered Him as one "of no reputation", and the crucifiers considered Him to lack understanding, and His enemies accounted Him to be without knowledge and intelligence, and concerning Jesus Paul spake against them, "The foolishness of God is wiser than the children of men."
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 5 -- Second Discourse on Simplicity

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: It is well known that the Apostles were the simplest of men, and it was for this reason Jesus chose them, that by their simplicity He might mock at the wisdom of the world, and that by their ignorance He might make manifest the emptiness of the learning of the wise and learned. And Paul said to certain men of his disciples who were boasting in the knowledge of the world, "Observe also your calling, my brethren, for there are not many among you who are wise according to the flesh."
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 4 -- On Faith: First Discourse on Simplicity

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: It is well known that the Apostles were the simplest of men, and it was for this reason Jesus chose them, that by their simplicity He might mock at the wisdom of the world, and that by their ignorance He might make manifest the emptiness of the learning of the wise and learned, even as Paul saith, "God chose the fools of this world to put its wise men to shame."
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 4 -- On Faith: First Discourse on Simplicity

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: And in teaching that not every man is able to be a hearer and a receiver of that wisdom which he had, Paul crieth out, saying, "We speak wisdom among the perfect: not the wisdom of this world nor that of the rulers of this world, which are brought to nought: but we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, which none of the wise men of the world hath been able to hear." The wisdom of this world is not sufficient for a foundation, nor is it able to receive the building of the wisdom of God, and for this reason our Lord placed simplicity in us for a foundation.
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 4 -- On Faith: First Discourse on Simplicity

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: And in teaching that not every man is able to be a hearer and a receiver of that wisdom which he had, Paul crieth out, saying, "We speak wisdom among the perfect: not the wisdom of this world nor that of the rulers of this world, which are brought to nought: but we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, which none of the wise men of the world hath been able to hear." The wisdom of this world is not sufficient for a foundation, nor is it able to receive the building of the wisdom of God, and for this reason our Lord placed simplicity in us for a foundation.
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 4 -- On Faith: First Discourse on Simplicity

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: Whosoever receiveth not the teaching of Christ and groweth not in virtues, his loss is the kingdom of heaven, and the happiness and delight which are sealed and preserved for the chosen of God, and that which the eye hath not seen, nor the ear heard, and which hath not gone up in the heart of man, and that intercourse which the perfect will have with Christ, and for the sake of which Christ Himself even came down from heaven to earth, and in the end this man's loss is his own person, together with the good things which are above nature.
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 5 -- Second Discourse on Simplicity

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: Do not thou then, O thou who hast denied the things which are seen, ask what kind of riches thou wilt receive in exchange for thy poverty, but be thou in earnest only to forsake thy poverty, and to hasten to possess them. Now what these riches are, and unto what they are like, Paul explaineth not unto thee, nor of what kind they are, for there is nothing which can be compared with them, nor how much they are, because they cannot be measured. "That which eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, and what hath not gone up in the heart of man, is what God hath prepared for them that love Him"; and the greatness of the reward is made manifest by these and such like words.
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 9 -- Second Discourse on Poverty

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: Now the foundation is set and laid, and is, according to the word of Paul, "Jesus Christ our God," and every man, howsoever he pleaseth, buildeth upon that foundation. For by His love the foundation hath been laid down once and for all to receive everything which might be set upon it, until the coming of the day of the revelation in which the work of every man will be tested and proved; and He who hath been the foundation stone in the corner of the building will go up and become the Judge and Head in the top of the building.

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: And according to what Paul himself spake, "If any man buildeth on this foundation gold, or silver, or stones of price, or wood, or hay, or stubble, each man's work shall be revealed, for that day shall reveal it, inasmuch as it shall be revealed by fire, and the fire shall prove each man's work of what sort it is." Now Paul likeneth the conduct of Christian life and character and the beauties of righteousness to gold and silver and precious stones, and among these faith is as gold, and the restraining of the passions and desires, and fasting, and self-denial and the other works of righteousness are as silver; and he likeneth to precious stones love, and peace, and hope, and pure thoughts, and holy meditations, and a mind which is wholly afraid in the Spirit, and which at all times reserveth in all its emotions wonder at God and admiration for the majesty of His Being, and an understanding which keepeth silence in trembling before the inexplicable and inexpressible mysteries of God. Now these heavenly thoughts, and emotions, and anxious fears, and life of the Spirit Paul calleth "precious stones;" and error and wickedness and the ministry of all the lusts he calleth wood, and hay, and stubble. And since the building itself is fixed in the ground every man can build and raise upon it whatsoever he pleaseth, until the day which shall decide is revealed.

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: Now when the body hath intercourse with the soul, and the soul with the spirit, and through the spirit with the Trinity, in very deed are accomplished the words, "The Lord is over all, and in us all", and, "Ye are the temple of the Lord, and the Spirit of God dwelleth in you." But Paul also frighteneth that soul which alloweth the body to become a minister unto fornication, saying, "Whosoever destroyeth the temple of God, God will destroy." And hereby he teacheth the soul not to allow the body to be corrupted by the union of fornication, because from this injury accrueth unto it, for together with the destruction of the body by its natural lusts, will the soul be condemned by the judgment which is for ever. And well did God ordain this retribution for the soul, though it is decreed for both the soul and the body by Him, because the soul in allowing the body to be debased unto the lusts of its nature will destroy it, and being able to restrain it, restraineth it not, and having the power to make it taste the sweetness of the lust for itself, the sweetness of its own corrupt lust, that is, the motions, and passions, and forms of which belong to shame, was pleasant unto it.
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 12 -- First Discourse on Fornication

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: And again in another place he saith, "We are fools for Christ's sake, and sick, and despised, and dishonoured, and we have nothing." And while in this world in which we live we possess nothing, we hold everything in that which is ours.

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: "Gluttons and drunkards shall not inherit the kingdom of God;" and read the passage, O disciple, and see unto what vices the Apostle compareth this wickedness—with soothsayers and destroyers, and other things like thereunto. And although the lust of the belly is not these, yet it leadeth unto them, for when the heart hath become gross through meats, straightway it driveth out from itself the remembrance of God, and when the memory of God hath departed from a man, what wickedness will he not do? and what iniquity will he be not moved to do?

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: And that a free man is not fettered by a lust for anything he sheweth by his freedom, and in that he hath the power and doth not make use thereof, he doubleth readily the freedom thereof, and he preserveth it from being dissipated, even as Paul writeth concerning this freedom, saying, "I have power to do everything, but not everything edifieth." And that thou mayest learn that it is thus with all other things, and especially in the matter of eating and not eating, he maketh known the power of his freedom and saith immediately after these words, "Meats of the belly, and the belly of meats, but God will bring both of them to nought."

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote:
And again, when the Apostle Paul is read, and he heareth from him, "Everything which was created by God is holy, and nothing is to be rejected if it be received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified through the word of God and prayer;" or another verse, "The belly for meats, and meats for the belly;" or that also which he spake, "Let not him that eateth not judge him that eateth." And in the other things like unto these which are written in the doctrine of Paul, the fool rejoiceth, and receiveth them gladly, without understanding the reason of the words.

And the glutton is not pleased to hear the other things which have been written by Paul upon fortitude and asceticism, either when he recounteth his numerous fastings, or when he crieth out to his disciples, saying, "Ye are dead unto the world," or when he writeth, "It is good for a man not to eat flesh, and not to drink wine," or his exhortation, "Through many tribulations it is meet for a man to enter into the kingdom of God," or his saying, "God shall bring both the belly and the food to nought;" and the reading of these and such like passages the glutton considereth unnecessary, and he is not pleased even to hear them.

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: Let us say unto each other that which hath been said unto us by the Apostle, "The belly for meats, and meats for the belly, but God will bring them both to nought." The body then is not for fornication, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body, to Whom be glory from us all for ever.

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: And that thou mayest learn that it is thus with all other things, and especially in the matter of eating and not eating, he maketh known the power of his freedom and saith immediately after these words, "Meats of the belly, and the belly of meats, but God will bring both of them to nought." Preserve then, O disciple, the habit of abstinence, that thou mayest also arrive at the power of freedom, and wean thyself, and eat not, that thou mayest draw nigh unto the state of eating without perceiving it; abstain from food by the power of thy soul, in order that the lusts which are mingled in thy members may be destroyed.

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: Craftiness in the soul is like a harlot in the street; for as the harlot speaketh with all men and putteth on all persons so that she may appear to be like unto every man, even so doth craftiness appear in every variety of opinion, and it prepareth the various kinds of ornamented forms which are required of it, that it may show itself to be like unto every man by them. And that which was written by the Apostle in integrity, "I have become all things unto all men, that I might profit all men", is wrought in the opposite manner by craftiness, which becometh all things unto all men that it may destroy all men, and that it may mock and laugh at all men.
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 5 -- Second Discourse on Simplicity

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: And as in worldly matters, if a man cannot perform properly the piece of work which he wisheth to do without setting himself free from all other work, and occupying himself with that alone, how much less can a man finish this spiritual labour unless he set himself free from the service of everything which is visible? Even as the blessed Paul also saith, "Every man who maketh a contest, keepeth his mind from everything"; and of what contest did he speak except the exercising of the body in the world? And if to a contest in which the body is engaged the service of carnal things is a hindrance, how much more will it be so to a spiritual contest? For in the one case, as regards the contest of the world, the contest, and the struggling therein, and the conquest therein, and also the things which retard the conquest therein, are one in nature, and they are all the children of one country, and although all these things are related to each other, the world with its cares and anxieties becometh an obstacle unto those who maintain the strife. How can a man fulfil the life here, then, which is a spiritual contest, and a service, and a life which is above the world, if he be tied unto and held fast by the things of the world?
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 9 -- Second Discourse on Poverty

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: Do thou then, even though all these things help thee, persevere in the patience which befitteth thy discipleship, and conquer the wicked mistress of all iniquity, and subdue thy body and afflict thy members, even as Paul also said, "I subdue my body, and bring it into subjection, lest peradventure I, who have preached to others, am myself rejected." And if Paul, although he, by the power of Grace, gained the victory over the passions, still had need to subdue his body, how much more have those, in whom there still live the lusts of the flesh, need to subdue their bodies by fasting and abstinence, and to fight and to overcome!

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: And that a free man is not fettered by a lust for anything he sheweth by his freedom, and in that he hath the power and doth not make use thereof, he doubleth readily the freedom thereof, and he preserveth it from being dissipated, even as Paul writeth concerning this freedom, saying, "I have power to do everything, but not everything edifieth."

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: For behold with us is poverty, but with the world there are riches; with us there is disgrace, but with it glory; with us there is humility, but with it pride; with us there is inferiority, but with it dominion; with us there is indigence, but with it possessions; with us there is hunger, but with it satiety; with us there is want, but with it abundance; with us there are afflictions, but with it pleasures; with us there is subjection, but with it command; with us there is the "narrow way," but with it the broad path; with us is the single garment which is limited by command, but with it are various kinds of fine raiment and apparel; with us is the order which restraineth us from our daily food, but with it are the treasures which are collected for generations and years; with us is the obligation to appear in neglect and contempt, but with it the appearance of pride and honour. All these things, and those which are like unto them, appear glorious to the world, and better in every respect than those which we have; but if we remove from the midst faith which is our true riches, even as our teacher Paul also testified concerning this in his word, "If in this life only we have hope in Christ, of all men we are the most miserable."

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: "Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of heaven," the blessed Paul teacheth us, or as a man might say, "So long as the motions of a man are established by flesh and blood he is unable to inherit the spiritual knowledge of Christ," which, as in a parable, he calleth the kingdom of heaven; and although this verse hath other meanings in respect of other passions, yet as regardeth the matter which is under discussion we may suitably apply it with this meaning. For the true kingdom is the knowledge which erreth not, and doubteth not, but seeth everything in its proper place distinctly, as well as things which are above nature, according to the capacity which is given unto created beings; and he whose life is established by means of motions of flesh and blood is unable to become the heir of this knowledge, and if it happen that he receive it by the tradition of words, he heareth the words from others, and it is not that knowledge which itself hath revealed itself in his soul, for this knowledge is beyond words, and beyond appellations and names.

author: Polycarp of Smyrna
quote: I am greatly grieved for Valens, who was once a presbyter among you, because he so little understands the place that was given him [in the Church]. I exhort you, therefore, that ye abstain from covetousness, and that ye be chaste and truthful. "Abstain from every form of evil." For if a man cannot govern himself in such matters, how shall he enjoin them on others? If a man does not keep himself from covetousness, he shall be defiled by idolatry, and shall be judged as one of the heathen. But who of us are ignorant of the judgment of the Lord? "Do we not know that the saints shall judge the world?" as Paul teaches. But I have neither seen nor heard of any such thing among you, in the midst of whom the blessed Paul laboured, and who are commended in the beginning of his Epistle. For he boasts of you in all those Churches which alone then knew the Lord; but we [of Smyrna] had not yet known Him. I am deeply grieved, therefore, brethren, for him (Valens) and his wife; to whom may the Lord grant true repentance! And be ye then moderate in regard to this matter, and "do not count such as enemies," but call them back as suffering and straying members, that ye may save your whole body. For by so acting ye shall edify yourselves.

author: Polycarp of Smyrna
quote: In like manner, let the young men also be blameless in all things, being especially careful to preserve purity, and keeping themselves in, as with a bridle, from every kind of evil. For it is well that they should be cut off from the lusts that are in the world, since "every lust warreth against the spirit;" and "neither fornicators, nor effeminate, nor abusers of themselves with mankind, shall inherit the kingdom of God," nor those who do things inconsistent and unbecoming. Wherefore, it is needful to abstain from all these things, being subject to the presbyters and deacons, as unto God and Christ. The virgins also must walk in a blameless and pure conscience.
